heading: 1.1 Cloud computing
text: Renting compute, storage, networking and services over the internet, on demand, instead of owning hardware. Shift from CapEx (buy servers upfront) to OpEx (pay as you use).

heading: 1.2 Shared responsibility model
text: The provider always owns physical hosts, network and datacenter. You always own your data, identities, and devices/accounts. Everything in between shifts by service type. Layer On-prem IaaS PaaS SaaS - - - - - Data, identities, access You You You You Applications You You You Provider Runtime / middleware You You Provider Provider OS You You Provider Provider Virtual network, hypervisor You Provider Provider Provider Physical hosts, datacenter You Provider Provider Provider

heading: 1.3 Cloud models
text: Public: shared Microsoft-owned infrastructure, pay-per-use, no hardware to maintain. Private: dedicated to one organization (on-prem or hosted); more control, higher cost. Hybrid: public + private/on-prem connected (e.g., Azure Arc, ExpressRoute, VPN). Multi-cloud: more than one cloud provider.

heading: 1.4 Consumption-based pricing
text: Pay only for what you use (per second/minute/hour, per GB, per million executions). No upfront cost, scale down to stop paying. Example: Azure Functions Consumption plan bills per execution and GB-seconds.

heading: 2\. Benefits of the cloud
text: High availability: SLA-backed uptime (e.g., 99.9% = \8.76 hrs downtime/year; 99.99% = \52 min/year). Composite SLA = product of the SLAs of the services in the path. Scalability: Vertical (scale up/down: bigger VM) vs horizontal (scale out/in: more instances). Prefer horizontal for stateless apps. Elasticity: auto-scale in and out with demand. Reliability: resilience via redundancy, self-healing, multi-region design. Predictability: performance (autoscale, load balancing) and cost (calculators, budgets, forecasts). Security and governance: compliance certifications, Azure Policy, Defender for Cloud. Manageability: manage of the cloud (autoscale, templates, monitoring) and in the cloud (Portal, CLI, PowerShell, REST APIs).

heading: 3\. Service types
text: You manage Examples Use when - - - - IaaS OS, runtime, apps, data Virtual Machines, VNets, Disks Lift-and-shift, full OS control PaaS Apps and data only App Service, Azure SQL, Functions Build apps without managing servers (most common for devs) SaaS Just use it (config, data) Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 Ready-made software Serverless (Functions, Logic Apps, Container Apps): PaaS variant where you write code/logic and pay per execution; scale to zero. \---

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 4\. Core architecture
heading: 4.1 Regions, region pairs, sovereign regions
text: Region: a set of datacenters connected by a low-latency network (e.g., Central India, East US). Pick by latency, compliance/data residency, service availability, and price. Region pair: two regions in the same geography, usually 300+ miles apart. Benefits: sequential platform updates (one at a time), prioritized recovery in a broad outage, and geo-redundant storage replicates to the pair. Sovereign regions: isolated instances for compliance/legal needs: Azure Government (US) and Azure China (21Vianet).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 4\. Core architecture
heading: 4.2 Availability Zones (AZs)
text: Physically separate datacenters (independent power, cooling, network) within one region; minimum 3 zones in zone-enabled regions. Protect against datacenter-level failure. Zonal services: pin to a specific zone (VMs, disks). Zone-redundant services: replicated across zones automatically (ZRS storage, zone-redundant SQL, Load Balancer Standard). Availability sets (older) protect against rack-level failures within a datacenter via fault/update domains. Prefer zones.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 4\. Core architecture
heading: 4.3 Datacenters
text: Physical buildings with servers, power, cooling and networking; Microsoft manages them. You never touch them but choose region/zone.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 4\. Core architecture
heading: 4.4 Resources and resource groups
text: Resource: any manageable item (VM, storage account, VNet). Resource group (RG): logical container for related resources sharing the same lifecycle. A resource lives in exactly one RG; resources can be moved between RGs. RGs can't be nested. Deleting an RG deletes everything in it. RG has a location (for metadata) but its resources can be in other regions. RBAC, policy, tags and locks can be applied at RG level and inherited.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 4\. Core architecture
heading: 4.5 Hierarchy: management groups, subscriptions
text: Management groups → Subscriptions → Resource groups → Resources Subscription: billing and access boundary; also holds limits/quotas. Common split: dev/test/prod. Management group: container for subscriptions to apply policy/RBAC at scale; up to 6 levels deep (excluding root); one root management group per tenant (Entra tenant). Policy and RBAC assigned at a higher scope are inherited downward.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 5\. Compute and networking
heading: 5.1 Compute types
text: Type Service Notes - - - Virtual machines Azure VMs, VM Scale Sets IaaS, full control Containers Container Instances (ACI), Container Apps, AKS Lightweight, portable Serverless Functions, Logic Apps Event-driven, pay per execution PaaS web hosting App Service Managed web apps/APIs

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 5\. Compute and networking
heading: 5.2 VM options
text: VM sizes/families: General purpose (B, D), Compute-optimized (F), Memory-optimized (E), Storage-optimized (L), GPU (N), HPC (H). Availability Sets: fault domains (power/network) + update domains (planned maintenance). Free; SLA 99.95%. Scale Sets (VMSS): identical VMs, autoscale by metrics/schedule, load-balanced. Azure Virtual Desktop: cloud-hosted Windows desktops/apps. Pricing options: Pay-as-you-go, Reserved Instances (1 or 3 yr, big discount), Savings Plans, Spot VMs (cheap, can be evicted; for interruptible batch work).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 5\. Compute and networking
heading: 5.3 Resources needed for a VM
text: Every VM needs: a resource group, VNet + subnet, NIC (network interface), OS disk (plus optional data disks), and an image/size. Optional: public IP, NSG, load balancer. Stop (deallocate) a VM to stop compute billing, but disks still cost money.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 5\. Compute and networking
heading: 5.4 Application hosting
text: Service Model Best for - - - App Service PaaS Web apps, REST APIs, mobile backends; deployment slots (blue/green), autoscale, built-in TLS; .NET, Java, Node, Python, PHP Azure Functions Serverless Event-driven snippets (HTTP, timer, queue, blob triggers); Consumption, Premium, Dedicated plans Container Instances Serverless containers Quick single containers, no orchestration Container Apps Serverless containers Microservices, KEDA autoscaling, scale to zero AKS Managed Kubernetes Complex orchestration; Azure manages the control plane, you manage nodes/workloads Static Web Apps Static hosting + APIs SPAs (React/Angular) with Functions backend

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 5\. Compute and networking
heading: 5.5 Virtual networking
text: VNet: private network in a region; you define address space (CIDR) and subnets. Resources in a VNet talk to each other by default. NSG (Network Security Group): stateful allow/deny rules by IP, port, protocol, priority (lower number = evaluated first); attach to subnet or NIC. Peering: connect VNets (same or different regions) over the Microsoft backbone; not transitive by default. VPN Gateway: encrypted tunnel over the internet (site-to-site, point-to-site). ExpressRoute: private dedicated connection to Azure, not over the public internet; higher reliability and lower latency. Load balancing options: Load Balancer: Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), regional. Application Gateway: Layer 7 (HTTP), regional, with WAF. Front Door: Layer 7, global, CDN + WAF. Traffic Manager: DNS-based global routing. Azure DNS: host DNS zones. Azure Firewall: managed network firewall. Bastion: browser-based RDP/SSH without exposing public IPs.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 5\. Compute and networking
heading: 5.6 Public and private endpoints
text: Public endpoint: service reachable via a public IP/URL (restrict with firewall rules). Private endpoint (Private Link): gives a PaaS service (Storage, SQL, Key Vault) a private IP in your VNet; traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone. Service endpoints extend VNet identity to a service but the service keeps its public endpoint.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 6\. Storage
heading: 6.1 Storage services (under one Storage Account)
text: Service Use - - Blob Unstructured object data (images, logs, backups, data lake) Files Managed SMB/NFS file shares Queue Simple async messaging (up to 64 KB messages) Table NoSQL key-attribute store Disks VM disks (Managed Disks)

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 6\. Storage
heading: 6.2 Access tiers (Blob)
text: Hot (frequent, highest storage cost, lowest access cost) → Cool (30+ days) → Cold (90+ days) → Archive (180+ days, offline, hours to rehydrate). Use lifecycle management policies to move data automatically.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 6\. Storage
heading: 6.3 Redundancy
text: Option Copies Protects from - - - LRS 3 in one datacenter Disk/rack failure ZRS 3 across AZs in one region Datacenter failure GRS LRS + 3 copies in paired region Regional outage GZRS ZRS + copy in paired region Zone + region failure RA-GRS / RA-GZRS As above + read access to secondary Read during outage

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 6\. Storage
heading: 6.4 Storage account
text: Globally unique name (3-24 lowercase letters/digits). Types: Standard general-purpose v2 (default), Premium (SSD; block blobs, file shares, page blobs). Secure with Entra ID/RBAC, SAS tokens, firewall/private endpoints, encryption at rest (always on).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 6\. Storage
heading: 6.5 Moving files
text: AzCopy: CLI for fast copy to/from blob and files. Azure Storage Explorer: GUI tool. Azure File Sync: sync on-prem file servers with Azure Files. Azure Data Box: physical device shipped for offline bulk transfer (TBs to PBs).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 6\. Storage
heading: 6.6 Migration
text: Azure Migrate: central hub to discover, assess and migrate servers, databases, web apps. Azure Database Migration Service: migrate databases with minimal downtime. Data Box for offline data (see above).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 7\. Identity, access and security
heading: 7.1 Directory services
text: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD): cloud identity provider (users, groups, apps, SSO). Not the same as on-prem AD DS. Entra Domain Services: managed domain services (LDAP, Kerberos, group policy) without running domain controllers. Entra Connect: sync on-prem AD identities to Entra ID (hybrid identity). External ID (B2B/B2C): guest access for partners/customers.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 7\. Identity, access and security
heading: 7.2 Authentication methods
text: SSO: sign in once, access many apps. MFA: something you know + have + are. Methods: Authenticator app, FIDO2 keys, SMS/voice (weakest). Passwordless: Windows Hello, Authenticator, FIDO2. SSPR: self-service password reset. Authentication vs authorization: AuthN = who are you; AuthZ = what can you do (OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect are the protocols).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 7\. Identity, access and security
heading: 7.3 Conditional Access
text: If-then policies evaluated at sign-in: signals (user, location, device, app, risk) → decision (block, require MFA, require compliant device). Needs Entra ID P1+.

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 7\. Identity, access and security
heading: 7.4 RBAC
text: Controls what authenticated identities can do on Azure resources. Role assignment = security principal (user/group/service principal/managed identity) + role definition + scope (management group, subscription, RG, resource). Inherited downward. Built-in roles: Owner (all + assign roles), Contributor (all except assigning roles), Reader (view only), User Access Administrator. Give least privilege at the narrowest scope. RBAC ≠ Entra roles (Entra roles manage the directory itself).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 7\. Identity, access and security
heading: 7.5 Zero Trust and defense in depth
text: Zero Trust: "never trust, always verify"; verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach. Defense in depth layers: Physical → Identity/Access → Perimeter (DDoS, firewall) → Network (NSG, segmentation) → Compute (patching) → Application → Data (encryption).

topic: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services › 7\. Identity, access and security
heading: 7.6 Microsoft Defender for Cloud
text: CSPM (posture management, Secure Score, recommendations) and CWPP (threat protection for VMs, containers, databases, storage). Works across Azure, on-prem and other clouds. \---

heading: 8.1 Factors affecting cost
text: Resource type and size, region, usage/consumption, bandwidth (inbound free; outbound charged), subscription type, reserved vs pay-as-you-go, Azure Hybrid Benefit (bring existing Windows/SQL licenses), Spot pricing, and support plan.

topic: Module 3: Management and Governance › 8\. Cost management
heading: 8.2 Pricing Calculator vs TCO Calculator
text: Pricing Calculator: estimate the monthly cost of Azure services you plan to use. TCO Calculator: compare on-prem cost vs Azure over a period (3-5 yrs) to build a migration business case.

topic: Module 3: Management and Governance › 8\. Cost management
heading: 8.3 Cost Management + Billing
text: Analyze spend by scope, set budgets, alerts, get forecasts, export data, and see recommendations.

topic: Module 3: Management and Governance › 8\. Cost management
heading: 8.4 Tags
text: Key-value metadata on resources/RGs/subscriptions (e.g., env=prod, owner=teamA, costcenter=123) for cost allocation, organization and automation. Not inherited by default; use Azure Policy to enforce/inherit.

heading: 9\. Governance and compliance
text: Azure Blueprints: packaged environment definitions (RBAC, policy, ARM templates, RGs). Deprecated by Microsoft; use Template Specs + Deployment Stacks and Azure Policy instead. Still appears in older course material. Azure Policy: creates rules on resources (e.g., allow only certain regions/SKUs, require tags). Effects: Deny, Audit, Append, Modify, DeployIfNotExists. Policy = what resources may look like; RBAC = who may do what. Resource locks: CanNotDelete or ReadOnly on subscription/RG/resource; inherited; override even Owner permissions until removed (only Owner/User Access Admin can remove). Microsoft Purview: data governance/compliance. Service Trust Portal: compliance reports and audits.

heading: 10\. Managing and deploying resources
text: Azure Portal: web GUI; good for exploring and one-off tasks. Not repeatable. Cloud Shell: browser-based Bash/PowerShell with CLI preinstalled. Azure CLI (az, cross-platform) and Azure PowerShell (Az module): scriptable, automatable. Azure Arc: extend Azure management (policy, monitoring, Defender) to on-prem, other-cloud servers, Kubernetes and data services. Azure Resource Manager (ARM): the single control plane; every request (Portal, CLI, SDK, REST) goes through it for auth, validation and deployment. Infrastructure as Code: ARM templates (JSON, declarative, idempotent) and Bicep (cleaner DSL that compiles to ARM). Also Terraform. az login az group create -n rg-demo -l centralindia az storage account create -n stdemo12345 -g rg-demo --sku Standard\_LRS az deployment group create -g rg-demo -f main.bicep az group delete -n rg-demo --yes --no-wait

heading: 11\. Monitoring
text: Azure Advisor: personalized recommendations in 5 areas: Reliability, Security, Performance, Cost, Operational Excellence. Azure Service Health: personalized view of Azure incidents. Includes Azure Status (global), Service Health (your services/regions), and Resource Health (a specific resource). Azure Monitor: collects metrics and logs across resources. Components: Metrics, Log Analytics (query with KQL), Alerts and action groups, Application Insights (APM for apps: traces, exceptions, dependencies), dashboards/workbooks. \---

Managed Identity: Azure-managed identity for your app, so it authenticates to Key Vault, Storage, SQL with no credentials in code. System-assigned (tied to the resource) or user-assigned (reusable). Service principal: identity for apps/automation (CI/CD) when managed identity isn't possible. Use DefaultAzureCredential in the Azure SDK: works with your login locally and managed identity in Azure.

heading: Git & GitHub
text: A practical guide to everything an entry-level software engineer needs to know about Git and GitHub: concepts, commands, workflows, and the mistakes to avoid.

heading: 1. Git vs GitHub
text: Git GitHub --- --- --- What Distributed version control system (VCS) Cloud platform that hosts Git repositories Runs Locally on your machine On the web Does Tracks changes, branches, merges Collaboration: pull requests, issues, code review, CI/CD Alternatives None really (Mercurial, SVN are legacy) GitLab, Bitbucket Why Git? Full history, safe experimentation via branches, offline work, and painless collaboration. ---

heading: 2. Installation & Setup
text: # Install sudo apt install git # Debian/Ubuntu brew install git # macOS winget install Git.Git # Windows git --version # Verify

heading: One-time configuration
text: git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@example.com" git config --global init.defaultBranch main git config --global core.editor "code --wait" # VS Code as editor git config --global pull.rebase false # merge on pull (or true for rebase) git config --list # View all settings git config user.name # View a single value Config levels: --system (all users) → --global (your user) → --local (this repo only; default).

heading: SSH authentication with GitHub (recommended)
text: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" # Generate key eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" && ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub # Copy → GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys ssh -T git@github.com # Test connection Alternative: HTTPS with a Personal Access Token (PAT). GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git operations. ---

heading: The three areas
text: Working Directory ──git add──▶ Staging Area (Index) ──git commit──▶ Local Repository ──git push──▶ Remote (GitHub) (your files) (what goes in next commit) (.git history)

heading: Key terms
text: Term Meaning --- --- Repository (repo) Project folder tracked by Git (contains a hidden .git/ directory) Commit Snapshot of staged changes with a unique SHA-1 hash, author, timestamp, message Branch A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit HEAD Pointer to your current commit/branch Remote A hosted copy of the repo (conventionally named origin) Upstream The remote branch your local branch tracks Origin Default name for the remote you cloned from Fork Your own server-side copy of someone else's repo Detached HEAD HEAD points to a commit directly, not a branch

heading: File states
text: Untracked → Staged → Committed → Modified → Staged → ... ---

heading: 4. Starting a Repository
text: git init # Create a new repo in current folder git init my-project # Create in a new folder git clone <url> # Copy a remote repo locally git clone <url> my-folder # Clone into a named folder git clone --depth 1 <url> # Shallow clone (latest commit only; fast) git clone -b <branch> <url> # Clone a specific branch ---

heading: Check status and differences
text: git status # Current state of working dir and staging area git status -s # Short format git diff # Unstaged changes git diff --staged # Staged changes (what will be committed) git diff main..feature # Compare two branches git diff <commit1> <commit2> # Compare two commits

heading: Stage changes
text: git add file.txt # Stage a file git add src/ # Stage a directory git add . # Stage everything in current directory git add -p # Interactively stage chunks (hunks); great for clean commits git rm file.txt # Delete file and stage the deletion git rm --cached file.txt # Untrack file but keep it on disk git mv old.txt new.txt # Rename/move and stage

heading: Commit
text: git commit -m "Add login validation" # Commit with message git commit -am "Fix typo" # Stage tracked files + commit (skips new files) git commit --amend -m "Better message" # Rewrite the last commit message git commit --amend --no-edit # Add staged changes to the last commit

heading: View history
text: git log # Full history git log --oneline # One line per commit git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate # Visual branch graph git log -n 5 # Last 5 commits git log --author="Name" # Filter by author git log --since="2 weeks ago" # Filter by date git log -p file.txt # History with diffs for one file git log --grep="bug" # Search commit messages git show <commit> # Details and diff of one commit git blame file.txt # Who last changed each line ---

heading: 6. Branching
text: Branches let you work on features or fixes in isolation without touching main. git branch # List local branches (* = current) git branch -a # List local and remote branches git branch -vv # Show tracking info and last commit git branch feature/login # Create branch git switch feature/login # Switch to branch (modern) git switch -c feature/login # Create and switch git checkout feature/login # Switch (older equivalent) git checkout -b feature/login # Create and switch (older equivalent) git branch -m new-name # Rename current branch git branch -d feature/login # Delete (only if merged) git branch -D feature/login # Force delete git push origin --delete feature/login # Delete remote branch ---

heading: 7. Merging & Rebasing
text: Both integrate changes from one branch into another, differently.

heading: Merge
text: git switch main git merge feature/login # Merge feature into main git merge --no-ff feature/login # Always create a merge commit git merge --squash feature/login # Combine all commits into one staged change git merge --abort # Cancel an in-progress merge Fast-forward: main hasn't moved, so Git just advances the pointer (no merge commit). Three-way merge: both branches diverged, so Git creates a merge commit.

heading: Rebase
text: Replays your commits on top of another branch for a linear history. git switch feature/login git rebase main # Replay feature commits on top of latest main git rebase --continue # After resolving conflicts git rebase --abort # Cancel rebase git rebase -i HEAD~3 # Interactive: squash, reword, reorder, drop last 3 commits Interactive rebase keywords: pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop.

heading: Merge vs Rebase
text: Merge Rebase --- --- --- History Preserves true history (non-linear) Linear, cleaner Safety Non-destructive Rewrites commits (new hashes) Use for Integrating into shared branches Cleaning up your own local/feature branch Golden rule: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch. ---

heading: 8. Resolving Merge Conflicts
text: Conflicts occur when two branches edit the same lines. <<<<<<< HEAD your current branch's version ======= incoming branch's version >>>>>>> feature/login Steps: git status # See conflicted files ("both modified") # 1. Open the files, choose/combine the correct code, delete the markers git add <resolved-file> # 2. Mark as resolved git commit # 3. Complete the merge (or: git rebase --continue) git checkout --ours file.txt # Take your version git checkout --theirs file.txt # Take the incoming version git mergetool # Launch a configured merge tool ---

heading: 9. Working with Remotes
text: git remote -v # List remotes git remote add origin <url> # Add a remote git remote set-url origin <new-url> # Change remote URL git remote remove origin # Remove a remote git fetch # Download changes, don't merge git fetch --prune # Also remove stale remote-tracking branches git pull # fetch + merge (or rebase) into current branch git pull --rebase # fetch + rebase git push origin main # Push branch git push -u origin feature/login # Push and set upstream (first push) git push # Push to the tracked upstream git push --force-with-lease # Safer force push (fails if remote changed)

heading: Fork workflow (open source)
text: git remote add upstream <original-repo-url> # Link the original repo git fetch upstream git switch main git merge upstream/main # Sync your fork with the original git push origin main Prefer --force-with-lease over --force. Never force-push to main. ---

heading: 10. Undoing Things
text: Choose the right tool depending on what you want to undo. Situation Command --- --- Discard unstaged changes in a file git restore file.txt Unstage a file (keep changes) git restore --staged file.txt Fix the last commit message git commit --amend Undo last commit, keep changes staged git reset --soft HEAD1 Undo last commit, keep changes unstaged git reset --mixed HEAD1 (default) Undo last commit, discard changes git reset --hard HEAD1 ⚠️ Undo a pushed commit safely git revert Remove untracked files git clean -fd ⚠️ (preview first with -n)

heading: Reset vs Revert
text: git reset moves the branch pointer back, rewriting history. Use only on local, unpushed commits. git revert creates a new commit that reverses an earlier one. Safe for shared branches. git revert <commit> # Undo a commit with a new commit git revert -m 1 <merge-commit> # Revert a merge commit git reset --hard origin/main # Make local branch match remote exactly ⚠️

heading: Recover "lost" work
text: git reflog # History of where HEAD has been (even after reset) git reset --hard <hash-from-reflog> # Restore to that state Reflog is your safety net. Commits are rarely truly gone (typically retained 90 days). ---

heading: 11. Stash
text: Temporarily shelve uncommitted changes to switch context. git stash # Stash tracked changes git stash -u # Include untracked files git stash push -m "wip: login form" # Stash with a message git stash list # View all stashes git stash show -p stash@{0} # View stash contents git stash pop # Apply latest stash and remove it git stash apply stash@{1} # Apply a stash and keep it git stash drop stash@{0} # Delete a stash git stash clear # Delete all stashes git stash branch new-branch # Create a branch from a stash ---

heading: 12. Tags & Releases
text: Tags mark specific commits, usually release versions (use Semantic Versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). git tag # List tags git tag v1.0.0 # Lightweight tag git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0" # Annotated tag (recommended) git tag -a v0.9.0 <commit> # Tag an older commit git push origin v1.0.0 # Push one tag git push origin --tags # Push all tags git tag -d v1.0.0 # Delete local tag git push origin --delete v1.0.0 # Delete remote tag git checkout v1.0.0 # Inspect code at a tag (detached HEAD) ---

heading: Cherry-pick: apply a specific commit to the current branch
text: git cherry-pick <commit> git cherry-pick A..B # A range of commits (A exclusive) git cherry-pick --abort

heading: Bisect: binary search to find the commit that introduced a bug
text: git bisect start git bisect bad # Current commit is broken git bisect good <known-good-commit> # Git checks out midpoints; test, then mark `good` or `bad` until found git bisect reset # Exit bisect

heading: Worktrees: multiple branches checked out in separate folders
text: git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix-branch git worktree list git worktree remove ../hotfix

heading: Submodules: embed another repo inside yours
text: git submodule add <url> path/ git submodule update --init --recursive

heading: Hooks: scripts that run on Git events
text: Located in .git/hooks/ (e.g., pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push). Share them via tools like Husky or pre-commit.

heading: Aliases: save keystrokes
text: git config --global alias.st status git config --global alias.co checkout git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all --decorate"

heading: Searching
text: git grep "TODO" # Search tracked files git log -S "functionName" # Find commits that added/removed a string ---

heading: 14. .gitignore
text: Tells Git which files to not track (build output, secrets, dependencies, OS/IDE files). # Dependencies node_modules/ venv/ # Build output dist/ build/ *.log # Secrets & environment .env *.pem # OS / IDE .DS_Store .vscode/ .idea/ # Negation: keep this file despite the rule above !important.log Notes: .gitignore only affects untracked files. If a file is already tracked: git rm --cached . Global ignore: git config --global core.excludesfile /.gitignore_global Generate templates at gitignore.io or from GitHub's gitignore repo. Never commit secrets. If you do, rotate the credential immediately; deleting the file later doesn't remove it from history. ---

heading: Linking issues and PRs
text: In a PR description or commit message, these keywords auto-close an issue on merge: Closes #42, Fixes #42, Resolves #42

heading: Branch protection (Settings → Branches)
text: Typical rules for main: require PR + approvals, require passing status checks, require up-to-date branches, block force pushes, require signed commits.

heading: GitHub CLI (gh)
text: gh auth login gh repo clone owner/repo gh repo create my-repo --public --clone gh issue list gh issue create --title "Bug" --body "Details" gh pr create --fill # Open a PR from current branch gh pr list gh pr checkout 123 # Check out someone's PR locally gh pr review 123 --approve gh pr merge 123 --squash gh run list # View Actions runs gh run watch ---

heading: 16. Pull Request Workflow
text: The standard flow on a team: # 1. Sync and branch git switch main git pull git switch -c feature/add-search # 2. Work and commit in small logical chunks git add -p git commit -m "feat(search): add search endpoint" # 3. Stay current with main git fetch origin git rebase origin/main # or: git merge origin/main # 4. Push and open a PR git push -u origin feature/add-search gh pr create --fill # or use the GitHub UI # 5. Address review feedback: commit and push again (PR updates automatically) # 6. After approval + green CI → merge → delete the branch git switch main && git pull git branch -d feature/add-search

heading: Merge options on GitHub
text: Option Result Best for --- --- --- Create a merge commit Preserves all commits + merge commit Keeping full history Squash and merge All commits collapse into one Clean main, messy feature branches Rebase and merge Commits replayed linearly, no merge commit Linear history with meaningful commits

heading: Writing a good PR
text: Small and focused: ideally under 400 lines changed Descriptive title; explain what and why; link the issue Include screenshots/test notes where relevant Self-review your diff before requesting review Use Draft PR for work in progress

heading: Reviewing code
text: Be specific, kind, and constructive; ask questions rather than demand changes Check correctness, readability, edge cases, tests, security, performance Use Approve, Request changes, or Comment appropriately Prefix nitpicks with nit: so they're clearly optional ---

heading: 17. GitHub Actions (CI/CD)
text: Automate tests, builds, and deployments. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/. # .github/workflows/ci.yml name: CI on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 20 cache: npm - run: npm ci - run: npm test - run: npm run build Vocabulary: workflow → job → step; runner (machine that executes jobs); action (reusable step); event (trigger); secret (encrypted variable, referenced as ${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}). Store sensitive values in Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions, never in code. ---

heading: 18. Branching Strategies
text: Strategy Description Best for --- --- --- GitHub Flow main is always deployable; short-lived feature branches → PR → merge Most web teams, continuous delivery Trunk-Based Development Tiny commits to main/short branches; feature flags High-velocity teams with strong CI Git Flow main, develop, feature/, release/, hotfix/ Scheduled releases, versioned software

heading: Branch naming
text: feature/user-authentication bugfix/null-pointer-checkout hotfix/payment-timeout chore/update-dependencies docs/api-readme ---

heading: 19. Commit Message Conventions
text: A commit message tells future readers why a change was made. Structure: <type>(<scope>): <short summary in imperative mood, ≤ 50 chars> <optional body: what and why, wrapped at 72 chars> <optional footer: Closes #123 / BREAKING CHANGE: ...> Conventional Commits types: Type Use --- --- feat New feature fix Bug fix docs Documentation only style Formatting (no logic change) refactor Restructure without behavior change test Add/modify tests chore Tooling, dependencies, config perf Performance improvement ci CI configuration Examples: feat(auth): add Google OAuth login fix(cart): prevent negative quantity on update docs: add setup instructions to README ✅ "Add retry logic to payment client" ❌ "fixed stuff", "changes", "wip", "asdf" ---

heading: Do
text: Commit small, atomic, logical changes Pull/rebase from main often to avoid giant conflicts Write meaningful commit messages and PR descriptions Use feature branches; never commit directly to main Review git status and git diff --staged before every commit Delete merged branches Use .gitignore from day one Run tests/linters locally (pre-commit hooks) before pushing Sign commits where required (git config --global commit.gpgsign true)

heading: Don't
text: ❌ Commit secrets, API keys, .env, or large binaries ❌ Force-push to shared branches ❌ Rebase already-pushed shared history ❌ Use git add . blindly (check what you're staging) ❌ Mix unrelated changes in one commit/PR ❌ Leave PRs open for weeks without updates ❌ Panic: almost everything is recoverable (git reflog)

heading: Large files
text: Use Git LFS for large binaries (images, datasets, models): git lfs install git lfs track "*.psd" git add .gitattributes ---

heading: 21. Troubleshooting Scenarios
text: Committed to the wrong branch git switch correct-branch git cherry-pick <commit> git switch wrong-branch git reset --hard HEAD~1 # Remove it from the wrong branch (if unpushed) Need to change the last commit (not yet pushed) git add forgotten-file.txt git commit --amend --no-edit git push rejected (non-fast-forward) git pull --rebase # Integrate remote changes, then git push Accidentally committed a secret Rotate/revoke the secret immediately. Remove it from history with git filter-repo (or BFG Repo-Cleaner). Force-push and notify collaborators. Detached HEAD: want to keep your work git switch -c rescue-branch Want to undo a merge that's already pushed git revert -m 1 <merge-commit> Local branch is a mess; reset to remote git fetch origin git reset --hard origin/<branch> # ⚠️ discards local changes and commits Remove a file from Git but keep it locally git rm --cached secret.txt && echo "secret.txt" >> .gitignore Find which commit broke something git bisect start && git bisect bad && git bisect good <hash> Fix an author name/email on the last commit git commit --amend --author="Name <email@example.com>" --no-edit Line-ending problems (Windows/Linux) git config --global core.autocrlf true # Windows git config --global core.autocrlf input # macOS/Linux ---

heading: Welcome
text: A short preface to the book: who you are, what the chapters cover, and how to read them.

heading: Arrays
text: An array is an ordered collection of values stored under numeric indexes, starting at 0. Arrays can hold values of any type, including other arrays and objects.

heading: Creating Arrays
text: const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]; const empty = []; const mixed = [1, "two", true, null, { a: 1 }]; const fromConstructor = new Array(3); // [ <3 empty items> ] const filled = Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i); // [0, 1, 2]

heading: Accessing and Updating
text: fruits[0]; // "apple" fruits[fruits.length - 1]; // "mango" fruits.at(-1); // "mango" fruits[1] = "grape"; // update fruits.length; // 3

heading: Adding and Removing Elements
text: Method Action --- --- push(x) Add to the end pop() Remove from the end unshift(x) Add to the start shift() Remove from the start splice(i, n, ...items) Remove/insert at an index const nums = [1, 2, 3]; nums.push(4); // [1, 2, 3, 4] nums.pop(); // [1, 2, 3] nums.unshift(0); // [0, 1, 2, 3] nums.shift(); // [1, 2, 3] nums.splice(1, 1); // removes 2 -> [1, 3] nums.splice(1, 0, 2); // inserts 2 -> [1, 2, 3]

heading: Searching
text: const nums = [10, 20, 30, 20]; nums.indexOf(20); // 1 nums.lastIndexOf(20); // 3 nums.includes(30); // true nums.find(n => n > 15); // 20 nums.findIndex(n => n > 15); // 1

heading: Iterating
text: const nums = [1, 2, 3]; nums.forEach(n => console.log(n)); for (const n of nums) console.log(n);

heading: Transforming
text: const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; nums.map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0); // [2, 4] nums.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // 15 nums.some(n => n > 4); // true nums.every(n => n > 0); // true

heading: Slicing, Joining, and Sorting
text: const nums = [3, 1, 2]; nums.slice(0, 2); // [3, 1] (does not modify original) nums.concat([4, 5]); // [3, 1, 2, 4, 5] [...nums, 4, 5]; // spread alternative nums.join("-"); // "3-1-2" nums.reverse(); // [2, 1, 3] (modifies original) nums.sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 3] (modifies original) sort() without a compare function sorts values as strings.

heading: Destructuring and Spread
text: const [first, second, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3, 4]; // first = 1, second = 2, rest = [3, 4] const copy = [...rest];

heading: Checking for an Array
text: Array.isArray([1, 2]); // true Array.isArray("abc"); // false

heading: Strings
text: A string is a sequence of characters used to represent text. Strings are immutable: methods return a new string instead of changing the original.

heading: Creating Strings
text: const single = 'Hello'; const double = "Hello"; const template = `Hello`; const fromConstructor = String(123); // "123"

heading: Template Literals
text: const name = "Sam"; const age = 25; `My name is ${name} and I am ${age}.`; `Line one Line two`; // multi-line

heading: Length and Character Access
text: const str = "JavaScript"; str.length; // 10 str[0]; // "J" str.charAt(4); // "S" str.at(-1); // "t"

heading: Changing Case
text: "hello".toUpperCase(); // "HELLO" "HELLO".toLowerCase(); // "hello"

heading: Searching
text: const str = "Hello, World"; str.indexOf("o"); // 4 str.lastIndexOf("o"); // 8 str.includes("World"); // true str.startsWith("Hello"); // true str.endsWith("World"); // true str.search(/W/); // 7

heading: Extracting Parts
text: const str = "JavaScript"; str.slice(0, 4); // "Java" str.slice(-6); // "Script" str.substring(4, 10); // "Script"

heading: Replacing
text: "a-b-c".replace("-", "+"); // "a+b-c" "a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+"); // "a+b+c" "a1b2".replace(/\d/g, "#"); // "a#b#"

heading: Trimming and Padding
text: " hi ".trim(); // "hi" " hi ".trimStart(); // "hi " " hi ".trimEnd(); // " hi" "5".padStart(3, "0"); // "005" "5".padEnd(3, "0"); // "500"

heading: Repeating and Concatenating
text: "ab".repeat(3); // "ababab" "Hello" + " " + "World"; // "Hello World" "Hello".concat(" World"); // "Hello World"

heading: Comparing
text: "a" === "a"; // true "apple" < "banana"; // true "a".localeCompare("b"); // -1

heading: Escape Characters
text: Sequence Meaning --- --- \n New line \t Tab \\ Backslash \' Single quote \" Double quote

heading: Iterating Over a String
text: for (const char of "abc") { console.log(char); }

heading: Loops
text: Loops run a block of code repeatedly until a condition is no longer met.

heading: for
text: for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 } Syntax: for (initialization; condition; update) { ... }

heading: while
text: Runs while the condition is true. The condition is checked before each iteration. let i = 0; while (i < 5) { console.log(i); i++; }

heading: do...while
text: Runs the block at least once, then checks the condition. let i = 0; do { console.log(i); i++; } while (i < 5);

heading: for...of
text: Iterates over the values of iterable objects such as arrays and strings. for (const fruit of ["apple", "banana"]) { console.log(fruit); } for (const char of "hi") { console.log(char); }

heading: for...in
text: Iterates over the enumerable property keys of an object. const user = { name: "Sam", age: 25 }; for (const key in user) { console.log(key, user[key]); } Prefer for...of for arrays. for...in is meant for objects.

heading: forEach
text: An array method that runs a function for each element. [1, 2, 3].forEach((n, index) => { console.log(index, n); });

heading: break
text: Exits the loop immediately. for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) { if (i === 3) break; console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2 }

heading: continue
text: Skips the rest of the current iteration. for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i === 2) continue; console.log(i); // 0, 1, 3, 4 }

heading: Nested Loops
text: for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { for (let j = 1; j <= 3; j++) { console.log(`${i} x ${j} = ${i * j}`); } }

heading: Labels
text: A label lets break or continue target an outer loop. outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) { if (j === 1) continue outer; console.log(i, j); } }

heading: Infinite Loops
text: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever. Always make sure the condition changes. while (true) { // must contain a break to stop break; }

heading: Functions
text: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a task. It can accept inputs (parameters) and return an output.

heading: Function Declaration
text: function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } greet("Sam"); // "Hello, Sam!" Function declarations are hoisted, so they can be called before they are defined.

heading: Function Expression
text: const greet = function (name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; }; Function expressions are not hoisted.

heading: Arrow Function
text: const greet = (name) => `Hello, ${name}!`; const add = (a, b) => a + b; const square = n => n * n; const log = () => { console.log("No parameters"); }; Arrow functions do not have their own this.

heading: Parameters and Arguments
text: function add(a, b) { // a, b are parameters return a + b; } add(2, 3); // 2, 3 are arguments

heading: Default Parameters
text: function greet(name = "Guest") { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } greet(); // "Hello, Guest!" greet("Sam"); // "Hello, Sam!"

heading: Rest Parameters
text: Collects any number of arguments into an array. function sum(...numbers) { return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0); } sum(1, 2, 3, 4); // 10

heading: Return Value
text: A function returns undefined if there is no return statement. A return ends the function immediately. function check(n) { if (n > 0) return "positive"; return "not positive"; }

heading: Returning Multiple Values
text: function minMax(arr) { return [Math.min(...arr), Math.max(...arr)]; } const [min, max] = minMax([3, 1, 2]);

heading: Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE)
text: A function that runs as soon as it is defined. (function () { console.log("Runs immediately"); })();

heading: Scope
text: Variables declared inside a function are not accessible outside it. function demo() { const inside = "local"; } // inside is not accessible here

heading: Recursion
text: A function that calls itself. function factorial(n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); } factorial(5); // 120

heading: Methods
text: A function stored as an object property. const user = { name: "Sam", sayHi() { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; }, }; user.sayHi();

heading: Functions as Values
text: Functions are first-class: they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. const operations = { add: (a, b) => a + b, multiply: (a, b) => a * b, }; operations.add(2, 3); // 5

heading: Callback Function
text: A callback function is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later by that function.

heading: Basic Example
text: function greet(name, callback) { console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`); callback(); } function done() { console.log("Greeting finished."); } greet("Sam", done); // Hello, Sam! // Greeting finished.

heading: Inline and Arrow Callbacks
text: greet("Sam", function () { console.log("Done"); }); greet("Sam", () => console.log("Done"));

heading: Callbacks with Arguments
text: function calculate(a, b, operation) { return operation(a, b); } calculate(2, 3, (x, y) => x + y); // 5 calculate(2, 3, (x, y) => x * y); // 6

heading: Callbacks in Built-in Methods
text: Many array methods accept callbacks. const nums = [1, 2, 3]; nums.map(n => n * 2); nums.filter(n => n > 1); nums.forEach(n => console.log(n));

heading: Synchronous Callbacks
text: Called immediately, in order, while the main function is running. [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => console.log(n));

heading: Asynchronous Callbacks
text: Called later, after an operation finishes. console.log("Start"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("Callback after 1 second"); }, 1000); console.log("End"); // Start // End // Callback after 1 second

heading: Error-First Callbacks
text: A common convention where the first argument of the callback is an error (or null). function fetchData(callback) { const success = true; if (success) { callback(null, { id: 1 }); } else { callback(new Error("Failed to fetch")); } } fetchData((error, data) => { if (error) { console.error(error.message); return; } console.log(data); });

heading: Callback Hell
text: Nesting many callbacks makes code hard to read and maintain. step1(function (result1) { step2(result1, function (result2) { step3(result2, function (result3) { console.log(result3); }); }); }); Ways to avoid it: use named functions, keep nesting shallow, or use Promises and async/await.

heading: Key Points
text: A callback is just a regular function passed as a value. Pass the function itself, not its result: greet("Sam", done), not greet("Sam", done()). Callbacks can run synchronously or asynchronously.

heading: Closures
text: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the scope where it was created, even after that outer scope has finished executing.

heading: Basic Example
text: function outer() { const message = "Hello"; function inner() { console.log(message); } return inner; } const fn = outer(); fn(); // "Hello" inner still has access to message even though outer has already returned.

heading: Counter Example
text: function createCounter() { let count = 0; return function () { count++; return count; }; } const counter = createCounter(); counter(); // 1 counter(); // 2 counter(); // 3 Each call to createCounter() creates its own separate count. const a = createCounter(); const b = createCounter(); a(); // 1 a(); // 2 b(); // 1

heading: Data Privacy
text: Closures can hide variables so they cannot be accessed directly from outside. function createAccount(balance) { return { deposit(amount) { balance += amount; return balance; }, getBalance() { return balance; }, }; } const account = createAccount(100); account.deposit(50); // 150 account.getBalance(); // 150 account.balance; // undefined

heading: Function Factories
text: function multiplier(factor) { return (number) => number * factor; } const double = multiplier(2); const triple = multiplier(3); double(5); // 10 triple(5); // 15

heading: Closures in Loops
text: With var, all callbacks share the same variable. for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); } // 3, 3, 3 With let, each iteration gets its own variable. for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); } // 0, 1, 2

heading: Lexical Scope
text: A closure works because of lexical scoping: a function can access variables from the scope where it was written, not where it is called. const x = "global"; function show() { console.log(x); } function run() { const x = "local"; show(); } run(); // "global"

heading: Key Points
text: Every function in JavaScript forms a closure over its surrounding scope. Closures keep variables alive as long as the function exists. Common uses: private variables, function factories, callbacks, and event handlers.

heading: setTimeout
text: setTimeout() runs a function once after a specified delay (in milliseconds).

heading: Syntax
text: setTimeout(callback, delay, arg1, arg2, ...); Parameter Description --- --- callback The function to run after the delay delay Time to wait in milliseconds (default 0) arg1, arg2, ... Optional arguments passed to the callback It returns a numeric ID (in browsers) that identifies the timer.

heading: Basic Example
text: setTimeout(() => { console.log("Runs after 2 seconds"); }, 2000);

heading: Passing Arguments
text: function greet(name, message) { console.log(`${message}, ${name}!`); } setTimeout(greet, 1000, "Sam", "Hello"); // Hello, Sam!

heading: Using a Named Function
text: function sayHi() { console.log("Hi!"); } setTimeout(sayHi, 1000); // pass the function, do not call it

heading: Cancelling with clearTimeout
text: const timerId = setTimeout(() => { console.log("This will not run"); }, 3000); clearTimeout(timerId);

heading: Asynchronous Behavior
text: setTimeout does not block the code that follows it. console.log("Start"); setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout"), 1000); console.log("End"); // Start // End // Timeout

heading: Zero Delay
text: Even with a delay of 0, the callback runs after the current code finishes. setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout"), 0); console.log("Sync"); // Sync // Timeout

heading: The this Keyword
text: In a regular function callback, this is not the surrounding object. Use an arrow function to keep it. const user = { name: "Sam", greet() { setTimeout(() => { console.log(`Hi, ${this.name}`); }, 1000); }, }; user.greet(); // Hi, Sam

heading: Chaining Delays
text: setTimeout(() => { console.log("Step 1"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("Step 2"); }, 1000); }, 1000);

heading: Key Points
text: The delay is a minimum wait time, not a guaranteed exact time. It runs the callback only once. Use clearTimeout(id) to cancel a pending timer.

heading: setInterval
text: setInterval() repeatedly runs a function at a fixed time interval (in milliseconds) until it is stopped.

heading: Syntax
text: setInterval(callback, interval, arg1, arg2, ...); Parameter Description --- --- callback The function to run repeatedly interval Time between each call in milliseconds arg1, arg2, ... Optional arguments passed to the callback It returns an ID (in browsers, a number) that identifies the interval.

heading: Basic Example
text: setInterval(() => { console.log("Runs every 1 second"); }, 1000);

heading: Stopping with clearInterval
text: const intervalId = setInterval(() => { console.log("Tick"); }, 1000); clearInterval(intervalId);

heading: Stopping After a Number of Runs
text: let count = 0; const intervalId = setInterval(() => { count++; console.log(`Run ${count}`); if (count === 5) { clearInterval(intervalId); } }, 1000);

heading: Passing Arguments
text: function greet(name) { console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`); } setInterval(greet, 2000, "Sam");

heading: Countdown Example
text: let seconds = 5; const timer = setInterval(() => { console.log(seconds); seconds--; if (seconds < 0) { clearInterval(timer); console.log("Done!"); } }, 1000);

heading: Clock Example
text: setInterval(() => { console.log(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()); }, 1000);

heading: Stopping After a Delay
text: const id = setInterval(() => console.log("Tick"), 1000); setTimeout(() => clearInterval(id), 5000); // stops after 5 seconds

heading: Key Points
text: The first call happens after the first interval, not immediately. The interval keeps running until clearInterval(id) is called. The interval is a minimum time; busy code can delay each run. Always store the ID so the interval can be cleared.

heading: this Keyword
text: this refers to the object that is executing the current code. Its value is determined by how a function is called, not where it is defined (except for arrow functions).

heading: Global Scope
text: console.log(this); Browser script: window (the global object). ES module: undefined. Node.js CommonJS module: module.exports (an empty object {} by default).

heading: Regular Function (Non-Strict Mode)
text: function show() { console.log(this); } show(); // window (browser) / globalThis (Node.js)

heading: Regular Function (Strict Mode)
text: "use strict"; function show() { console.log(this); } show(); // undefined

heading: Object Method
text: When a function is called as a method, this is the object before the dot. const user = { name: "Sam", greet() { console.log(this.name); }, }; user.greet(); // "Sam"

heading: Losing this
text: Extracting a method from its object loses this. const greet = user.greet; greet(); // undefined (or error in strict mode) setTimeout(user.greet, 1000); // `this` is not `user` Fixes: setTimeout(user.greet.bind(user), 1000); setTimeout(() => user.greet(), 1000);

heading: Arrow Functions
text: Arrow functions do not have their own this. They use this from the surrounding scope at the time they are defined. const user = { name: "Sam", regular() { return this.name; }, arrow: () => { return this.name; // `this` is the outer scope, not `user` }, }; user.regular(); // "Sam" user.arrow(); // undefined

heading: Arrow Function Inside a Method
text: const timer = { seconds: 0, start() { setInterval(() => { this.seconds++; // `this` is `timer` }, 1000); }, };

heading: Nested Regular Function
text: const user = { name: "Sam", greet() { function inner() { console.log(this.name); // `this` is not `user` } inner(); }, }; user.greet(); // undefined

heading: Constructor Function
text: With new, this is the newly created object. function User(name) { this.name = name; } const user = new User("Sam"); user.name; // "Sam"

heading: Class
text: class User { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } greet() { return this.name; } } const user = new User("Sam"); user.greet(); // "Sam" const fn = user.greet; fn(); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (class code is strict)

heading: Explicit Binding: call, apply, bind
text: function greet(greeting) { return `${greeting}, ${this.name}`; } const person = { name: "Sam" }; greet.call(person, "Hello"); // "Hello, Sam" greet.apply(person, ["Hello"]); // "Hello, Sam" const bound = greet.bind(person); bound("Hello"); // "Hello, Sam"

heading: DOM Event Handlers

heading: Currying
text: Currying is a technique that transforms a function taking multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument. f(a, b, c) becomes f(a)(b)(c)

heading: Basic Example
text: // Normal function function add(a, b) { return a + b; } add(2, 3); // 5 // Curried function function curriedAdd(a) { return function (b) { return a + b; }; } curriedAdd(2)(3); // 5

heading: Arrow Function Version
text: const add = a => b => a + b; add(2)(3); // 5

heading: Three Arguments
text: const volume = l => w => h => l * w * h; volume(2)(3)(4); // 24

heading: Partial Application
text: A curried function can be called with some arguments now and the rest later. const multiply = a => b => a * b; const double = multiply(2); const triple = multiply(3); double(5); // 10 triple(5); // 15

heading: Why Currying Works: Closures
text: Each inner function remembers the arguments from the outer functions through closure. function greet(greeting) { return function (name) { return `${greeting}, ${name}!`; }; } const sayHello = greet("Hello"); sayHello("Sam"); // "Hello, Sam!" sayHello("Alex"); // "Hello, Alex!"

heading: Generic curry Function
text: function curry(fn) { return function curried(...args) { if (args.length >= fn.length) { return fn.apply(this, args); } return function (...nextArgs) { return curried.apply(this, [...args, ...nextArgs]); }; }; } function sum(a, b, c) { return a + b + c; } const curriedSum = curry(sum); curriedSum(1)(2)(3); // 6 curriedSum(1, 2)(3); // 6 curriedSum(1)(2, 3); // 6 curriedSum(1, 2, 3); // 6 fn.length is the number of parameters the original function expects.

heading: Practical Example
text: const log = level => message => `[${level}] ${message}`; const info = log("INFO"); const error = log("ERROR"); info("Server started"); // "[INFO] Server started" error("Server crashed"); // "[ERROR] Server crashed"

heading: Key Points
text: Currying turns a multi-argument function into nested single-argument functions. It relies on closures to remember earlier arguments. It helps create reusable, specialized functions.

heading: Promise
text: A Promise is an object that represents the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value.

heading: States
text: State Meaning --- --- pending Initial state, not yet finished fulfilled Operation completed successfully rejected Operation failed Once a Promise is fulfilled or rejected, it is settled and its state cannot change.

heading: Creating a Promise
text: const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const success = true; if (success) { resolve("Operation succeeded"); } else { reject(new Error("Operation failed")); } }); resolve(value) marks the Promise as fulfilled. reject(error) marks the Promise as rejected.

heading: Consuming a Promise
text: promise .then(result => console.log(result)) .catch(error => console.error(error.message)) .finally(() => console.log("Finished")); Method Runs when --- --- then() The Promise is fulfilled catch() The Promise is rejected finally() The Promise settles, either way

heading: Asynchronous Example
text: function delay(ms) { return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); } delay(1000).then(() => console.log("1 second passed"));

heading: Promise Chaining
text: Each then() returns a new Promise, so calls can be chained. Promise.resolve(1) .then(n => n + 1) // 2 .then(n => n * 2) // 4 .then(n => console.log(n)); // 4 A value returned from then() is passed to the next then(). A returned Promise is awaited before continuing.

heading: Error Handling in Chains
text: An error thrown anywhere in the chain skips to the nearest catch(). Promise.resolve() .then(() => { throw new Error("Something went wrong"); }) .then(() => console.log("Skipped")) .catch(error => console.error(error.message));

heading: Shortcuts
text: Promise.resolve("done"); // already fulfilled Promise.reject(new Error("failed")); // already rejected

heading: Callbacks vs Promises
text: // Callbacks getData(function (a) { getMore(a, function (b) { console.log(b); }); }); // Promises getData() .then(a => getMore(a)) .then(b => console.log(b));

heading: Key Points
text: A Promise is either pending, fulfilled, or rejected. Use then, catch, and finally to handle the result. Chaining avoids deeply nested callbacks. Always handle rejections with catch().

heading: Promise APIs
text: The Promise object provides static methods for working with multiple Promises at once.

heading: Promise.all()
text: Waits for all Promises to fulfill. Rejects immediately if any Promise rejects. const p1 = Promise.resolve(1); const p2 = Promise.resolve(2); const p3 = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(3), 1000)); Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]).then(results => { console.log(results); // [1, 2, 3] }); Promise.all([p1, Promise.reject(new Error("Failed")), p3]) .catch(error => console.error(error.message)); // "Failed" Returns an array of results in the same order as the input. Fails fast on the first rejection.

heading: Promise.allSettled()
text: Waits for all Promises to settle, whether fulfilled or rejected. It never rejects. Promise.allSettled([ Promise.resolve("ok"), Promise.reject(new Error("failed")), ]).then(results => console.log(results)); // [ // { status: "fulfilled", value: "ok" }, // { status: "rejected", reason: Error: failed } // ]

heading: Promise.race()
text: Settles as soon as the first Promise settles (fulfilled or rejected). const slow = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve("slow"), 2000)); const fast = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve("fast"), 500)); Promise.race([slow, fast]).then(result => console.log(result)); // "fast" Common use: adding a timeout to an operation. const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("Timed out")), 3000) ); Promise.race([fetch("https://api.example.com/data"), timeout]);

heading: Promise.any()
text: Fulfills as soon as the first Promise fulfills. Ignores rejections unless all Promises reject. Promise.any([ Promise.reject(new Error("fail 1")), Promise.resolve("success"), Promise.reject(new Error("fail 2")), ]).then(result => console.log(result)); // "success" If all Promises reject, it rejects with an AggregateError. Promise.any([ Promise.reject(new Error("fail 1")), Promise.reject(new Error("fail 2")), ]).catch(error => { console.log(error.name); // "AggregateError" console.log(error.errors.length); // 2 });

heading: Promise.resolve()
text: Returns a Promise that is fulfilled with the given value. Promise.resolve("done").then(console.log); // "done"

heading: Promise.reject()
text: Returns a Promise that is rejected with the given reason. Promise.reject(new Error("failed")).catch(error => console.error(error.message));

heading: Comparison
text: Method Fulfills when Rejects when --- --- --- Promise.all All fulfill Any one rejects Promise.allSettled All settle Never Promise.race First settles with fulfillment First settles with rejection Promise.any Any one fulfills All reject

heading: Async & Await
text: async and await provide a cleaner way to work with Promises, letting asynchronous code be written in a synchronous style.

heading: async Function
text: An async function always returns a Promise. async function greet() { return "Hello"; } greet().then(console.log); // "Hello" Returning a value wraps it in a resolved Promise. Throwing an error returns a rejected Promise.

heading: await
text: await pauses the execution of an async function until the Promise settles, then returns its resolved value. function delay(ms) { return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); } async function run() { console.log("Start"); await delay(1000); console.log("After 1 second"); } run(); await can only be used inside an async function (or at the top level of an ES module).

heading: Fetching Data
text: async function getUser() { const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/user"); const data = await response.json(); return data; }

heading: Error Handling with try...catch
text: async function getUser() { try { const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/user"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Request failed"); } return await response.json(); } catch (error) { console.error(error.message); } finally { console.log("Done"); } }

heading: Sequential Execution
text: Each await waits for the previous one to finish. async function sequential() { const a = await taskA(); // waits const b = await taskB(); // then runs return [a, b]; }

heading: Parallel Execution
text: Start the tasks first, then await them together. async function parallel() { const [a, b] = await Promise.all([taskA(), taskB()]); return [a, b]; }

heading: async Arrow Functions
text: const fetchData = async () => { const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/data"); return response.json(); };

heading: await in Loops
text: async function processItems(items) { for (const item of items) { await process(item); // one at a time } }

heading: Key Points
text: async makes a function return a Promise. await waits for a Promise without blocking the rest of the program. Use try...catch to handle rejected Promises. Use Promise.all to run independent tasks in parallel.

heading: Debouncing
text: Debouncing is a technique that delays running a function until a specified time has passed since the last time it was called. If the function is called again before the delay ends, the timer resets.

heading: Explanation
text: Imagine a user typing in a search box. Without debouncing, an API request would fire on every keystroke. With debouncing, the request fires only after the user stops typing for a set time (for example, 500ms). Keystrokes: a b c d e (pause) Timer: reset reset reset reset reset --> runs once

heading: Common Use Cases
text: Search box suggestions Auto-saving a form Window resize handlers Validating input after the user stops typing

heading: Basic Implementation
text: function debounce(fn, delay) { let timerId; return function (...args) { clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = setTimeout(() => { fn.apply(this, args); }, delay); }; } How it works: timerId is kept in a closure, so it persists between calls. Each call clears the previous timer. A new timer starts, and the function runs only if no new call arrives within delay.

heading: Usage
text: function search(query) { console.log("Searching for:", query); } const debouncedSearch = debounce(search, 500); debouncedSearch("j"); debouncedSearch("ja"); debouncedSearch("jav"); // Only "Searching for: jav" is logged, 500ms after the last call

heading: With an Input Event
text: const input = document.querySelector("#search"); input.addEventListener( "input", debounce((event) => { console.log(event.target.value); }, 500) );

heading: Leading Edge Option
text: Run the function immediately on the first call, then ignore calls until the delay passes without activity. function debounce(fn, delay, immediate = false) { let timerId; return function (...args) { const callNow = immediate && !timerId; clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = setTimeout(() => { timerId = null; if (!immediate) fn.apply(this, args); }, delay); if (callNow) fn.apply(this, args); }; } const onClick = debounce(() => console.log("Clicked"), 1000, true);

heading: Adding a Cancel Method
text: function debounce(fn, delay) { let timerId; function debounced(...args) { clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay); } debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timerId); return debounced; } const save = debounce(() => console.log("Saved"), 1000); save(); save.cancel(); // nothing is logged

heading: Key Points
text: Debouncing runs the function only after calls stop for the given delay. Each new call resets the timer. It is implemented with setTimeout, clearTimeout, and a closure.

heading: Throttling
text: Throttling is a technique that ensures a function runs at most once in a given time interval, no matter how many times it is triggered.

heading: Explanation
text: If an event fires continuously (such as scrolling), a throttled handler runs at regular intervals instead of on every event. Events: | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | Throttle: | | | | (runs once per interval)

heading: Common Use Cases
text: Scroll event handlers Window resize handlers Mouse move tracking Preventing repeated button clicks Rate-limiting API calls

heading: Implementation 1: Using a Flag and setTimeout
text: function throttle(fn, limit) { let inThrottle = false; return function (...args) { if (inThrottle) return; fn.apply(this, args); inThrottle = true; setTimeout(() => { inThrottle = false; }, limit); }; }

heading: Implementation 2: Using Timestamps
text: function throttle(fn, limit) { let lastCall = 0; return function (...args) { const now = Date.now(); if (now - lastCall >= limit) { lastCall = now; fn.apply(this, args); } }; }

heading: Usage
text: function onScroll() { console.log("Scroll position:", window.scrollY); } window.addEventListener("scroll", throttle(onScroll, 200)); // runs at most once every 200ms const log = throttle((msg) => console.log(msg), 1000); log("a"); // runs log("b"); // ignored log("c"); // ignored // after 1 second, the next call will run

heading: Implementation with Trailing Call
text: The basic versions drop calls made during the wait. This version also runs the last call after the interval. function throttle(fn, limit) { let lastCall = 0; let timerId; return function (...args) { const now = Date.now(); const remaining = limit - (now - lastCall); if (remaining <= 0) { clearTimeout(timerId); lastCall = now; fn.apply(this, args); } else { clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = setTimeout(() => { lastCall = Date.now(); fn.apply(this, args); }, remaining); } }; }

heading: Debouncing vs Throttling
text: Debouncing Throttling --- --- Runs after calls stop for a set delay Runs at regular intervals during continuous calls Resets the timer on every call Ignores calls until the interval ends Example: search box input Example: scroll handler

heading: Key Points
text: Throttling limits a function to one execution per time interval. It can be implemented with a flag plus setTimeout, or with timestamps. It uses a closure to remember state between calls.

heading: Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
text: When an event happens on an element, it travels through the DOM tree in phases. Understanding these phases explains why a click on a child can trigger handlers on its parents.

topic: DOM & DOM Manipulation › Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
heading: Event Propagation Phases
text: Capturing (trickling) phase: the event travels down from window to the target element. Target phase: the event reaches the target element. Bubbling phase: the event travels back up from the target to window.

topic: DOM & DOM Manipulation › Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
heading: Event Bubbling (Default)
text: By default, event listeners run in the bubbling phase. The innermost element's handler runs first, then its parents'. document.getElementById("grandparent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("grandparent"); }); document.getElementById("parent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("parent"); }); document.getElementById("child").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("child"); }); // Clicking the button logs: // child // parent // grandparent

topic: DOM & DOM Manipulation › Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
heading: Event Trickling (Capturing)
text: Pass true (or { capture: true }) as the third argument to listen during the capturing phase. Outer elements run first. document.getElementById("grandparent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("grandparent"); }, true); document.getElementById("parent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("parent"); }, true); document.getElementById("child").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("child"); }, true); // Clicking the button logs: // grandparent // parent // child

topic: DOM & DOM Manipulation › Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
heading: Capturing and Bubbling Together

heading: Event Delegation
text: Event delegation is a technique where a single event listener is attached to a parent element to handle events for all of its children, including children added later. It works because of event bubbling.

text: list.addEventListener("click", (event) => { if (event.target.matches("li.active")) { console.log("Active item clicked"); } });

heading: Handling Multiple Actions
text: const actions = { save() { console.log("Saving"); }, edit() { console.log("Editing"); }, delete() { console.log("Deleting"); }, }; document.querySelector("#toolbar").addEventListener("click", (event) => { const action = event.target.dataset.action; if (action && actions[action]) { actions[action](); } });

heading: Benefits
text: Fewer event listeners, so less memory use. Works for elements added or removed dynamically. Less code to set up and clean up.

heading: Limitations
text: Only works for events that bubble (not focus, blur, etc.; use focusin and focusout instead). If a child calls event.stopPropagation(), the parent listener will not run. Very generic listeners high in the tree, such as on document, can add unnecessary work.

heading: Key Points
text: Attach the listener to a common parent. Use event.target to find which child triggered the event. Use closest() when the target may be a nested element.

heading: async & defer attributes
text: async executes the script the moment it finishes downloading (which pauses HTML parsing), whereas defer waits for the HTML parsing to completely finish before executing the script in the order it appears on the page. DEFAULT script tag: HTML parsing is paused for download and execution The scripts are executed immediately upon discovery/ arrival Execution Order: The scripts are executed in an ordered manner(as they appear in HTML). DOM Dependent? : Safe(if placed at the bottom) script async tag: HTML parsing is paused only during execution. The scripts are executed immediately after download completes. Execution Order: Unordered(load-first basis) DOM Dependent? : Unsafe(may run before DOM is ready) script defer tag: HTML Parsing is never paused. The scripts are executed after the DOM is fully parsed. Execution Order: Ordered(as they appear in HTML) DOM Dependent? : Safe(always runs after dom is ready) When to Use Which Use async when: The script is completely independent. It does not rely on other scripts. It does not need to manipulate the DOM. Examples: Analytics tools like Google Analytics, ad tracking pixels, or heatmaps. Use defer when: The script relies on the full DOM being built. The script depends on, or is depended on by, another script. Examples: UI interaction scripts, application bootloaders, or frameworks like React or Vue packages.

heading: local storage & session storage
text: localStorage and sessionStorage are Web Storage APIs that store key-value pairs in the browser. Keys and values are always stored as strings.

heading: Differences
text: Feature localStorage sessionStorage --- --- --- Lifetime Stays until manually cleared Cleared when the tab is closed Scope Shared across all tabs of the same origin Limited to a single tab Capacity About 5 MB About 5 MB Sent to server No No

heading: Methods
text: Both share the same API. localStorage.setItem("name", "Sam"); // save localStorage.getItem("name"); // "Sam" localStorage.removeItem("name"); // remove one item localStorage.clear(); // remove everything localStorage.length; // number of items localStorage.key(0); // key at index 0 sessionStorage.setItem("token", "abc123"); sessionStorage.getItem("token"); // "abc123"

heading: Shorthand Access
text: localStorage.theme = "dark"; console.log(localStorage.theme); // "dark"

heading: Missing Keys
text: localStorage.getItem("unknown"); // null

heading: Storing Objects and Arrays
text: Values are converted to strings, so use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse. const user = { name: "Sam", age: 25 }; localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify(user)); const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user")); console.log(saved.name); // "Sam" Without JSON.stringify: localStorage.setItem("user", user); localStorage.getItem("user"); // "[object Object]"

heading: Looping Through Items
text: for (let i = 0; i < localStorage.length; i++) { const key = localStorage.key(i); console.log(key, localStorage.getItem(key)); }

heading: Storage Event
text: Fires in other tabs of the same origin when localStorage changes. window.addEventListener("storage", (event) => { console.log(event.key, event.oldValue, event.newValue); });

heading: Common Use Cases
text: localStorage: theme preference, saved settings, cached data. sessionStorage: form data for the current tab, temporary state.

heading: Key Points
text: Data is stored as strings only. Data is scoped to the origin (protocol, domain, and port). Do not store sensitive data such as passwords, since the storage is readable by any script on the page.

heading: Constructor Functions
text: A constructor function is a regular function used with the new keyword to create multiple objects with the same structure. By convention, its name starts with a capital letter. function User(name, age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; this.greet = function () { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; }; } const user1 = new User("Sam", 25); const user2 = new User("Alex", 30); user1.greet(); // "Hi, I'm Sam"

topic: Object Oriented JS › Object literal, Constructors
heading: What new Does
text: Creates a new empty object. Sets the object's prototype to the constructor's prototype. Runs the constructor with this bound to the new object. Returns the object (unless the constructor returns another object).
