topic: Object Oriented JS › Object literal, Constructors
heading: Key Points
text: Use object literals for single objects. Use constructor functions (with new) to create many objects of the same shape. Methods defined inside a constructor are duplicated for every object.

heading: Object prototype
text: Every JavaScript object has an internal link to another object called its prototype. When a property is not found on an object, JavaScript looks for it on the object's prototype, and then on that prototype's prototype, and so on.

heading: [[Prototype]], __proto__, and prototype
text: Term Meaning --- --- [[Prototype]] The internal link from an object to its prototype __proto__ Accessor for an object's [[Prototype]] (legacy) Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) The recommended way to read [[Prototype]] Function.prototype / prototype A property on constructor functions, used as the [[Prototype]] of objects created with new

heading: Prototype Chain
text: const arr = [1, 2, 3]; arr.push(4); // found on Array.prototype arr.hasOwnProperty; // found on Object.prototype Object.getPrototypeOf(arr) === Array.prototype; // true Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype; // true Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype); // null (end of chain) The chain is: arr → Array.prototype → Object.prototype → null.

heading: Property Lookup
text: const animal = { eats: true }; const dog = Object.create(animal); dog.barks = true; dog.barks; // true (own property) dog.eats; // true (found on prototype) dog.flies; // undefined (not found anywhere in the chain)

heading: Own vs Inherited Properties
text: Object.hasOwn(dog, "barks"); // true Object.hasOwn(dog, "eats"); // false "eats" in dog; // true (checks the whole chain)

heading: Constructor Functions and prototype
text: Methods placed on the constructor's prototype are shared by all instances instead of being copied. function User(name) { this.name = name; } User.prototype.greet = function () { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; }; const user1 = new User("Sam"); const user2 = new User("Alex"); user1.greet(); // "Hi, I'm Sam" user1.greet === user2.greet; // true (same function) Object.getPrototypeOf(user1) === User.prototype; // true

heading: The constructor Property
text: User.prototype.constructor === User; // true user1.constructor === User; // true

heading: Adding Methods to Built-in Prototypes
text: Array.prototype.last = function () { return this[this.length - 1]; }; [1, 2, 3].last(); // 3 Modifying built-in prototypes is discouraged because it can cause conflicts.

heading: Creating Objects with a Chosen Prototype
text: const proto = { hello() { return "Hello"; }, }; const obj = Object.create(proto); obj.hello(); // "Hello" const noProto = Object.create(null); // object with no prototype

heading: Getting and Setting Prototypes
text: Object.getPrototypeOf(obj); Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, newProto); // works, but can hurt performance

heading: Shadowing
text: An own property with the same name hides the prototype's property. const base = { greet() { return "base"; } }; const child = Object.create(base); child.greet = function () { return "child"; }; child.greet(); // "child"

heading: Key Points
text: Every object has a prototype (except objects created with Object.create(null)). Property lookup walks up the prototype chain until null. Methods on Constructor.prototype are shared across all instances. Use Object.getPrototypeOf instead of __proto__ in new code.

heading: Prototype inheritance
text: Prototype inheritance lets one object inherit properties and methods from another object through the prototype chain.

heading: Inheriting with Object.create
text: const animal = { eat() { return `${this.name} is eating`; }, }; const dog = Object.create(animal); dog.name = "Rex"; dog.bark = function () { return `${this.name} says woof`; }; dog.eat(); // "Rex is eating" (inherited) dog.bark(); // "Rex says woof" (own)

topic: Object Oriented JS › Prototype inheritance › Inheritance with Constructor Functions
heading: Step 1: Parent Constructor
text: function Animal(name) { this.name = name; } Animal.prototype.eat = function () { return `${this.name} is eating`; };

topic: Object Oriented JS › Prototype inheritance › Inheritance with Constructor Functions
heading: Step 2: Child Constructor
text: function Dog(name, breed) { Animal.call(this, name); // inherit instance properties this.breed = breed; } Animal.call(this, name) runs the parent constructor with this set to the new Dog.

topic: Object Oriented JS › Prototype inheritance › Inheritance with Constructor Functions
heading: Step 3: Link the Prototypes
text: Dog.prototype = Object.create(Animal.prototype); Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog; // restore the constructor reference

topic: Object Oriented JS › Prototype inheritance › Inheritance with Constructor Functions
heading: Step 4: Add Child Methods
text: Dog.prototype.bark = function () { return `${this.name} says woof`; };

topic: Object Oriented JS › Prototype inheritance › Inheritance with Constructor Functions
heading: Using It
text: const rex = new Dog("Rex", "Labrador"); rex.eat(); // "Rex is eating" (from Animal.prototype) rex.bark(); // "Rex says woof" (from Dog.prototype) rex instanceof Dog; // true rex instanceof Animal; // true The chain is: rex → Dog.prototype → Animal.prototype → Object.prototype → null.

heading: Overriding Methods
text: Dog.prototype.eat = function () { const base = Animal.prototype.eat.call(this); return `${base} (and wagging its tail)`; }; rex.eat(); // "Rex is eating (and wagging its tail)"

heading: Why Not Dog.prototype = Animal.prototype?
text: Dog.prototype = Animal.prototype; // wrong Both would share the same object, so adding a method to Dog.prototype would also add it to Animal.prototype. Object.create(Animal.prototype) creates a separate object that links to it.

heading: Why Not Dog.prototype = new Animal()?
text: This runs the parent constructor at setup time and can leave unwanted properties on the prototype. Object.create(Animal.prototype) avoids that.

heading: Checking Inheritance
text: Animal.prototype.isPrototypeOf(rex); // true rex instanceof Animal; // true Object.getPrototypeOf(rex) === Dog.prototype; // true

heading: Setting the Prototype Directly
text: Object.setPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype, Animal.prototype);

heading: Key Points
text: Objects inherit through the prototype chain. Use Parent.call(this, ...) to inherit instance properties. Use Object.create(Parent.prototype) to inherit methods. Reset Child.prototype.constructor after replacing the prototype.

heading: ES6 Classes & Inheritance

Methods are placed on the class's prototype and shared by all instances. A class must be called with new.

heading: Object Destructuring
text: Object destructuring extracts properties from an object into separate variables using a concise syntax.

heading: Basic Syntax
text: const user = { name: "Sam", age: 25, city: "Ahmedabad" }; const { name, age } = user; console.log(name); // "Sam" console.log(age); // 25 Variable names must match the property names.

text: const { country: userCountry = "India" } = user;

heading: Rest Operator

text: const employee = { id: 1, profile: { firstName: "Sam", address: { city: "Ahmedabad", pin: "380001" }, }, }; const { profile: { firstName, address: { city }, }, } = employee; console.log(firstName); // "Sam" console.log(city); // "Ahmedabad" Note: profile and address themselves are not created as variables here.

heading: Destructuring in Function Parameters

heading: Object.keys()

heading: Object.fromEntries()

heading: Object.freeze() and Object.isFrozen()

heading: Object.seal() and Object.isSealed()

heading: Object.preventExtensions() and Object.isExtensible()

heading: Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor() and Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors()

heading: Object.is()

topic: Object Oriented JS › Built-in Static Object Methods
heading: Object.hasOwn()

heading: Key Points
text: keys, values, and entries list an object's own enumerable data. freeze, seal, and preventExtensions limit changes to an object. defineProperty controls property behavior in detail. Object.hasOwn is the modern replacement for hasOwnProperty.

heading: Nullish coalescing
text: The nullish coalescing operator (??) returns the right-hand value only when the left-hand value is null or undefined. Otherwise, it returns the left-hand value.

heading: Syntax
text: const result = value ?? defaultValue;

heading: Basic Example
text: null ?? "default"; // "default" undefined ?? "default"; // "default" "hello" ?? "default"; // "hello"

heading: Difference from ||
text: The operator falls back for any falsy value. The ?? operator falls back only for null and undefined. 0 || 10; // 10 0 ?? 10; // 0 "" || "text"; // "text" "" ?? "text"; // "" false || true; // true false ?? true; // false NaN || 5; // 5 NaN ?? 5; // NaN

heading: Practical Example
text: function setVolume(volume) { const level = volume ?? 50; console.log(level); } setVolume(0); // 0 setVolume(undefined); // 50 setVolume(null); // 50

heading: Nullish Assignment (??=)
text: Assigns a value only if the variable is null or undefined. let user = { name: "Sam", age: null }; user.age ??= 18; user.name ??= "Guest"; console.log(user); // { name: "Sam", age: 18 }

heading: Chaining
text: const name = null ?? undefined ?? "Guest"; // "Guest"

heading: Mixing with || and &&
text: ?? cannot be combined directly with or && without parentheses. const a = null || undefined ?? "x"; // SyntaxError const b = (null || undefined) ?? "x"; // "x"

heading: Key Points
text: ?? treats only null and undefined as missing values. Use it when 0, "", and false are valid values. ??= assigns a default only when the value is null or undefined.

heading: Optional chaining
text: Optional chaining (?.) lets you safely access deeply nested properties, methods, or array items. If a value in the chain is null or undefined, the expression short-circuits and returns undefined instead of throwing an error.

heading: The Problem
text: const user = {}; user.address.city; // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

heading: Property Access
text: const user = { name: "Sam", address: { city: "Ahmedabad" } }; user?.address?.city; // "Ahmedabad" user?.contact?.phone; // undefined (no error)

heading: Method Calls
text: const user = { greet() { return "Hello"; }, }; user.greet?.(); // "Hello" user.sayBye?.(); // undefined (no error)

heading: Array Items
text: const users = [{ name: "Sam" }]; users?.[0]?.name; // "Sam" users?.[5]?.name; // undefined

heading: Dynamic Keys
text: const key = "name"; user?.[key]; // "Sam"

heading: Short-Circuiting
text: When the left side is null or undefined, the rest of the chain is not evaluated. let count = 0; const user = null; user?.update(count++); console.log(count); // 0

heading: With Default Values
text: const city = user?.address?.city || "Unknown";

heading: Only for null and undefined
text: Optional chaining checks only for null and undefined, not other falsy values. const obj = { count: 0, name: "" }; obj?.count; // 0 obj?.name; // ""

heading: Limitations
text: // Cannot be used on the left side of an assignment user?.name = "Sam"; // SyntaxError

heading: Key Points
text: ?. returns undefined if the value before it is null or undefined. Works with properties (?.), methods (?.()), and brackets (?.[]). Prevents TypeError when accessing nested data.

heading: Regular Expressions
text: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern used to match character combinations in strings.

heading: Creating a Regex
text: const regex1 = /hello/; // literal const regex2 = new RegExp("hello"); // constructor const withFlags = /hello/gi; const dynamic = new RegExp(`${word}`, "g"); // useful for dynamic patterns

heading: Flags
text: Flag Meaning --- --- g Global: find all matches i Case-insensitive m Multiline: ^ and $ match each line s Dot matches newlines u Unicode support y Sticky: match from lastIndex only d Include match indices

heading: test()
text: Returns true or false. /hello/.test("hello world"); // true /hello/.test("Hi"); // false

heading: exec()
text: Returns match details or null. const result = /(\d+)-(\d+)/.exec("Call 123-456"); result[0]; // "123-456" result[1]; // "123" result[2]; // "456" result.index; // 5

heading: String matchAll()
text: Returns an iterator of all matches, including groups. Requires the g flag. const matches = "a1b2".matchAll(/([a-z])(\d)/g); for (const m of matches) { console.log(m[0], m[1], m[2]); // "a1" "a" "1", then "b2" "b" "2" }

heading: String replace() and replaceAll()
text: "a-b-c".replace(/-/g, "+"); // "a+b+c" "John Smith".replace(/(\w+) (\w+)/, "$2 $1"); // "Smith John" "a-b-c".replaceAll(/-/g, "+"); // "a+b+c" "abc".replace(/b/, (match) => match.toUpperCase()); // "aBc"

heading: String search() and split()
text: "hello world".search(/world/); // 6 "a1b2c3".split(/\d/); // ["a", "b", "c", ""]

heading: Character Classes
text: Pattern Matches --- --- . Any character except newline \d Digit (0-9) \D Non-digit \w Letter, digit, or underscore \W Not a word character \s Whitespace \S Non-whitespace [abc] Any of a, b, or c [^abc] Anything except a, b, or c [a-z] Any lowercase letter

heading: Anchors and Boundaries
text: Pattern Matches --- --- ^ Start of string (or line with m) $ End of string (or line with m) \b Word boundary \B Not a word boundary /^hello/.test("hello world"); // true /world$/.test("hello world"); // true /\bcat\b/.test("a cat sat"); // true

heading: Quantifiers
text: Pattern Matches --- --- 0 or more + 1 or more ? 0 or 1 {3} Exactly 3 {2,} 2 or more {2,4} Between 2 and 4 /a+/.exec("caaat")[0]; // "aaa" /\d{3}/.test("123"); // true

heading: Greedy vs Lazy
text: Quantifiers are greedy by default. Add ? to make them lazy. "bolditalic".match(/<.+>/)[0]; // "bolditalic" "bolditalic".match(/<.+?>/)[0]; // ""

heading: Non-Capturing Groups
text: /(?:ab)+/.test("ababab"); // true, without creating a capture group

heading: Named Groups
text: const m = "2025-10-15".match(/(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})-(?<day>\d{2})/); m.groups.year; // "2025" m.groups.month; // "10"

heading: Backreferences
text: /(\w)\1/.test("hello"); // true ("ll")

heading: Alternation
text: /cat|dog/.test("I have a dog"); // true

heading: Lookahead and Lookbehind
text: /\d+(?= dollars)/.exec("100 dollars")[0]; // "100" (positive lookahead) /\d+(?! dollars)/.exec("100 euros")[0]; // "100" (negative lookahead) /(?<=\$)\d+/.exec("$50")[0]; // "50" (positive lookbehind) /(?<!\$)\b\d+/.exec("USD 50")[0]; // "50" (negative lookbehind)

heading: Escaping Special Characters
text: Special characters: . + ? ^ $ { } ( ) [ ] \ /\./.test("a.b"); // matches a literal dot /\$\d+/.test("$50"); // matches a literal $

heading: The Global Flag and lastIndex
text: With g or y, test() and exec() remember their position. const re = /a/g; re.test("aa"); // true (lastIndex = 1) re.test("aa"); // true (lastIndex = 2) re.test("aa"); // false (lastIndex reset to 0)

heading: Common Examples
text: /^\d{10}$/.test("9876543210"); // 10-digit number /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test("a@b.com"); // simple email check /^#?([a-f0-9]{6}|[a-f0-9]{3})$/i.test("#ff00aa"); // hex color /^\s+|\s+$/g; // leading/trailing whitespace /^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d).{8,}$/.test("Passw0rdX"); // 8+ chars, 1 uppercase, 1 digit

heading: Key Points
text: Create with /pattern/flags or new RegExp(). Use test() to check a match and match() / matchAll() to extract matches. Use groups to capture parts and replace() to transform text. Quantifiers are greedy by default; add ? for lazy matching.

heading: Set Data Structure
text: A Set is a collection of unique values. A value can appear only once in a Set, and values can be of any type.

heading: Creating a Set
text: const set = new Set(); const numbers = new Set([1, 2, 3, 3, 2]); // Set(3) { 1, 2, 3 } const letters = new Set("hello"); // Set(4) { "h", "e", "l", "o" }

heading: Basic Methods
text: const set = new Set(); set.add(1); set.add(2); set.add(2); // ignored (already exists) set.has(1); // true set.has(5); // false set.delete(1); // true (removed) set.size; // 1 set.clear(); // remove all values add() returns the Set, so calls can be chained. set.add("a").add("b").add("c");

heading: Uniqueness
text: Values are compared using the "same-value-zero" rule, similar to ===, except that NaN equals NaN. const set = new Set([NaN, NaN, 0, -0]); set.size; // 2 (NaN once, 0 once) Objects are compared by reference. const s = new Set(); s.add({ a: 1 }); s.add({ a: 1 }); s.size; // 2 (two different objects)

heading: Iterating Over a Set
text: Values are iterated in insertion order. const set = new Set(["a", "b", "c"]); for (const value of set) { console.log(value); } set.forEach((value) => console.log(value)); set.values(); // iterator of values set.keys(); // same as values() set.entries(); // iterator of [value, value] pairs

heading: Converting Between Set and Array
text: const set = new Set([1, 2, 3]); const arr1 = [...set]; const arr2 = Array.from(set); const backToSet = new Set(arr1);

heading: Removing Duplicates from an Array
text: const nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]; const unique = [...new Set(nums)]; // [1, 2, 3]

heading: Union
text: const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]); const b = new Set([3, 4, 5]); const union = new Set([...a, ...b]); // Set { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }

heading: Intersection
text: const intersection = new Set([...a].filter((x) => b.has(x))); // Set { 3 }

heading: Difference
text: const difference = new Set([...a].filter((x) => !b.has(x))); // Set { 1, 2 }

heading: Symmetric Difference
text: const symDiff = new Set( [...a].filter((x) => !b.has(x)).concat([...b].filter((x) => !a.has(x))) ); // Set { 1, 2, 4, 5 }

heading: Subset Check
text: const isSubset = [...a].every((x) => b.has(x));

heading: Built-in Set Methods (Modern JavaScript)
text: Newer JavaScript engines include these methods directly. a.union(b); a.intersection(b); a.difference(b); a.symmetricDifference(b); a.isSubsetOf(b); a.isSupersetOf(b); a.isDisjointFrom(b);

heading: Set vs Array
text: Feature Set Array --- --- --- Duplicates Not allowed Allowed Access by index No Yes Order Insertion order Index order Check if value exists has() (fast) includes() (slower for large data) Size size length

heading: Common Use Cases
text: Removing duplicate values Fast membership checks Tracking visited items Finding common or different items between collections

heading: WeakSet
text: A WeakSet holds only objects, keeps them weakly (they can be garbage collected), is not iterable, and has no size. const weak = new WeakSet(); const obj = {}; weak.add(obj); weak.has(obj); // true weak.delete(obj);

heading: Key Points
text: A Set stores unique values and preserves insertion order. Main methods: add, has, delete, clear, and the size property. [...new Set(array)] is the quickest way to remove duplicates. Use has() for fast lookups.

heading: 1. Servers in Node.js
text: A server is a system that provides resources, data, services, or programs to other computers (clients) over a network. In Node.js, a server is primarily used to handle and respond to client requests over the HTTP protocol. Node.js servers are highly efficient due to their event-driven, non-blocking I/O architecture, which allows: Handling multiple client requests simultaneously. Avoiding the need to create new threads for each request. Reducing resource overhead and improving application performance.

topic: Chapter 02-JS on the Server › Chapter 02: JavaScript on the Server
heading: 2. The V8 JavaScript Engine
text: The V8 engine is an open-source JavaScript engine developed by Google, primarily used in Chrome and Node.js. It is optimized for high performance through Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation, which compiles JavaScript into machine code at runtime. Key features of V8 include: JIT Compilation: Converts JavaScript into optimized machine code dynamically during execution. Garbage Collection: Automatically manages memory, preventing leaks and maintaining performance. Efficient Execution: Optimizes frequently used code paths to improve runtime speed.

topic: Chapter 02-JS on the Server › Chapter 02: JavaScript on the Server
heading: 3. Node.js Code Conversion: High-Level to Machine Code
text: JavaScript is a high-level interpreted language, meaning it needs to be converted into machine code before execution by the CPU. The V8 engine manages this conversion through the following steps: Parsing: - V8 reads the JavaScript code and checks for syntax errors. - Converts the code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). Intermediate Representation (IR) Generation: - The AST is transformed into an Intermediate Representation (IR), a lower-level, platform-independent form of the code. Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation: - The IR is compiled into machine code dynamically at runtime. - V8 continuously optimizes the machine code based on runtime performance, ensuring efficient execution. This conversion process enables Node.js applications to run at high speed while maintaining flexibility and scalability. ---

Here's an example: // In file app.js const greet = require('./greet'); console.log(greet('World')); // Output: Hello, World! #### Exporting Multiple Functions/Variables To export multiple functions or variables, attach them to the `module.exports` object: // In file utils.js const add = (a, b) => a + b; const subtract = (a, b) => a - b; module.exports = { add, subtract }; #### Importing Multiple Exports To import multiple exports from a module, use destructuring: // In file app.js const { add, subtract } = require('./utils'); console.log(add(5, 3)); // Output: 8 console.log(subtract(5, 3)); // Output: 2 #### How `require` Works When you use `require` to import a module, Node.js executes the code in the module file. Only the properties of `module.exports` are exposed to the importing file. Example: // In file data.js const secret = 'hidden'; const publicData = 'visible'; module.exports = publicData; // In file app.js const data = require('./data'); console.log(data); // Output: visible console.log(secret); // Error: secret is not defined In the example above, `secret` is not accessible outside `data.js` because it was not exported using `module.exports`. #### .mjs vs. .cjs Modules ##### .cjs Modules (CommonJS) - **File Extension:** `.js` or `.cjs` - **Module System:** CommonJS - **Usage:** `require()` and `module.exports` Example: // In file common.js module.exports = function() { / ... / }; ##### .mjs Modules (ES Modules) - **File Extension:** `.mjs` - **Module System:** ES Modules (ESM) - **Usage:** `import` and `export` Example: // In file module.mjs return Hello, ${name}!; } ###### Importing in .mjs // In file app.mjs console.log(greet('World')); // Output: Hello, World! #### Differences Between .mjs and .cjs - **Syntax:** `.cjs` uses `require` and `module.exports`, while `.mjs` uses `import` and `export`. - **Compatibility:** `.mjs` is the standard ES Module syntax and is compatible with modern JavaScript, while `.cjs` is used for legacy Node.js modules. - **Use Case:** Use `.mjs` for new projects or when using features of ES Modules, and `.cjs` for legacy code or when using the CommonJS module system. #### Summary - `module.exports` is used to export functions, objects, or variables from a module. - `require` imports these exports into another module. - `.cjs` modules use CommonJS syntax (`require` and `module.exports`), while `.mjs` modules use ES Module syntax (`import` and `export`). - These kind of pattern used for import export in Nodejs ## Chapter 05-Diving into Nodejs github repo ### Understanding IIFE, Module Privacy, and `require` in Node.js #### Overview This repository provides an in-depth look into Immediately Invoked Function Expressions (IIFE) in Node.js, how module variables and functions can be kept private, and the detailed mechanism of the `require` statement in Node.js. #### Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE) An Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE) is a design pattern in JavaScript that executes a function immediately after its creation. It is often used to create a private scope and avoid polluting the global namespace. ##### Syntax (function() { // Code inside here is private })(); ##### Parameters IIFEs can accept parameters, allowing them to use values from the outer scope without exposing them: (function(param) { console.log(param); })(5); // Logs 5 In this example, `param` is only accessible within the IIFE and does not affect the outer scope. ##### Use in Node.js In Node.js, IIFEs can be particularly useful for managing module scope and creating private variables and functions. Here are a few key points on how IIFEs are used in Node.js: 1. **Encapsulation**: IIFEs allow developers to encapsulate logic and variables within a module. This means that variables and functions defined inside the IIFE are not accessible from outside the module, helping to avoid potential conflicts and unintentional usage. 2. **Avoiding Globals**: By wrapping code in an IIFE, you prevent variables and functions from leaking into the global namespace. This is especially important in Node.js, where global scope pollution can lead to hard-to-debug issues. 3. **Creating Module-like Structures**: Although Node.js modules use CommonJS for encapsulation, IIFEs can still be useful for creating self-contained code blocks within modules or libraries. ##### Example in Node.js Here is an example demonstrating how an IIFE can be used to create private variables and functions within a Node.js module: // myModule.js const myModule = (function() { const privateVariable = 'I am private'; function privateFunction() { console.log('This is a private function'); } return { publicFunction: function() { console.log('This is a public function'); privateFunction(); // Accesses private function } }; })(); module.exports = myModule; In this example: - `privateVariable` and `privateFunction` are private to the IIFE and cannot be accessed from outside the module. - `publicFunction` is exposed and accessible when the module is required elsewhere. #### Module Privacy in Node.js In Node.js, each module has its own scope, which means that variables and functions defined in a module are private to that module by default. You can control what is exposed to other modules using the `module.exports` or `exports` object. ##### Example // myModule.js const privateVariable = 'I am private'; function privateFunction() { console.log('This is a private function'); } module.exports = { publicFunction: function() { console.log('This is a public function'); } }; In this example: - `privateVariable` and `privateFunction` are private to `myModule.js`. - Only `publicFunction` is exposed and accessible when the module is required elsewhere. #### `require` Mechanism in Node.js The `require` statement in Node.js is used to import modules. heading: npm
text: A practical, SDE-1-level guide to npm (Node Package Manager), covering how npm works, how to manage dependencies, how packages are resolved and executed, how to publish packages, and how to troubleshoot real-world Node.js projects.

heading: What is npm?
text: npm originally stood for Node Package Manager. It is the default package manager for Node.js and consists broadly of: A CLI used from the terminal. A registry where packages are published and downloaded. A package/dependency resolution system. A package metadata and versioning ecosystem. npm allows developers to: Install third-party libraries. Install development tools. Manage project dependencies. Run project scripts. Publish reusable packages. Share code across projects. Reproduce dependency installations across machines and CI environments. Example: npm install express This generally: Resolves the requested package and its dependencies. Downloads the required package metadata/artifacts. Places packages under node_modules. Updates package.json. Updates package-lock.json. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Node.js, npm, and npx
text: These three are related but serve different purposes.

heading: Node.js
text: Node.js is the JavaScript runtime. node app.js runs JavaScript using Node.js.

heading: npm
text: npm manages packages and project dependencies. npm install express

heading: npx
text: npx executes package binaries. For example: npx eslint . You can think of them as: Node.js -> Runs JavaScript npm -> Installs/manages packages npx -> Executes package-provided CLI binaries Modern npm distributions include npx. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Installing and Verifying npm
text: Installing Node.js normally installs npm as well. Check versions: node -v npm -v npx -v Useful diagnostic command: npm doctor The exact output depends on the installed Node.js/npm versions and operating system. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Registry
text: The npm registry is the package repository used by npm. The default public registry is: https://registry.npmjs.org/ A package can contain: Package name Version Description Dependencies Entry points README License Repository metadata Published files Search packages: npm search express View package metadata: npm view express View a specific field: npm view express version npm view express dependencies npm view express dist.tarball ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: package.json
text: package.json is one of the most important files in a Node.js project. Create one: npm init or: npm init -y A basic example: { "name": "my-app", "version": "1.0.0", "description": "Example Node.js application", "main": "index.js", "scripts": { "start": "node index.js", "dev": "node --watch index.js", "test": "node --test" }, "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" }, "devDependencies": { "eslint": "^9.0.0" }, "engines": { "node": ">=20" }, "license": "MIT" }

heading: name
text: Package/project name. "name": "my-app" For published packages, the name must follow npm naming rules.

heading: version
text: The package's current version. "version": "1.0.0"

heading: description
text: Short description of the package.

heading: main
text: Historically used as the CommonJS entry point. "main": "index.js" For modern packages, exports is often preferred.

heading: type
text: Controls how .js files are interpreted. "type": "module" means .js files are treated as ES modules. Without it, .js files are generally treated as CommonJS unless another rule applies.

heading: scripts
text: Defines commands that can be run using npm. "scripts": { "dev": "node --watch src/index.js", "start": "node src/index.js" } Run: npm run dev npm start

heading: dependencies
text: Packages required by the application at runtime. "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" }

heading: devDependencies
text: Packages required primarily for development, testing, linting, building, etc. "devDependencies": { "eslint": "^9.0.0" }

heading: peerDependencies
text: Used when the package expects the consuming project to provide a compatible dependency. Common in: React libraries UI component libraries Plugins Framework integrations Example: "peerDependencies": { "react": ">=18" }

heading: optionalDependencies
text: Dependencies that are allowed to fail during installation without necessarily failing the entire installation.

heading: bundledDependencies
text: Dependencies that are included inside the published package. Use this only when there is a concrete reason; ordinary dependencies are normally preferable.

heading: engines
text: Specifies supported runtime versions. "engines": { "node": ">=20" } This communicates compatibility expectations but should not be treated as a substitute for runtime enforcement. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: package-lock.json
text: package-lock.json records the dependency tree resolved for a project. It helps provide: Reproducible installations. Exact package versions. Integrity information. Dependency relationships. Faster and more deterministic CI installations. A simplified relationship is: package.json | | declares acceptable versions v package-lock.json | | records resolved versions v node_modules | | contains installed packages

text: For applications, generally yes. Commit: package.json package-lock.json Do not normally commit: node_modules/ ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: node_modules
text: node_modules contains installed dependencies. Example: project/ ├── node_modules/ ├── src/ ├── package.json └── package-lock.json You normally should not manually edit files inside node_modules. If dependencies become corrupted, a common clean reinstall is: rm -rf node_modules npm ci On Windows PowerShell, an equivalent approach is: Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules npm ci ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Dependencies vs Dev Dependencies vs Peer Dependencies
text: This distinction is important in professional development.

topic: Dependencies vs Dev Dependencies vs Peer Dependencies
heading: dependencies
text: Required for the application to run. Example: "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" }

topic: Dependencies vs Dev Dependencies vs Peer Dependencies

text: Used by libraries when the host application is expected to provide a dependency. Example: "peerDependencies": { "react": ">=18" }

topic: Dependencies vs Dev Dependencies vs Peer Dependencies › peerDependencies
heading: Rule of thumb
text: Ask: "Does the production application need this package to execute?" If yes, it is generally a dependency. If it is only required to build, test, lint, format, or develop the project, it is generally a devDependency. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Semantic Versioning
text: npm packages commonly use Semantic Versioning (SemVer). Format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH Example: 2.4.7 means: 2 -\> MAJOR 4 -\> MINOR 7 -\> PATCH

heading: MAJOR
text: Breaking API changes. 2.x.x -> 3.x.x

heading: MINOR
text: Backward-compatible features. 2.4.x -> 2.5.x

heading: Version Ranges
text: npm supports version ranges.

heading: Exact version
text: "express": "5.1.0" Only that version is requested.

heading: Caret
text: "express": "^5.1.0" Generally permits compatible updates that do not change the left-most non-zero major/minor compatibility boundary. For a normal major version: ^5.1.0 allows versions: >=5.1.0 <6.0.0

heading: Tilde
text: "express": "~5.1.0" Generally allows patch-level updates: >=5.1.0 <5.2.0

heading: Wildcards
text: "express": "5.x" or: "express": "*" Avoid overly broad ranges unless there is a specific reason. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

text: npm install express Shortcut: npm i express

heading: Install a development dependency
text: npm install --save-dev eslint Shortcut: npm i -D eslint

heading: Install a specific version
text: npm install express@5.1.0

heading: Install the latest version
text: npm install express@latest

heading: Install a package globally
text: npm install -g typescript Use global installation mainly for tools that you intentionally want available system-wide. Project dependencies should normally be local.

heading: Install all project dependencies
text: npm install npm reads package.json and the lockfile when available. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Removing and Updating Packages
text: Remove: npm uninstall express Update packages within their declared ranges: npm update Check outdated dependencies: npm outdated View installed dependency tree: npm ls View a specific package: npm ls express ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Scripts
text: Scripts are commands defined in package.json. Example: { "scripts": { "dev": "node --watch src/server.js", "start": "node src/server.js", "lint": "eslint .", "test": "node --test" } } Run: npm run dev npm start npm run lint npm test Some scripts have special shorthand: npm start npm test npm restart npm stop

heading: Why scripts matter
text: They standardize project commands. Instead of asking every developer to remember: node --watch src/server.js the project can provide: npm run dev This becomes particularly valuable in teams and CI/CD pipelines. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npx
text: npx runs executables supplied by npm packages. Example: npx eslint . For a package that exposes a CLI: npx <package-command> A useful mental model: npm install -> acquire/manage packages npx -> execute package binaries For reproducible project tooling, prefer using the project's locally installed version rather than relying on an unrelated global installation. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Local installation
text: npm install eslint --save-dev The package is available to the project. Typical location: node_modules/.bin/ npm scripts automatically make local binaries available on PATH.

heading: Global installation
text: npm install -g eslint The package is installed into npm's global prefix. Check the global prefix: npm prefix -g

topic: Global vs Local Packages › Global installation
heading: Best practice
text: For project-specific tooling: Prefer local installation. This avoids "works on my machine" problems caused by different global versions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: How npm Resolves Dependencies
text: Suppose your application depends on: A and A depends on: B The resulting graph is: Application └── A └── B Now suppose another package also requires B: Application ├── A │ └── B └── C └── B npm tries to construct a valid dependency tree while avoiding unnecessary duplication. The exact tree depends on: Requested version ranges. npm version. Peer dependencies. Existing lockfile. Platform. Optional dependencies. Package metadata. Understanding npm as a dependency graph resolver, rather than merely a downloader, is important for debugging. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm install vs npm ci
text: This is a very common SDE-1 and production question.

heading: npm install
text: Used for normal development. npm install It can: Resolve dependencies. Update the lockfile when necessary. Install packages. Reconcile package.json and the lockfile.

heading: npm ci
text: Primarily intended for clean, automated, reproducible installations. npm ci Important characteristics: Requires a compatible lockfile. Installs from the lockfile. Removes existing node_modules before installation. Does not intentionally update the lockfile. Commonly used in CI/CD.

topic: npm install vs npm ci › npm ci

Dependency Trees and Deduplication
text: Use: npm ls to inspect dependencies. A project can accidentally contain multiple versions of the same package: node_modules/ ├── package-a/ │ └── node_modules/ │ └── lodash@4.x └── lodash@4.x npm can sometimes deduplicate compatible dependencies. Command: npm dedupe However, do not assume every duplicate can or should be removed. Different packages may legitimately require incompatible versions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Workspaces
text: Workspaces allow multiple packages to live in one repository. Example: monorepo/ ├── package.json ├── package-lock.json └── packages/ ├── api/ │ └── package.json ├── web/ │ └── package.json └── shared/ └── package.json Root package.json: { "private": true, "workspaces": [ "packages/*" ] } Workspaces are useful for: Monorepos. Shared libraries. Frontend + backend repositories. Internal packages. Shared TypeScript utilities. Example: npm install from the root can install workspace dependencies. Run a workspace script: npm run build --workspace=web Workspaces are different from simply having multiple unrelated Node.js projects in the same Git repository. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Configuration and .npmrc
text: npm configuration can be controlled using: .npmrc Configuration can exist at different levels, including: Project level. User level. Global level. Environment variables / CLI flags. Inspect configuration: npm config list Get a specific value: npm config get registry Set a value: npm config set registry https://registry.npmjs.org/

heading: Important caution
text: Never commit credentials or authentication tokens into .npmrc. For private registries, authentication should be handled securely using environment variables, CI secrets, or supported npm authentication mechanisms. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Environment Variables and Secrets
text: Do not put secrets directly into: package.json .npmrc Git source code Bad: { "someToken": "actual-secret-value" } Prefer environment variables and secret managers. For CI/CD, configure secrets through the CI platform. A common .gitignore includes: node_modules/ .env .env.* Be careful: some projects intentionally commit non-secret .env.example files. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Private Registries and Scoped Packages
text: npm supports scoped packages: @company/package-name Example: npm install @company/shared-utils Organizations can use private registries to distribute internal packages. A project can configure a registry for a scope: @company:registry=https://registry.example.com/ This allows different scopes to resolve through different registries. Private package authentication should be configured securely and never hard-coded into source control. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Publishing an npm Package
text: Before publishing, ensure: { "name": "my-package", "version": "1.0.0" } Login: npm login Inspect what will be published: npm pack --dry-run This is extremely useful because it shows which files will be included. Publish: npm publish For scoped public packages, depending on package configuration: npm publish --access public

heading: Versioning before publishing
text: Patch: npm version patch Minor: npm version minor Major: npm version major These commands update the package version and typically create the corresponding Git metadata depending on configuration.

topic: Publishing an npm Package › Versioning before publishing
heading: Important
text: Do not treat publishing as: write code -> npm publish A professional release process should also consider: Tests. Build output. Package contents. README. License. Versioning. Changelog. Security. Compatibility. Access control. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Package Entry Points and Exports
text: A package needs a clear public API. Historically: { "main": "index.js" } Modern packages can use: { "exports": { ".": "./dist/index.js" } } exports provides stronger control over which files consumers can import. Example: { "exports": { ".": "./dist/index.js", "./utils": "./dist/utils.js" } } Then consumers can use: import packageName from "package-name"; or: import { helper } from "package-name/utils"; depending on the package's module format and exports. A key concept: exports defines the package's supported public import surface. This can prevent consumers from depending on internal implementation files. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: CommonJS vs ESM
text: Node.js supports both major JavaScript module systems.

heading: CommonJS
text: const express = require("express"); module.exports = myFunction;

heading: ES Modules
text: import express from "express"; export default myFunction; A package can declare ESM behavior using: { "type": "module" } CommonJS can explicitly use: .cjs ES modules can explicitly use: .mjs

heading: Why SDE-1 developers should understand this
text: Many npm errors are actually module-system errors: require is not defined Cannot use import statement outside a module ERR_REQUIRE_ESM When debugging, inspect: package.json "type" File extensions Package exports Whether the dependency is CommonJS or ESM ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Lifecycle and Pre/Post Scripts
text: npm supports lifecycle scripts. For example: { "scripts": { "prebuild": "npm run clean", "build": "tsc", "postbuild": "node scripts/postbuild.js" } } Running: npm run build can cause: prebuild ↓ build ↓ postbuild There are also lifecycle events associated with installation and publishing.

heading: Security consideration
text: Lifecycle scripts can execute code during package installation or other npm operations. This is one reason dependency trust and supply-chain security matter. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Security
text: npm projects are exposed to software supply-chain risks. Major categories include: Malicious packages. Compromised dependencies. Vulnerable dependencies. Typosquatting. Dependency confusion. Malicious install scripts. Credential leakage. Stale dependencies. Untrusted transitive dependencies.

heading: Typosquatting
text: An attacker may publish a package with a name similar to a popular package. Example concept: popular-package populer-package Always verify package names before installing.

heading: Dependency confusion
text: An internal package name can accidentally resolve to a malicious public package if registry configuration is incorrect. Scoped private packages and explicit registry configuration help reduce this risk. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Auditing and Vulnerability Management
text: Check vulnerabilities: npm audit Attempt automatic fixes: npm audit fix Be careful with aggressive upgrades because security fixes can introduce breaking changes. You should understand: Direct dependency ↓ Transitive dependency ↓ Vulnerable package A vulnerability may exist in a package you never directly installed. Useful commands: npm audit npm ls <package-name> npm explain <package-name> npm explain can help identify why a package exists in the dependency tree. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Reproducible Builds and CI/CD
text: A production Node.js project should aim for reproducible dependency installation. Typical CI flow: Clone repository ↓ Install Node.js ↓ npm ci ↓ Run lint ↓ Run tests ↓ Build ↓ Package/deploy Example: npm ci npm test npm run build The lockfile is important because different developers should not randomly receive different transitive dependency versions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Caching
text: npm maintains a local cache. Inspect: npm cache verify Clean the cache only when there is a concrete reason: npm cache clean --force Do not make cache deletion your default response to every npm problem. Many npm issues are caused by: Incorrect package versions. Peer dependency conflicts. Broken lockfiles. Registry/authentication issues. Node/npm incompatibility. Platform-specific optional dependencies. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 1. "Module not found"
text: Example: Cannot find module 'express' Check: npm ls express If missing: npm install express Also verify that you are running the command from the correct project directory. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 2. Delete node_modules and reinstall
text: When the dependency installation is genuinely corrupted: rm -rf node_modules npm ci On Windows PowerShell: Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules npm ci ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 3. package-lock.json conflict
text: If package.json and the lockfile are inconsistent, understand why before deleting the lockfile. For a clean CI environment: npm ci requires the lockfile to satisfy npm's expectations. Do not blindly delete package-lock.json as a first troubleshooting step. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 4. Peer dependency conflict
text: You may see errors such as: ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree First understand the conflicting package requirements. Inspect: npm ls npm explain <package> Avoid immediately using: npm install --legacy-peer-deps as a permanent solution. It can bypass dependency resolution protections and leave an invalid or unsupported combination. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 5. EACCES / permission errors
text: On Unix-like systems, permission errors can happen when npm directories are owned by another user. Investigate: npm config get prefix Avoid solving the problem by routinely running npm with: sudo npm install A correct Node/npm installation and user-level configuration is preferable. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 6. Registry problems
text: Check: npm config get registry Expected public registry: https://registry.npmjs.org/ If using a company registry, verify: Registry URL. Authentication. Scope configuration. Network/VPN. Proxy configuration. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 7. Network errors
text: Common errors include: ETIMEDOUT ECONNRESET EAI_AGAIN Possible causes: Internet connectivity. DNS. Proxy. VPN. Corporate firewall. Registry outage. Do not immediately assume the package itself is broken. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: 8. "Works on my machine"
text: Check: node -v npm -v Then compare: Node.js version npm version package.json package-lock.json OS CPU architecture environment variables Use: npm ci in CI to reduce environment-dependent dependency differences. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Performance and Dependency Hygiene
text: A good SDE-1 should not only know how to install packages but also understand the cost of dependencies. Consider: Number of dependencies. Package size. Transitive dependency count. Startup overhead. Security exposure. Maintenance status. License compatibility. Runtime vs build-time usage. Before adding a dependency, ask: Do I really need it? Is the package maintained? Is the API stable? Is it secure? Is the package size reasonable? Can the functionality be implemented safely without another dependency? Do not add a large library for a trivial utility unless the trade-off makes sense. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: (Open Web Application Security Project OR Open Worldwide Application Security Project)
What is DevSecOps?
text: It refers to the integration of security practices into a DevOps software delivery model. It is the practice of integrating security into every phase of the software development lifecycle (SDLC) instead of treating it as a final gate before release. In a DevSecOps model, security objectives are integrated as early as possible in the lifecycle of software development and security considerations are important throughout the lifecycle.

heading: Vulnerabilities
text: A security vulnerability is a software code flaw or a system misconfiguration that hackers can use to gain unauthorized access to a system or network. A vulnerability is a weakness in software, configuration, or process that an attacker can exploit to compromise confidentiality, integrity, or availability (the CIA triad).

heading: Exploit
text: An exploit is the method hackers used to exploit a vulnerability and exploit is typically a piece of custom software or a sequence of commands.

heading: Threat
text: A threat is the actual or hypothetical event in which one or more exploits vulnerability to mount an attack.

heading: Key terminology
text: Term Definition - - Vulnerability A weakness (e.g., unsanitized input) Threat Something that could exploit a weakness (attacker, malware) Exploit Code or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability. Risk Likelihood x impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability. Attack Surface Sum of all points where an attacker can interact with the system (APIs, forms, ports, dependencies). Payload The malicious data sent during an attack. Zero-day A vulnerability with no available patch, often unknown to the vendor. PoC Proof of Concept: demonstrates that a vulnerability is exploitable.

heading: What is DevOps?
text: A set of practices that combines software development and IT Operations. It aims to shorten the Systems Development Lifecycle and provides continuous delivery with high software availability.

heading: DevOps vs DevSecOps
text: Aspect DevOps DevSecOps - - - Goal Deliver software faster and more reliably Deliver software faster, reliably, and securely Security Timing Often a late-stage review/gate Continuous, from planning onward Ownership Dev + Ops Dev + Sec + Ops Pipeline Build -> Test -> Deploy Build -> Security scans -> Test -> Policy checks -> Deploy -> Runtime monitoring Cost of fixing bugs Security bugs found late are expensive Found early, cheap to fix Culture Collaboration between dev and ops Collaboration between dev, ops and security Compliance Manual audits Automated, continuous compliance checks Feedback Loop Test failures Test failures plus vulnerability findings in PRs/IDE

heading: Advantages of DevSecOps over DevOps
text: faster delivery improved security posture reduced costs enabling greater overall business access improving security integration and pace enhancing the value of DevOps
