topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › 1.CWE: Common Weakness Enumeration
heading: 1.Porous Defenses
text: A porous defenses weakness is one that could allow users to bypass or spoof authentication and authorization processes. Authentication verifies the identity of someone trying to access a system while authorization is set of access and usage permissions assigned to the user. Porous defense weakness examples: Weak password encoding insufficiently protected credentials missing or single factor authentication insecurely inherited permissions sessions that do not expire in a timely manner.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › 1.CWE: Common Weakness Enumeration
heading: 2. Risky Resource Management
text: Risky management of resources such as memory, functions and open-source frameworks. Examples: out of bound read/ write buffer overflow path traversal

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › 1.CWE: Common Weakness Enumeration
heading: 3. Insecure Interaction Between Components
text: Many applications today send and receive data across a wide range of services, threads and processes. The way different components interact with each other can introduce vulnerabilities. Examples: cross-site-scripting cross-site request forgery backdoor attacks scripting attacks worms trojan horses other exploits...

heading: 2. OWASP Top 10
text: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is an open community dedicated to enabling organizations to develop, purchase, and maintain applications and APIs that can be trusted.

heading: What are Application Security Risks?
text: Attackers can potentially use many different paths through your application to do harm to your business or organization. Each of these ways poses a potential risk that needs to be investigated.

heading: Data Factors to determine application security lists:
text: There are data factors that are listed for each of the Top Ten Categories, here is what they mean: CWEs Mapped: The number of CWEs mapped to a category by the Top Ten team. Incidence Rate: Incidence rate is the percentage of applications vulnerable to that CWE from the population tested by that org for that year. Weighted Exploit: The Exploit sub-score from CVSSv2 and CVSSv3 scores assigned to CVEs mapped to CWEs, normalized, and placed on a 10pt scale. Weighted Impact: The Impact sub-score from CVSSv2 and CVSSv3 scores assigned to CVEs mapped to CWEs, normalized, and placed on a 10pt scale. (Testing) Coverage: The percentage of applications tested by all organizations for a given CWE. Total Occurrences: Total number of applications found to have the CWEs mapped to a category. Total CVEs: Total number of CVEs in the NVD DB that were mapped to the CWEs mapped to a category. Formula: (Max Incidence Rate % \ 1000) + (Max Coverage % \ 100) + (Avg Exploit \ 10) + (Avg Impact \ 20) + (Sum Occurrences / 10000) = Risk Score

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A01: Broken Access Control
heading: Description.
text: Access control enforces policy such that users cannot act outside of their intended permissions. Failures typically lead to unauthorized information disclosure, modification or destruction of all data, or performing a business function outside the user's limits. Common access control vulnerabilities include: Violation of the principle of least privilege, commonly known as deny by default, where access should only be granted for particular capabilities, roles, or users, but is available to anyone. Bypassing access control checks by modifying the URL (parameter tampering or force browsing), internal application state, or the HTML page, or by using an attack tool that modifies API requests. Permitting viewing or editing someone else's account by providing its unique identifier (insecure direct object references) An accessible API with missing access controls for POST, PUT, and DELETE. Elevation of privilege. Acting as a user without being logged in or or gaining privileges beyond those expected of the logged in user (e.g. admin access). Metadata manipulation, such as replaying or tampering with a JSON Web Token (JWT) access control token, a cookie or hidden field manipulated to elevate privileges, or abusing JWT invalidation. CORS misconfiguration allows API access from unauthorized or untrusted origins. Force browsing (guessing URLs) to authenticated pages as an unauthenticated user or to privileged pages as a standard user.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A01: Broken Access Control
heading: How to prevent.
text: Access control is only effective when implemented in trusted server-side code or serverless APIs, where the attacker cannot modify the access control check or metadata. Except for public resources, deny by default. Implement access control mechanisms once and reuse them throughout the application, including minimizing Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) usage. Model access controls should enforce record ownership rather than allowing users to create, read, update, or delete any record. Unique application business limit requirements should be enforced by domain models. Disable web server directory listing and ensure file metadata (e.g., .git) and backup files are not present within web roots. Log access control failures, alert admins when appropriate (e.g., repeated failures). Implement rate limits on API and controller access to minimize the harm from automated attack tooling. Stateful session identifiers should be invalidated on the server after logout. Stateless JWT tokens should be short-lived to minimize the window of opportunity for an attacker. For longer-lived JWTs, consider using refresh tokens and following OAuth standards to revoke access. Use well-established toolkits or patterns that provide simple, declarative access controls. Developers and QA staff should include functional access control in their unit and integration tests.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A02: Security Misconfiguration
heading: Description.
text: Security misconfiguration is when a system, application, or cloud service is set up incorrectly from a security perspective, creating vulnerabilities. The application might be vulnerable if: It is missing appropriate security hardening across any part of the application stack or improperly configured permissions on cloud services. Unnecessary features are enabled or installed (e.g., unnecessary ports, services, pages, accounts, testing frameworks, or privileges). Default accounts and their passwords are still enabled and unchanged. A lack of central configuration for intercepting excessive error messages. Error handling reveals stack traces or other overly informative error messages to users. For upgraded systems, the latest security features are disabled or not configured securely. Excessive prioritization of backward compatibility leading to insecure configuration. The security settings in the application servers, application frameworks (e.g., Struts, Spring, ASP.NET), libraries, databases, etc., are not set to secure values. The server does not send security headers or directives, or they are not set to secure values. Without a concerted, repeatable application security configuration hardening process, systems are at a higher risk.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A02: Security Misconfiguration
heading: How to prevent.
text: Secure installation processes should be implemented, including: A repeatable hardening process enabling the fast and easy deployment of another environment that is appropriately locked down. Development, QA, and production environments should all be configured identically, with different credentials used in each environment. This process should be automated to minimize the effort required to set up a new secure environment. A minimal platform without any unnecessary features, components, documentation, or samples. Remove or do not install unused features and frameworks. A task to review and update the configurations appropriate to all security notes, updates, and patches as part of the patch management process (see A03 Software Supply Chain Failures). Review cloud storage permissions (e.g., S3 bucket permissions). A segmented application architecture provides effective and secure separation between components or tenants, with segmentation, containerization, or cloud security groups (ACLs). Sending security directives to clients, e.g., Security Headers. An automated process to verify the effectiveness of the configurations and settings in all environments. Proactively add a central configuration to intercept excessive error messages as a backup. If these verifications are not automated, they should be manually verified annually at a minimum. Use identity federation, short-lived credentials, or role-based access mechanisms provided by the underlying platform instead of embedding static keys or secrets in code, configuration files, or pipelines.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A03: Software Supply Chain Failures
heading: Description.
text: Software supply chain failures are breakdowns or other compromises in the process of building, distributing, or updating software. They are often caused by vulnerabilities or malicious changes in third-party code, tools, or other dependencies that the system relies on. You are likely vulnerable if: you do not carefully track the versions of all components that you use (both client-side and server-side). This includes components you directly use as well as nested (transitive) dependencies. the software is vulnerable, unsupported, or out of date. This includes the OS, web/application server, database management system (DBMS), applications, APIs and all components, runtime environments, and libraries. you do not scan for vulnerabilities regularly and subscribe to security bulletins related to the components you use. you do not have a change management process or tracking of changes within your supply chain, including tracking IDEs, IDE extensions and updates, changes to your organization's code repository, sandboxes, image and library repositories, the way artifacts are created and stored, etc. Every part of your supply chain should be documented, especially changes. you have not hardened every part of your supply chain, with a special focus on access control and the application of least privilege. your supply chain systems do not have any separation of duty. No single person should be able to write code and promote it all the way to production without oversight from another human being. components from untrusted sources, across any part of the tech stack, are used in or can impact on production environments. you do not fix or upgrade the underlying platform, frameworks, and dependencies in a risk-based, timely fashion. This commonly happens in environments when patching is a monthly or quarterly task under change control, leaving organizations open to days or months of unnecessary exposure before fixing vulnerabilities. software developers do not test the compatibility of updated, upgraded, or patched libraries. you do not secure the configurations of every part of your system (see A02:2025-Security Misconfiguration). your CI/CD pipeline has weaker security than the systems it builds and deploys, especially if it is complex.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A04: Cryptographic Failures
heading: Description.
text: Generally speaking, all data in transit should be encrypted at the transport layer (OSI layer 4). Previous hurdles such as CPU performance and private key/certificate management are now handled by CPUs having instructions designed to accelerate encryption (eg: AES support) and private key and certificate management being simplified by services like LetsEncrypt.org with major cloud vendors providing even more tightly integrated certificate management services for their specific platforms. Beyond securing the transport layer, it is important to determine what data needs encryption at rest as well as what data needs extra encryption in transit (at the application layer, OSI layer 7). For example, passwords, credit card numbers, health records, personal information, and business secrets require extra protection, especially if that data falls under privacy laws, e.g., EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), or regulations such as PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS). For all such data: Are any old or weak cryptographic algorithms or protocols used either by default or in older code? Are default crypto keys in use, are weak crypto keys generated, are keys re-used, or is proper key management and rotation missing? Are crypto keys checked into source code repositories? Is encryption not enforced, e.g., are any HTTP headers (browser) security directives or headers missing? Is the received server certificate and the trust chain properly validated? Are initialization vectors ignored, reused, or not generated sufficiently secure for the cryptographic mode of operation? Is an insecure mode of operation such as ECB in use? Is encryption used when authenticated encryption is more appropriate? Are passwords being used as cryptographic keys in the absence of a password based key derivation function? Is randomness used that was not designed to meet cryptographic requirements? Even if the correct function is chosen, does it need to be seeded by the developer, and if not, has the developer over-written the strong seeding functionality built into it with a seed that lacks sufficient entropy/unpredictability? Are deprecated hash functions such as MD5 or SHA1 in use, or are non-cryptographic hash functions used when cryptographic hash functions are needed? Are cryptographic error messages or side channel information exploitable, for example in the form of padding oracle attacks? Can the cryptographic algorithm be downgraded or bypassed?

heading: Description
text: An injection vulnerability is an application flaw that allows untrusted user input to be sent to an interpreter (e.g. a browser, database, the command line) and causes the interpreter to execute parts of that input as commands. An application is vulnerable to attack when: User-supplied data is not validated, filtered, or sanitized by the application. Dynamic queries or non-parameterized calls without context-aware escaping are used directly in the interpreter. Unsanitized data is used within object-relational mapping (ORM) search parameters to extract additional, sensitive records. Potentially hostile data is directly used or concatenated. The SQL or command contains the structure and malicious data in dynamic queries, commands, or stored procedures. Some of the more common injections are SQL, NoSQL, OS command, Object Relational Mapping (ORM), LDAP, and Expression Language (EL) or Object Graph Navigation Library (OGNL) injection. The concept is identical among all interpreters. Detection is best achieved by a combination of source code review along with automated testing (including fuzzing) of all parameters, headers, URL, cookies, JSON, SOAP, and XML data inputs. The addition of static (SAST), dynamic (DAST), and interactive (IAST) application security testing tools into the CI/CD pipeline can also be helpful to identify injection flaws before production deployment.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A06: Insecure Design
heading: Description
text: Insecure design is a broad category representing different weaknesses, expressed as “missing or ineffective control design.” Insecure design is not the source for all other Top Ten risk categories. Note that there is a difference between insecure design and insecure implementation. We differentiate between design flaws and implementation defects for a reason, they have different root causes, take place at different times in the development process, and have different remediations. A secure design can still have implementation defects leading to vulnerabilities that may be exploited. An insecure design cannot be fixed by a perfect implementation as needed security controls were never created to defend against specific attacks. One of the factors that contributes to insecure design is the lack of business risk profiling inherent in the software or system being developed, and thus the failure to determine what level of security design is required. Three key parts of having a secure design are: Gathering Requirements and Resource Management Creating a Secure Design Having a Secure Development Lifecycle

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A07: Authentication Failures
heading: Description
text: When an attacker is able to trick a system into recognizing an invalid or incorrect user as legitimate, this vulnerability is present. There may be authentication weaknesses if the application: Permits automated attacks such as credential stuffing, where the attacker has a breached list of valid usernames and passwords. More recently this type of attack has been expanded to include hybrid password attacks credential stuffing (also known as password spray attacks), where the attacker uses variations or increments of spilled credentials to gain access, for instance trying Password1!, Password2!, Password3! and so on. Permits brute force or other automated, scripted attacks that are not quickly blocked. Permits default, weak, or well-known passwords, such as "Password1" or "admin" username with an "admin" password. Allows users to create new accounts with already known-breached credentials. Allows use of weak or ineffective credential recovery and forgot-password processes, such as "knowledge-based answers," which cannot be made safe. Uses plain text, encrypted, or weakly hashed passwords data stores (see A04:2025-Cryptographic Failures). Has missing or ineffective multi-factor authentication. Allows use of weak or ineffective fallbacks if multi-factor authentication is not available. Exposes session identifier in the URL, a hidden field, or another insecure location that is accessible to the client. Reuses the same session identifier after successful login. Does not correctly invalidate user sessions or authentication tokens (mainly single sign-on (SSO) tokens) during logout or a period of inactivity. Does not correctly assert the scope and intended audience of the provided credentials.

heading: A08: Software or Data Integrity Failures

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A08: Software or Data Integrity Failures
heading: Description
text: Software and data integrity failures relate to code and infrastructure that does not protect against invalid or untrusted code or data being treated as trusted and valid. An example of this is where an application relies upon plugins, libraries, or modules from untrusted sources, repositories, and content delivery networks (CDNs). An insecure CI/CD pipeline without consuming and providing software integrity checks can introduce the potential for unauthorized access, insecure or malicious code, or system compromise. Another example of this is a CI/CD that pulls code or artifacts from untrusted places and/or doesn’t verify them before use (by checking the signature or similar mechanism). Lastly, many applications now include auto-update functionality, where updates are downloaded without sufficient integrity verification and applied to the previously trusted application. Attackers could potentially upload their own updates to be distributed and run on all installations. Another example is where objects or data are encoded or serialized into a structure that an attacker can see and modify is vulnerable to insecure deserialization.

heading: How To Prevent
text: Use digital signatures or similar mechanisms to verify the software or data is from the expected source and has not been altered. Ensure libraries and dependencies, such as npm or Maven, are only consuming trusted repositories. If you have a higher risk profile, consider hosting an internal known-good repository that's vetted. Ensure that there is a review process for code and configuration changes to minimize the chance that malicious code or configuration could be introduced into your software pipeline. Ensure that your CI/CD pipeline has proper segregation, configuration, and access control to ensure the integrity of the code flowing through the build and deploy processes. Ensure that unsigned or unencrypted serialized data is not received from untrusted clients and subsequently used without some form of integrity check or digital signature to detect tampering or replay of the serialized data.

heading: A09: Security Logging and Alerting Failure
Description
text: Without logging and monitoring, attacks and breaches cannot be detected, and without alerting it is very difficult to respond quickly and effectively during a security incident. Insufficient logging, continuous monitoring, detection, and alerting to initiate active responses occurs any time: Auditable events, such as logins, failed logins, and high-value transactions, are not logged or logged inconsistently (for instance, only logging successful logins, but not failed attempts). Warnings and errors generate no, inadequate, or unclear log messages. The integrity of logs is not properly protected from tampering. Logs of applications and APIs are not monitored for suspicious activity. Logs are only stored locally, and not properly backedup. Appropriate alerting thresholds and response escalation processes are not in place or effective. Alerts are not received or reviewed within a reasonable amount of time. Penetration testing and scans by dynamic application security testing (DAST) tools (such as Burp or ZAP) do not trigger alerts. The application cannot detect, escalate, or alert for active attacks in real-time or near real-time. You are vulnerable to sensitive information leakage by making logging and alerting events visible to a user or an attacker (see A01:2025-Broken Access Control), or by logging sensitive information that should not be logged (such as PII or PHI). You are vulnerable to injections or attacks on the logging or monitoring systems if log data is not correctly encoded. The application is missing or mishandling errors and other exceptional conditions, such that the system is unaware there was an error, and is therefore unable to log there was a problem. Adequate ‘use cases’ for issuing alerts are missing or outdated to recognize a special situation. Too many false positive alerts make it impossible to distinguish important alerts from unimportant ones, resulting in them being recognized too late or not at all (physical overload of the SOC team). Detected alerts cannot be processed correctly because the playbook for the use case is incomplete, out of date, or missing.

topic: DevOps vs DevSecOps › A10: Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
heading: Description
text: Mishandling exceptional conditions in software happens when programs fail to prevent, detect, and respond to unusual and unpredictable situations, which leads to crashes, unexpected behavior, and sometimes vulnerabilities. This can involve one or more of the following 3 failings; the application doesn’t prevent an unusual situation from happening, it doesn’t identify the situation as it is happening, and/or it responds poorly or not at all to the situation afterwards. Exceptional conditions can be caused by missing, poor, or incomplete input validation, or late, high level error handling instead at the functions where they occur, or unexpected environmental states such as memory, privilege, or network issues, inconsistent exception handling, or exceptions that are not handled at all, allowing the system to fall into an unknown and unpredictable state. Any time an application is unsure of its next instruction, an exceptional condition has been mishandled. Hard-to-find errors and exceptions can threaten the security of the whole application for a long time. Many different security vulnerabilities can happen when we mishandle exceptional conditions, such as logic bugs, overflows, race conditions, fraudulent transactions, or issues with memory, state, resource, timing, authentication, and authorization. These types of vulnerabilities can negatively affect the confidentiality, availability, and/or integrity of a system or it’s data. Attackers manipulate an application's flawed error handling to strike this vulnerability.

heading: Syntax Writing Order:
text: When writing a SELECT statement in ⁠PostgreSQL, clauses must be written in this exact sequence: SELECT column\_list FROM table\_name JOIN other\_table ON condition WHERE row\_filter\_conditions GROUP BY grouping\_columns HAVING group\_filter\_conditions WINDOW window\_name AS (window\_spec) ORDER BY sorting\_columns LIMIT number\_of\_rows OFFSET number\_to\_skip;

heading: Clauses Execution Order:
text: STEP CLAUSE PostgreSQL Execution - - - 1. FROM/JOIN Selects the base tables and merges them to create the initial dataset. 2. WHERE Filters out rows that do not meet individual conditions. 3. GROUP BY Collapses the remaining individual rows into groups. 4. HAVING Filters out aggregated groups that do not meet specified criteria. 5. WINDOW Executes window functions (like ROW\_NUMBER()) over the grouped data. 6. SELECT Emits the final columns and evaluates expressions or structural aliases. 7. DISTINCT Scans the columns to eliminate any duplicate result rows. 8. ORDER BY Sorts the final result set in ascending or descending order. 9. LIMIT/OFFSET Trims the result set to skip a specific number of rows or keep only the top rows. Alias Visibility: Because SELECT runs after WHERE and GROUP BY, you cannot use column aliases inside those clauses. For example, SELECT price \ 2 AS double\_price ... WHERE double\_price > 10 will throw an error. ORDER BY Capabilities: Because ORDER BY executes after SELECT, you can use your SELECT aliases or positional numbers (like ORDER BY 1) to sort your data. WHERE vs. HAVING: Use WHERE to filter raw rows before aggregation, and use HAVING only to filter aggregated values (like COUNT(\) or SUM()).

heading: AGGREGATE FUNCTIONS
text: The five most used SQL aggregate functions are COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), and MAX(). General Syntax Structure Aggregate functions are generally placed in the SELECT list and are frequently paired with a GROUP BY clause to summarize categories. SELECT column\_name, AGGREGATE\_FUNCTION(column\_to\_aggregate)   FROM table\_name   WHERE condition   GROUP BY column\_name   HAVING AGGREGATE\_FUNCTION(column\_to\_aggregate) > value; General-Purpose Aggregates COUNT(\): Counts total input rows. COUNT(expression): Counts rows with non-null values. SUM(expression): Calculates the total of numeric values. AVG(expression): Computes the arithmetic mean. MIN(expression): Finds the minimum value. MAX(expression): Finds the maximum value. ARRAY\_AGG(expression): Concatenates input values into an array. STRING\_AGG(expression, delimiter): Concatenates values into a single string. JSON\_AGG(expression): Aggregates rows into a JSON array. JSONB\_AGG(expression): Aggregates rows into a JSONB array. JSON\_OBJECT\_AGG(key, value): Aggregates key-value pairs into a JSON object. JSONB\_OBJECT\_AGG(key, value): Aggregates key-value pairs into a JSONB object. BOOL\_AND(expression): Returns true if all values are true. BOOL\_OR(expression): Returns true if any value is true. EVERY(expression): Identical equivalent to BOOL\_AND. XMLAGG(expression): Concatenates XML values across input rows. Statistical Aggregates STDDEV(expression): Alias for sample standard deviation. STDDEV\_SAMP(expression): Computes sample standard deviation. STDDEV\_POP(expression): Computes population standard deviation. VARIANCE(expression): Alias for sample variance. VAR\_SAMP(expression): Computes sample variance. VAR\_POP(expression): Computes population variance. CORR(Y, X): Computes the correlation coefficient. COVAR\_POP(Y, X): Computes population covariance. COVAR\_SAMP(Y, X): Computes sample covariance. Linear Regression Aggregates REGR\_COUNT(Y, X): Counts rows where both inputs are non-null. REGR\_AVGX(Y, X): Computes independent variable average. REGR\_AVGY(Y, X): Computes dependent variable average. REGR\_SLOPE(Y, X): Computes the least-squares-fit slope. REGR\_INTERCEPT(Y, X): Computes the y-intercept value. REGR\_R2(Y, X): Computes the square of correlation coefficient. REGR\_SXX(Y, X): Computes independent "sum of squares". REGR\_SYY(Y, X): Computes dependent "sum of squares". REGR\_SXY(Y, X): Computes "sum of products".

heading: EXTRACT & CASE
text: The EXTRACT() function retrieves specific subfields (like year, month, day, hour, or minute) from a date, time, timestamp, or interval value. It returns a value of type numeric (or double precision in older versions) Common Field Subfields YEAR: The full calendar year. QUARTER: The quarter of the year (1 to 4). MONTH: The month number (1 to 12). DAY: The day of the month (1 to 31). DOW: The day of the week (0 = Sunday, 1 = Monday, ..., 6 = Saturday). ISODOW: The ISO 8601 day of the week (1 = Monday, ..., 7 = Sunday). DOY: The day of the year (1 to 365/366). HOUR: The hour component (0 to 23). MINUTE: The minute component (0 to 59). SECOND: The seconds component, including fractional seconds. EPOCH: The total number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. Examples: SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM TIMESTAMP '2026-07-18 14:30:15') AS order\_year,   EXTRACT(MONTH FROM TIMESTAMP '2026-07-18 14:30:15') AS order\_month,   EXTRACT(DAY FROM TIMESTAMP '2026-07-18 14:30:15') AS order\_day; SELECT EXTRACT(HOUR FROM CURRENT\_TIMESTAMP) AS current\_hour; SELECT \   FROM transactions   WHERE EXTRACT(MONTH FROM transaction\_date) = 5; 2. The CASE expression function acts like an if-then-else statement to add conditional logic directly inside your SQL queries. It runs through conditions in order and returns a value as soon as the first condition is met. Example-1: SELECT   product\_name,   price,   CASE   WHEN price < 10 THEN 'Budget'   WHEN price BETWEEN 10 AND 50 THEN 'Normal'   ELSE 'Premium'   END AS price\_category FROM products; Example-2: SELECT   employee\_name,   department\_id,   CASE department\_id   WHEN 1 THEN 'Engineering'   WHEN 2 THEN 'Marketing'   WHEN 3 THEN 'Sales'   ELSE 'Other'   END AS department\_name FROM employees; Advanced Placement: You are not limited to using CASE in SELECT lists. You can place it inside other clauses. You can embed a CASE expression in almost any statement or clause that accepts a value, column name, or logic check. SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, JOIN (specifically ON) Clauses, SET Clause (in UPDATE Statements, VALUES Clause (in INSERT Statements),Nested inside another CASE Expression.

heading: GENERATE_SERIES
text: GENERATE\_SERIES() generate\_series() is a built-in Set Returning Function (SRF) used to create ordered lists of numbers, dates, or timestamps on the fly. It behaves like a virtual table, making it highly effective for generating test data, filling missing gaps in reporting timelines, or replacing programmatic loops. Syntax Overview: generate\_series(start, stop \[, step]) start: The beginning value of your sequence. stop: The termination limit; the sequence will not cross this value. step: (Optional) The increment/decrement size. Defaults to 1 for numeric data types. Basic Examples: Generating Numbers: You can generate a sequential list of integers, bigints, or numeric fractions. Default step (1): SELECT \ FROM generate\_series(1, 5); -- Returns: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Custom step: SELECT \ FROM generate\_series(10, 50, 10); -- Returns: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 Counting backwards (Requires a negative step): SELECT \ FROM generate\_series(5, 1, -1); -- Returns: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1   2. Generating Dates \& Timestamps: When generating time series, the step parameter must be specified as an INTERVAL. Daily interval: SELECT generate\_series(   '2026-07-01'::timestamp,   '2026-07-05'::timestamp,   '1 day'::interval   ) AS days; Hourly interval: SELECT generate\_series(   '2026-07-19 00:00'::timestamp,   '2026-07-19 04:00'::timestamp,   '1 hour'::interval   ) AS hours;

heading: TO_CHAR, TRIM
text: 1\. TO\_CHAR() converts data types like dates, timestamps, or numbers into formatted text strings. The TO\_CHAR() function formats timestamp, interval, integer, float, or numeric data into structured text based on a template. Syntax: TO\_CHAR(value, 'format\_pattern') Common Examples Format Current Date: Formats a date into a standard YYYY-MM-DD layout. SELECT TO\_CHAR(CURRENT\_DATE, 'YYYY-MM-DD'); -- Result: '2026-07-19' Format Time with AM/PM: Extracts 12-hour formatted time with minutes and indicators. SELECT TO\_CHAR(NOW(), 'HH12:MI AM'); -- Result: '05:29 PM' Format Currency \& Decimals: Rounds numbers and maps local currency or thousands separators. SELECT TO\_CHAR(12345.67, '$99,999.99'); -- Result: ' $12,345.67' 2\. The TRIM() Function The TRIM() function strips blank spaces or designated unwanted characters from the edges of text strings. Syntax: TRIM(\[LEADING TRAILING BOTH] \[characters] FROM string) Note: If no positioning or character targets are passed, it defaults to stripping spaces from BOTH ends. Common Examples: Remove Surrounding Spaces: Cleans white space off both sides. SELECT TRIM(' hello world '); -- Result: 'hello world' Remove Leading Characters Only: Strips target elements from the start. SELECT TRIM(LEADING '0' FROM '00012345'); -- Result: '12345' Remove Specific Multi-Character Sets: Strips any matching character from the edge sets. SELECT TRIM(BOTH 'xyz' FROM 'xyxTomxx'); -- Result: 'Tom'

heading: ROLL_UP
text: ROLLUP is a subclause of the GROUP BY clause that allows you to calculate multiple levels of subtotals and a grand total within a single query. It generates hierarchical grouping sets based on the order of the columns provided, reducing the columns from right to left. How ROLLUP Works: When you pass columns to ROLLUP(c1, c2, c3), PostgreSQL assumes a hierarchy where c1 > c2 > c3. It will automatically compute aggregates for the following combinations: (c1, c2, c3) — Detailed group totals. (c1, c2) — Subtotals for each combination of c1 and c2. (c1) — Subtotals for each c1. () — Grand total across the entire table. Basic Syntax: SELECT column1, column2, SUM(column3)   FROM table\_name   GROUP BY ROLLUP (column1, column2); Examples: 1. Consider a sales table containing regional sales data:   region category amount - - - North Electronics 1000 North Electronics 500 South Furniture 1500   SELECT region, category, SUM(amount) AS total\_sales   FROM sales   GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, category)   ORDER BY region, category; Expected Output: region category total\_sales Explanation - - - - North Electronics 1000 Normal Group North Furniture 500 Normal Group North NULL 1500 North Region Subtotal South Electronics 1500 Normal Group South NULL 1500 South Region Subtotal NULL NULL 3000 Grand Total Differentiating NULLs with GROUPING(): When using ROLLUP, rows containing subtotals output a NULL for the columns that have been rolled up. To avoid confusion between a natural NULL in your data and a NULL generated by ROLLUP, you can use the GROUPING() function: SELECT   CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'All Regions' ELSE region END as region,   CASE WHEN GROUPING(category) = 1 THEN 'All Categories' ELSE category END as category,   SUM(amount) AS total\_sales   FROM sales   GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, category); Partial ROLLUP: If you want a grand total and specific subtotals but don't want to roll up every single column, you can leave columns outside the ROLLUP function: GROUP BY region, ROLLUP(category); -- This skips the individual category breakdown subtotals

heading: WINDOW Functions
text: PostgreSQL window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them into a single output row. The basic syntax requires an OVER clause, which controls how rows are grouped (PARTITION BY) and sorted (ORDER BY): SELECT column, function() OVER (PARTITION BY group\_col ORDER BY sort\_col) FROM table; Ranking Functions: These functions assign numerical rankings or sequential positions to rows within a partition. ROW\_NUMBER(): Assigns a unique sequential integer to each row starting at 1. RANK(): Assigns rankings with gaps for duplicate values (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE\_RANK(): Assigns rankings without any gaps for duplicate values (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 3). PERCENT\_RANK(): Calculates the relative rank of a row as a percentage between 0 and 1. CUME\_DIST(): Calculates the cumulative distribution of a value (relative position) within the partition. NTILE(num\_buckets): Splits rows into a specific number of approximately equal buckets and assigns a bucket ID. Value \& Offset Functions: These functions allow you to grab values from other rows without performing complex self-joins. LAG(col, offset, default): Fetches data from a previous row at a specific offset. LEAD(col, offset, default): Fetches data from a subsequent row at a specific offset. FIRST\_VALUE(col): Returns the value from the very first row in the window frame. LAST\_VALUE(col): Returns the value from the very last row in the window frame. NTH\_VALUE(col, n): Returns the value from the exact n-th row in the window frame. Aggregate Functions (Used as Window Functions): Standard aggregate functions automatically act as window functions when paired with an OVER clause. Instead of a total summary, they produce running calculations. SUM(col): Computes running totals. AVG(col): Computes moving averages. COUNT(col): Computes cumulative counts. MIN(col) / MAX(col): Finds the lowest or highest value in the window.

heading: Basic-Queries
text: ###Retrieve everything from a table: How can you retrieve all the information from the cd.facilities table? Ans. SELECT FROM cd.facilities; ###Retrieve specific columns from a table: You want to print out a list of all of the facilities and their cost to members. How would you retrieve a list of only facility names and costs? Ans: SELECT name, membercost FROM cd.facilities; ###Control which rows are retrieved: How can you produce a list of facilities that charge a fee to members? Ans: SELECT FROM cd.facilities WHERE membercost != 0; ###Control which rows are retrieved - part 2: How can you produce a list of facilities that charge a fee to members, and that fee is less than 1/50th of the monthly maintenance cost? Return the facid, facility name, member cost, and monthly maintenance of the facilities in question. Ans: SELECT facid, name, membercost, monthlymaintenance FROM cd.facilities WHERE membercost != 0 AND membercost < (monthlymaintenance / 50); ###Basic string searches: How can you produce a list of all facilities with the word 'Tennis' in their name? Ans. SELECT FROM cd.facilities WHERE name LIKE '%Tennis%'; ###Matching against multiple possible values: How can you retrieve the details of facilities with ID 1 and 5? Try to do it without using the OR operator. Ans: SELECT FROM cd.facilities WHERE facid IN (1, 5); ###Classify results into buckets: How can you produce a list of facilities, with each labelled as 'cheap' or 'expensive' depending on if their monthly maintenance cost is more than $100? Return the name and monthly maintenance of the facilities in question. Ans: SELECT name, CASE WHEN monthlymaintenance < 100 THEN 'cheap' ELSE 'expensive' END AS cost FROM cd.facilities; ###Working with dates: How can you produce a list of members who joined after the start of September 2012? Return the memid, surname, firstname, and joindate of the members in question. Ans: SELECT memid, surname, firstname, joindate FROM cd.members WHERE joindate > '2012-09-01'; ###Removing duplicates, and ordering results: How can you produce an ordered list of the first 10 surnames in the members table? The list must not contain duplicates. Ans: SELECT DISTINCT surname FROM cd.members ORDER BY surname LIMIT 10; ###Combining results from multiple queries: You, for some reason, want a combined list of all surnames and all facility names. Yes, this is a contrived example :-). Produce that list! Ans: SELECT surname FROM cd.members UNION SELECT name FROM cd.facilities AS surname; ###Simple aggregation: You'd like to get the signup date of your last member. How can you retrieve this information? Ans: SELECT MAX(joindate) AS latest FROM cd.members; ###More aggregation: You'd like to get the first and last name of the last member(s) who signed up - not just the date. How can you do that? Ans: SELECT firstname, surname, joindate FROM cd.members WHERE joindate = (SELECT MAX(joindate) FROM cd.members);

heading: Joins&SubQueries
text: Retrieve the start times of members' bookings: How can you produce a list of the start times for bookings by members named 'David Farrell'? Ans: SELECT starttime FROM cd.bookings bk INNER JOIN cd.members mems ON (bk.memid = mems.memid) WHERE mems.firstname = 'David' AND mems.surname = 'Farrell'; SELECT starttime FROM cd.bookings WHERE memid = (SELECT memid FROM cd.members WHERE firstname = 'David' and surname = 'Farrell'); Work out the start times of bookings for tennis courts: How can you produce a list of the start times for bookings for tennis courts, for the date '2012-09-21'? Return a list of start time and facility name pairings, ordered by the time. Ans: SELECT bks.starttime AS start, facs.name AS name FROM cd.facilities facs INNER JOIN cd.bookings bks ON (bks.facid = facs.facid) WHERE facs.name LIKE '%Tennis Court%' AND bks.starttime >= '2012-09-21' AND bks.starttime <= '2012-09-22' ORDER BY start; Produce a list of all members who have recommended another member:How can you output a list of all members who have recommended another member? Ensure that there are no duplicates in the list, and that results are ordered by (surname, firstname). Ans: SELECT DISTINCT mems1.firstname, mems1.surname FROM cd.members mems1 INNER JOIN cd.members mems2 ON (mems1.memid = mems2.recommendedby) ORDER BY surname, firstname; Produce a list of all members, along with their recommender: How can you output a list of all members, including the individual who recommended them (if any)? Ensure that results are ordered by (surname, firstname). Ans: SELECT mems.firstname AS memfname, mems.surname AS memsname, recs.firstname AS recfname, recs.surname AS recsname FROM cd.members mems LEFT OUTER JOIN cd.members recs ON (mems.recommendedby = recs.memid) ORDER BY memsname, memfname; Produce a list of all members who have used a tennis court: How can you produce a list of all members who have used a tennis court? Include in your output the name of the court, and the name of the member formatted as a single column. Ensure no duplicate data, and order by the member name followed by the facility name. heading: Common Table Expressions allow us to, effectively, create our own temporary tables for the duration of a query - they're largely a convenience to help us make more readable SQL. Using the WITH RECURSIVE modifier, however, it's possible for us to create recursive queries. This is enormously advantageous for working with tree and graph-structured data - imagine retrieving all of the relations of a graph node to a given depth, for example.
This category shows you some basic recursive queries that are possible using our dataset.

Return member ID and name, and order by ascending member id. Ans. WITH RECURSIVE recommendeds(memid) AS (   SELECT memid FROM cd.members WHERE recommendedby = 1     UNION ALL     SELECT mems.memid FROM recommendeds recs   INNER JOIN cd.members mems ON (mems.recommendedby = recs.memid) ) SELECT recs.memid, mems.firstname, mems.surname FROM recommendeds recs INNER JOIN cd.members mems ON (recs.memid = mems.memid) ORDER BY memid; 3. text: A concise guide to the five core building blocks of React: JSX, Functional Components, Props & State, Conditional Rendering, and Lists & Keys. Examples use modern React (18+) with function components and Hooks. ---

heading: 1. JSX
text:
JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. It is not required by React, but it is the standard way to describe UI. Build tools (Babel, Vite, etc.) compile it into plain JavaScript calls. const element =

Hello, React!

; // Compiles to roughly: const element = React.createElement("h1", null, "Hello, React!");

heading: Rules of components
text: Name them in PascalCase (UserCard, not userCard). Keep them pure: given the same props and state, return the same JSX. Don't mutate props or external variables while rendering. Never define a component inside another component. It is re-created on every render and loses its state. Prefer small, single-purpose components. ---

heading: State rules
text: 1. Never mutate state directly. Always use the setter. count = count + 1; // ❌ won't trigger a re-render setCount(count + 1); // ✅ 2. Updating from the previous value? Use the functional form. setCount((prev) => prev + 1); // ✅ always uses the latest value 3. Treat objects and arrays as immutable. Create new copies. const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: "Asha", age: 24 }); setUser({ ...user, age: 25 }); // ✅ object const [items, setItems] = useState([1, 2]); setItems([...items, 3]); // ✅ add setItems(items.filter((i) => i !== 2)); // ✅ remove setItems(items.map((i) => (i === 1 ? 10 : i))); // ✅ update 4. State updates are asynchronous (batched). The state variable doesn't change until the next render. setCount(count + 1); console.log(count); // still the OLD value 5. Keep state minimal. If a value can be computed from existing state or props, compute it during render instead of storing it.

heading: Component Architecture
text: This guide covers three topics: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components Lifting State Up Component Modularity & Composition ---

heading: 1. Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
text: Form elements ( , , ) naturally keep their own value in the DOM. React gives you two ways to handle that value. Controlled Uncontrolled --- --- --- Source of truth React state The DOM Reading the value From state, at any time From a ref, when needed (usually on submit) Updating onChange → setState The browser handles it Re-renders per keystroke Yes No Initial value value defaultValue

topic: Component Architecture › 1. Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
heading: Controlled components
text: The input's value is driven by React state. Every change goes through a handler, so React always knows the current value. import { useState } from "react"; function SignupForm() { const [email, setEmail] = useState(""); const handleSubmit = (e) => { e.preventDefault(); console.log("Submitted:", email); }; return ( <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> <input type="email" value={email} // value comes from state onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} // state updates on every change /> <button type="submit">Sign up</button> </form> ); } Multiple fields with one handler: function ProfileForm() { const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: "", email: "", role: "dev" }); const handleChange = (e) => { const { name, value } = e.target; setForm((prev) => ({ ...prev, [name]: value })); }; return ( <form> <input name="name" value={form.name} onChange={handleChange} /> <input name="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} /> <select name="role" value={form.role} onChange={handleChange}> <option value="dev">Developer</option> <option value="design">Designer</option> </select> </form> ); } Checkboxes use checked, not value: <input type="checkbox" checked={isSubscribed} onChange={(e) => setIsSubscribed(e.target.checked)} /> Why choose controlled: Instant validation and formatting as the user types Enable or disable buttons based on input Reset or prefill the form by setting state Keep multiple inputs in sync One predictable source of truth Trade-offs: more boilerplate, and a re-render on each keystroke (rarely a problem unless the form is very large).

topic: Component Architecture › 1. Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
heading: Uncontrolled components
text: The DOM holds the value. You read it with a ref when you need it. import { useRef } from "react"; function SearchForm() { const inputRef = useRef(null); const handleSubmit = (e) => { e.preventDefault(); console.log("Searching:", inputRef.current.value); }; return ( <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> <input ref={inputRef} defaultValue="" /> <button type="submit">Search</button> </form> ); } Reading all fields with FormData: function ContactForm() { const handleSubmit = (e) => { e.preventDefault(); const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(e.target)); console.log(data); // { name: "...", message: "..." } }; return ( <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> <input name="name" defaultValue="" /> <textarea name="message" defaultValue="" /> <button type="submit">Send</button> </form> ); } File inputs are always uncontrolled, because their value is read-only: <input type="file" ref={fileRef} /> // fileRef.current.files[0] Why choose uncontrolled: Simple forms where you only need values on submit Less code and no re-render per keystroke File inputs Integrating with non-React code Trade-offs: you can't easily validate live, transform input as it's typed, or drive other UI from the value.

topic: Component Architecture › 1. Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components

Never switch an input between controlled and uncontrolled during its life. Initialize state with "", not undefined: const [name, setName] = useState(); // ❌ undefined → uncontrolled, then controlled const [name, setName] = useState(""); // ✅ always controlled

heading: 2. Lifting State Up
text: When two or more components need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent and pass it down through props. The parent becomes the single source of truth, and children communicate changes back through callback props. Parent (owns state) / \ value ↓ ↓ value ChildA ChildB ↑ onChange (callback)

heading: The problem
text: Sibling components can't share state directly. Each keeps its own copy, so they drift out of sync. function CelsiusInput() { const [temp, setTemp] = useState(""); // local to this component return <input value={temp} onChange={(e) => setTemp(e.target.value)} />; } function FahrenheitInput() { const [temp, setTemp] = useState(""); // a separate copy: not synced! return <input value={temp} onChange={(e) => setTemp(e.target.value)} />; }

heading: The solution: lift the state
text: Step 1: Make the children controlled by props. Remove their local state. Step 2: Move the state to the parent. Step 3: Pass the value and a change handler down. function TemperatureInput({ label, value, onChange }) { return ( <label> {label} <input value={value} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)} /> </label> ); } const toFahrenheit = (c) => (c * 9) / 5 + 32; const toCelsius = (f) => ((f - 32) * 5) / 9; function Converter() { // Single source of truth: store only Celsius const [celsius, setCelsius] = useState(""); const fahrenheit = celsius === "" ? "" : toFahrenheit(Number(celsius)).toFixed(1); const handleFahrenheitChange = (f) => setCelsius(f === "" ? "" : toCelsius(Number(f)).toFixed(1)); return ( <> <TemperatureInput label="Celsius" value={celsius} onChange={setCelsius} /> <TemperatureInput label="Fahrenheit" value={fahrenheit} onChange={handleFahrenheitChange} /> </> ); } Both inputs always agree because they read from one state. Note that fahrenheit is derived during render, not stored separately.

A child can't change the parent's state directly. It calls a function the parent passed down. function Product({ product, onAddToCart }) { return (

{product.name}

); } function Shop() { const [cart, setCart] = useState([]); const addToCart = (product) => setCart((prev) => [...prev, product]); return ( <> {/* sibling reads the same state */} ); }

heading: Guidelines
text: Lift state to the closest common ancestor, no higher than necessary. Keep one source of truth per piece of data. Don't duplicate it in multiple places. Derive values instead of storing them when they can be computed from existing state or props. Name callback props with on... (onChange, onSubmit) and handlers with handle.... Data flows down (props), events flow up (callbacks). This is React's one-way data flow.

heading: Warning signs
text: Symptom Likely cause --- --- Two components show inconsistent data Duplicated state, so lift it up Props passed through many layers that don't use them Prop drilling: restructure with composition (see section 3) A parent re-renders and slows down State lifted higher than needed; move it closer to where it's used ---

heading: Avoiding prop drilling with composition
text: Instead of passing props through layers that don't use them, pass the finished element down. // ❌ Prop drilling: Page and Header only forward `user` <Page user={user} /> // → <Header user={user} /> → <Avatar user={user} /> // ✅ Composition: build the element at the top and pass it in function App() { const user = useUser(); return <Page header={<Header avatar={<Avatar user={user} />} />} />; } Intermediate components stay simple and no longer need to know about user.

heading: Best practices
text: Prefer props and composition over deep conditionals and giant components. Keep components presentational (UI only) where possible, and place data fetching and logic in parents or hooks. Give props clear, descriptive names, and set sensible defaults. Spread extra props (...rest) onto the root element so consumers can customize. Avoid over-abstraction: don't create a reusable component until you actually reuse it (roughly the "rule of three"). Colocate files (component, styles, tests) that change together.

heading: Component design checklist
text: [ ] Does it do one job? [ ] Is it configurable through props? [ ] Can I name it clearly? [ ] Is the state as low in the tree as it can be (but high enough to be shared)? heading: React Hooks
text: Hooks let function components use state, side effects, refs, and shared data. This guide covers five essentials: useState useEffect useRef Context API (useContext) Custom Hooks ---

heading: 1. useState
text: Adds state to a function component. When state changes, the component re-renders. import { useState } from "react"; const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue);

heading: Basic example
text:
function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return (

Count: {count}

); }

heading: Functional updates
text: When the new value depends on the previous one, pass a function. It always receives the latest value. setCount((prev) => prev + 1);

heading: Lazy initial state
text: If the initial value is expensive to compute, pass a function. It runs only on the first render. const [data, setData] = useState(() => JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("data")) ?? []);

heading: Objects and arrays: never mutate, always copy
text: const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: "Asha", age: 24 }); setUser((prev) => ({ ...prev, age: 25 })); // update object const [items, setItems] = useState([]); setItems((prev) => [...prev, "new"]); // add setItems((prev) => prev.filter((i) => i !== "old")); // remove setItems((prev) => prev.map((i) => (i.id === 1 ? { ...i, done: true } : i))); // update

heading: Key points
text: The setter replaces state. For objects, spread the old values yourself. Updates are batched and asynchronous: the variable keeps its old value until the next render. Calling the setter with the same value skips the re-render. Call useState at the top level of a component, never inside loops or conditions. ---

heading: 2. useEffect
text: Runs side effects after render: data fetching, subscriptions, timers, DOM updates, and syncing with external systems. import { useEffect } from "react"; useEffect(() => { // effect code return () => { // optional cleanup }; }, [dependencies]);

heading: The dependency array
text: Dependency array When the effect runs --- --- Omitted After every render [] Once, after the first render (mount) [a, b] After the first render and whenever a or b changes useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count}`; }); // every render useEffect(() => { console.log("Mounted"); }, []); // mount only useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count}`; }, [count]); // when count changes

heading: Cleanup
text:
The returned function runs before the next effect and when the component unmounts. Use it to avoid leaks. function Clock() { const [time, setTime] = useState(new Date()); useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setTime(new Date()), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); // cleanup }, []); return

{time.toLocaleTimeString()}

; } Event listeners follow the same pattern: useEffect(() => { const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth); window.addEventListener("resize", onResize); return () => window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize); }, []);

Error: {error}

{user.name}

; } The effect callback cannot be async directly. Define an async function inside it, or use promises as above.

heading: Key points
text: Include every reactive value (props, state, functions) used inside the effect in the dependency array. Missing dependencies cause stale values. Unstable dependencies (new objects/functions each render) cause infinite loops. Don't use effects for things you can calculate during render or handle in an event handler. In development with Strict Mode, effects run twice on mount to help you catch missing cleanup. This does not happen in production.

heading: 3. useRef
text: Returns a mutable object { current: value } that persists across renders. Changing it does not trigger a re-render. import { useRef } from "react"; const ref = useRef(initialValue); ref.current; // read or write

heading: Use case 1: Access a DOM element

Timers, previous values, counters, and flags are good candidates. function Stopwatch() { const [seconds, setSeconds] = useState(0); const intervalRef = useRef(null); const start = () => { if (intervalRef.current) return; intervalRef.current = setInterval(() => setSeconds((s) => s + 1), 1000); }; const stop = () => { clearInterval(intervalRef.current); intervalRef.current = null; }; return (

{seconds}s

); }

heading: Use case 3: Track the previous value
text: function usePrevious(value) { const ref = useRef(); useEffect(() => { ref.current = value; }, [value]); return ref.current; // value from the previous render }

text: useState useRef --- --- --- Triggers re-render on change ✅ Yes ❌ No Persists across renders ✅ ✅ Use for Data shown in the UI DOM access, timers, values the UI doesn't display Update style Via setter Mutate ref.current directly

heading: Key points
text: Don't read or write ref.current during rendering (except for initial setup). Do it in event handlers or effects. ref.current is null until the element mounts. If the UI needs to show the value, use state, not a ref. ---

heading: 4. Context API (useContext)
text: Shares data across the component tree without passing props through every level (avoids "prop drilling").

heading: The three steps
text: 1. Create the context import { createContext } from "react"; export const ThemeContext = createContext("light"); // default value 2. Provide a value import { useState } from "react"; export function ThemeProvider({ children }) { const [theme, setTheme] = useState("light"); const toggleTheme = () => setTheme((t) => (t === "light" ? "dark" : "light")); return ( <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, toggleTheme }}> {children} </ThemeContext.Provider> ); } 3. Consume it with useContext import { useContext } from "react"; function ThemeButton() { const { theme, toggleTheme } = useContext(ThemeContext); return ( <button onClick={toggleTheme}> Current: {theme}. Click to switch. </button> ); } Wrap your app: function App() { return ( <ThemeProvider> <Header /> <ThemeButton /> </ThemeProvider> ); }

heading: Recommended pattern: wrap in a custom hook
text: Cleaner imports and a helpful error when used outside the provider. export function useTheme() { const context = useContext(ThemeContext); if (context === undefined) { throw new Error("useTheme must be used within a ThemeProvider"); } return context; } // Usage const { theme, toggleTheme } = useTheme(); For this to work, create the context with createContext(undefined).

text: Every component that calls useContext(X) re-renders whenever the context value changes. Passing a new object to value on every render (value={{ a, b }}) re-renders all consumers each time. Keep the value stable (for example with useMemo) in performance-sensitive trees. A component uses the value from the nearest Provider above it. If there is none, it gets the default value. Good for: theme, authenticated user, language/locale. Not ideal for rapidly changing data. ---

text: This guide covers four topics: Virtual DOM & Reconciliation Re-render Triggers Memoization Hooks Code Splitting & Lazy Loading ---

heading: Virtual DOM
text:
The Virtual DOM (VDOM) is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM: a tree of plain objects describing what the UI should look like. Updating real DOM nodes is relatively expensive, so React does its work on this cheap in-memory tree first and only touches the real DOM when necessary. // This JSX...

heading: How an update works
text: 1. State or props change 2. React calls your component → produces a NEW virtual tree (Render phase) 3. React compares the new tree with the previous one (diffing) (Reconciliation) 4. React applies only the minimal changes to the real DOM (Commit phase) Phase What happens Pure? --- --- --- Render Components run and return JSX. React builds the new virtual tree. ✅ Must be pure (no side effects) Reconciliation React diffs old vs new trees to find what changed. Internal Commit Real DOM is updated; refs are set; effects run. Side effects allowed (useEffect) "Rendering" means React calling your component function. It does not necessarily mean the browser repaints or the DOM changes.

heading: Reconciliation
text: Reconciliation is the algorithm React uses to diff two trees. A fully general tree diff is O(n³), so React uses two heuristics to make it O(n): Elements of different types produce different trees. Keys hint which child elements are stable across renders.

heading: Keys and state
text: State is tied to a component's position in the tree plus its key. Changing a key resets that component's state. This is a useful trick: // Switching userId gives <Profile> a fresh instance with fresh state <Profile key={userId} userId={userId} />

heading: 2. Re-render Triggers
text: A component re-renders when React needs to call it again to figure out the new UI. There are only a few causes.

heading: What triggers a re-render
text: Trigger Details --- --- 1. State change Calling a useState or useReducer setter with a new value (compared with Object.is) 2. Parent re-renders By default, all children re-render when the parent does, even if their props didn't change 3. Context change Every component that reads the context via useContext re-renders when the Provider's value changes 4. Force update / key change A changed key remounts the component Props changing is not a separate trigger. Props only change because a parent re-rendered. The parent re-rendering is the real cause.

heading: What does NOT trigger a re-render
text: Changing a useRef value (ref.current = ...) Mutating a variable declared outside the component Directly mutating state (state.push(x)): React never sees it Calling a setter with the same value (React bails out, though the component function may run once more before it stops)

heading: Is a re-render bad?
text: Not necessarily. Re-rendering is cheap for most components, and React only updates the DOM if the output changed. Optimize only when you can measure a problem (slow typing, laggy interactions, large lists).

heading: Reducing unnecessary re-renders
text: Technique When to use --- --- Move state closer to where it's used First choice; costs nothing Pass expensive subtrees as children Wrapper holds frequently changing state Split contexts by concern Avoid one big context everyone consumes Memoization (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback) Measured, repeated, expensive work ---

heading: 3. Memoization Hooks
text: Memoization caches the result of a computation and reuses it until its inputs change. React offers useMemo and useCallback for hooks, plus React.memo for components. They only skip work when dependencies are unchanged.

heading: useMemo: cache a calculated value
text: const memoizedValue = useMemo(() => computeExpensive(a, b), [a, b]); function ProductList({ products, filter }) { const filtered = useMemo( () => products.filter((p) => p.category === filter), [products, filter] ); return filtered.map((p) => <Product key={p.id} product={p} />); } React recomputes only when products or filter changes. Other re-renders reuse the cached array. Use it for: Genuinely expensive calculations (filtering/sorting large lists, heavy math) Keeping an object or array reference stable when passing it to a memoized child or as a hook dependency

heading: useCallback: cache a function
text: const memoizedFn = useCallback(() => doSomething(a, b), [a, b]); useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps). It returns the same function reference between renders until a dependency changes. Why does this matter? Functions are recreated on every render, so each render produces a new reference. That breaks memoized children: function Parent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); const handleClick = () => console.log("clicked"); // new function every render return ( <> <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button> <Child onClick={handleClick} /> </> ); } Even if Child is wrapped in React.memo, the new handleClick prop makes it re-render. Fix with useCallback: const handleClick = useCallback(() => console.log("clicked"), []);

heading: React.memo: skip re-rendering a component
text: Wraps a component so it re-renders only if its props changed (shallow comparison). const Child = React.memo(function Child({ onClick, label }) { console.log("Child rendered"); return <button onClick={onClick}>{label}</button>; }); The three work together: function Parent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); const [text, setText] = useState(""); const handleSave = useCallback(() => save(text), [text]); // stable function const config = useMemo(() => ({ mode: "dark", text }), [text]); // stable object return ( <> <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button> <input value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)} /> <Child onSave={handleSave} config={config} /> {/* skips render when count changes */} </> ); } const Child = React.memo(function Child({ onSave, config }) { /* ... */ }); useCallback and useMemo on their own don't prevent child re-renders. They only help when the child is wrapped in React.memo (or receives the value as a hook dependency).

heading: Comparison
text: useMemo useCallback React.memo --- --- --- --- Caches A value A function A component's output Returns Result of calling the function The function itself A memoized component Re-computes when Dependencies change Dependencies change Props change (shallow) Typical use Expensive calculations, stable objects Stable handlers passed to children Prevent child re-renders

heading: Dependency rules
text: List every reactive value the function reads in the dependency array. Missing dependencies cause stale values (the function sees old state). Passing [] means "create once", so be sure nothing inside changes. Dependencies are compared with Object.is, so a new object or array each render invalidates the cache. const total = useMemo(() => items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0), [items]); Avoid stale closures with functional updates: const increment = useCallback(() => setCount((c) => c + 1), []); // no `count` dependency needed

heading: When NOT to memoize
text: Memoization isn't free: it adds code, uses memory, and the dependency comparison itself costs time. ❌ Cheap calculations (simple math, small arrays) ❌ Components that almost always receive new props anyway ❌ Everywhere "just in case" ✅ Measured slowness (verify with the React DevTools Profiler) ✅ Large lists, heavy computations, memoized children that receive callbacks or objects ✅ Stabilizing values used as dependencies of other hooks (useEffect, useMemo) Order of attack: fix structure first (move state down, composition), then memoize if a measured problem remains. ---

heading: 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
text: By default, bundlers combine your whole app into one JavaScript file. Users download code for pages and features they may never visit. Code splitting breaks the bundle into smaller chunks, and lazy loading fetches those chunks only when they're needed. The result is a smaller initial download and a faster first load. Without splitting: [ one big bundle: Home + Dashboard + Settings + Charts + Editor ] With splitting: [ main: Home ] → loads [ Dashboard ] / [ Settings ] / [ Charts ] on demand

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Dynamic import()
text: The standard JavaScript mechanism. It returns a Promise and tells the bundler to create a separate chunk. // Static import: always in the main bundle import { heavyFunction } from "./heavy"; // Dynamic import: separate chunk, loaded on demand const module = await import("./heavy"); module.heavyFunction();

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: React.lazy + Suspense
text:
React.lazy renders a dynamically imported component as a regular component. Suspense shows a fallback while the chunk loads. import { lazy, Suspense } from "react"; const Dashboard = lazy(() => import("./Dashboard")); function App() { return ( Loading...

}> ); } Requirements: The lazy module must have a default export. A lazy component must render inside a boundary. Call lazy() at the module top level, never inside a component (it would reset on every render). Named exports: re-map them to default. const Chart = lazy(() => import("./Charts").then((module) => ({ default: module.LineChart })) );

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Strategy 1: Route-based splitting (most common)
text: Each page becomes its own chunk. This is usually the best first step because users only need one page at a time. import { lazy, Suspense } from "react"; import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from "react-router-dom"; const Home = lazy(() => import("./pages/Home")); const Dashboard = lazy(() => import("./pages/Dashboard")); const Settings = lazy(() => import("./pages/Settings")); function App() { return ( <BrowserRouter> <Suspense fallback={<PageSpinner />}> <Routes> <Route path="/" element={<Home />} /> <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} /> <Route path="/settings" element={<Settings />} /> </Routes> </Suspense> </BrowserRouter> ); }

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Strategy 2: Component-based splitting
text:
Defer heavy components that aren't visible right away: modals, charts, rich-text editors, maps. const HeavyChart = lazy(() => import("./HeavyChart")); function Report() { const [show, setShow] = useState(false); return ( <> {show && ( Loading chart...

}> )} ); } The chart's code is downloaded only when the button is clicked.

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Strategy 3: Library-based splitting
text: Load large libraries only at the moment you use them. async function exportToPdf(data) { const { jsPDF } = await import("jspdf"); // fetched on demand const doc = new jsPDF(); doc.text(JSON.stringify(data), 10, 10); doc.save("report.pdf"); }

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Suspense boundaries
text: Place boundaries thoughtfully. Where you put them determines what shows a fallback. // One boundary: whole section shows a single spinner <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}> <Sidebar /> <Content /> </Suspense> // Separate boundaries: each part loads independently <Suspense fallback={<SidebarSkeleton />}><Sidebar /></Suspense> <Suspense fallback={<ContentSkeleton />}><Content /></Suspense> Use skeleton/placeholder fallbacks matching the final layout to reduce layout shift. Nest boundaries so a slow chunk doesn't blank the entire page.

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Handling load failures
text:
Network issues can make a chunk fail to load. Wrap lazy components in an Error Boundary so the app doesn't crash. class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component { state = { hasError: false }; static getDerivedStateFromError() { return { hasError: true }; } render() { if (this.state.hasError) return

Something went wrong. Please retry.

; return this.props.children; } } }>

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Preloading to hide load time
text: Start fetching a chunk before the user needs it, for example on hover. const loadSettings = () => import("./pages/Settings"); const Settings = lazy(loadSettings); <Link to="/settings" onMouseEnter={loadSettings}>Settings</Link>

topic: Performance & Rendering › 4. Code Splitting & Lazy Loading
heading: Best practices
text: Start with route-level splitting, then split heavy components as needed. Don't split tiny components: each chunk costs an extra network request. Keep above-the-fold, critical UI in the main bundle. Always provide a meaningful fallback and an Error Boundary. Inspect bundle size with a bundle analyzer to find what's worth splitting. Test on a throttled network to feel the loading experience. ---

heading: Webpack
text: A practical and in-depth reference to Webpack 5: core concepts, configuration, optimization, internals, and interview-ready knowledge.

heading: 1\. What is Webpack and Why Use It
text: Webpack is a static module bundler for JavaScript applications. It starts from one or more entry points, builds a dependency graph of every module your project needs (JS, CSS, images, fonts, JSON, WASM, etc.), and emits one or more bundles that browsers (or Node.js) can load.

topic: 1\. What is Webpack and Why Use It
heading: Problems it solves
text: Problem How Webpack helps - - Many tags, order-sensitive, global scope pollution Module system with a single dependency graph; scoped modules Browsers lacking support for newer syntax or module formats Transpilation via loaders (Babel, TypeScript), format interop Non-JS assets (CSS, images, fonts) Treated as modules via loaders / asset modules Large bundles, slow load Code splitting, tree shaking, minification, lazy loading Cache invalidation Content hashing, deterministic IDs, runtime chunk Developer experience Dev server, Hot Module Replacement, source maps Sharing code across apps Module Federation

topic: 1\. What is Webpack and Why Use It
heading: Key characteristics
text: Everything is a module (via loaders / asset modules). Supports ESM, CommonJS, AMD, and mixes of them. Highly configurable and extensible (loaders + plugins + hooks). Built on Tapable, an event/hook system that powers the whole architecture. Has a persistent filesystem cache (v5) for fast rebuilds.

heading: 2\. Core Concepts
text: Entry ──► Module graph ──► Loaders transform ──► Chunks ──► Output bundles ▲ ▲ Plugins hook into every stage Concept Purpose - - Entry Where Webpack starts building the dependency graph Output Where and how bundles are emitted Loaders Transform individual files (non-JS to JS, TS to JS, SCSS to CSS) Plugins Extend Webpack across the whole build lifecycle (HTML generation, minification, env injection) Mode development, production, or none; sets built-in optimizations Module Any file Webpack processes Chunk A group of modules bundled together (a unit of splitting) Bundle The final emitted file(s), generally one per chunk Dependency graph The tree/graph of module relationships Runtime / Manifest Small bootstrap code that wires modules and chunks together at runtime \\Module vs Chunk vs Bundle\\: modules are the source units, chunks are logical groupings created during the build, and bundles are the actual files written to disk. \---

heading: 3\. Installation and Quick Start
text: mkdir my-app \&\& cd my-app npm init -y npm install --save-dev webpack webpack-cli webpack-dev-server Project layout: my-app/ ├── src/ │ └── index.js ├── dist/ ├── package.json └── webpack.config.js src/index.js: import { greet } from './greet'; document.body.textContent = greet('Webpack'); webpack.config.js: const path = require('path'); module.exports = { mode: 'development', entry: './src/index.js', output: { filename: 'main.js', path: path.resolve(\_\_dirname, 'dist'), clean: true, }, }; package.json scripts: { "scripts": { "dev": "webpack serve --open", "build": "webpack --mode production", "watch": "webpack --watch" } } Run npm run build; output lands in dist/. Webpack 5 requires Node.js 10.13+ (use a currently supported LTS in practice). \---

heading: 4\. Configuration Basics
text: Webpack config is a JS module that exports an object, an array of objects (multi-compiler), a function, or a Promise. // webpack.config.js module.exports = { mode: 'production', entry: {}, output: {}, module: { rules: \[] }, plugins: \[], resolve: {}, optimization: {}, devServer: {}, devtool: 'source-map', externals: {}, target: 'web', cache: {}, performance: {}, stats: 'errors-warnings', watchOptions: {}, experiments: {}, };

Array (multiple independent builds) module.exports = \[ { name: 'client', target: 'web', entry: './src/client.js' }, { name: 'server', target: 'node', entry: './src/server.js' }, ]; // 3. Promise (async config) module.exports = async () => ({ /\* ... \*/ });

heading: TypeScript config
text: Name the file webpack.config.ts (requires ts-node and @types/webpack/@types/node): import type { Configuration } from 'webpack'; const config: Configuration = { mode: 'production', entry: './src/index.ts' }; export default config;

heading: ESM config
text: Use webpack.config.mjs or "type": "module" in package.json. \---

heading: 5\. Entry Points
text: // Single entry entry: './src/index.js' // Multiple files merged into one chunk entry: \['./src/polyfills.js', './src/index.js'] // Multiple entries (multi-page apps) entry: { home: './src/home.js', admin: './src/admin.js', } // Entry descriptor (advanced) entry: { main: { import: './src/index.js', dependOn: 'shared', // share modules with another entry filename: 'pages/\[name].js', }, shared: \['react', 'react-dom'], worker: { import: './src/worker.js', runtime: false }, } // Dynamic entry entry: () => ({ app: './src/app.js' }) dependOn avoids duplicating shared modules between entries. runtime: 'single' or a runtime name lets multiple entries share one runtime chunk. heading: 21\. Module Federation (Micro-Frontends)
text: Introduced in Webpack 5. Lets separately built and deployed applications share modules at runtime. // Remote app (exposes modules) new ModuleFederationPlugin({ name: 'checkout', filename: 'remoteEntry.js', exposes: { './Cart': './src/Cart' }, shared: { react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^18.0.0' }, 'react-dom': { singleton: true } }, }); // Host app (consumes) new ModuleFederationPlugin({ name: 'shell', remotes: { checkout: 'checkout@https://cdn.example.com/checkout/remoteEntry.js' }, shared: { react: { singleton: true }, 'react-dom': { singleton: true } }, }); const Cart = React.lazy(() => import('checkout/Cart')); Key concepts: Host / Remote: consumer and provider (an app can be both). shared: dedupes libraries; singleton enforces a single instance (critical for React, context). Version negotiation: requiredVersion, strictVersion, eager. Needs an async boundary (import('./bootstrap')) in the entry so shared modules can negotiate before use. Trade-offs: runtime failures if a remote is down, version skew, harder typing (use generated types or @module-federation/\ tooling), and testing complexity. \---
