heading: 23\. Writing a Custom Loader
text: A loader is a function that receives source and returns transformed source. // loaders/replace-loader.js module.exports = function (source, sourceMap, meta) { const options = this.getOptions(); // validate with schema-utils in real loaders this.cacheable(true); // result can be cached const result = source.replace(/\_\_NAME\_\_/g, options.name); return result; // or this.callback(null, result, sourceMap, meta) }; // Async loader module.exports = function (source) { const callback = this.async(); doAsyncWork(source).then(r => callback(null, r), callback); }; // Raw (Buffer) loader module.exports.raw = true; // Pitching phase (runs left→right before the normal phase) module.exports.pitch = function (remainingRequest, precedingRequest, data) {}; Usage: { test: /\\.txt$/, use: { loader: path.resolve('loaders/replace-loader.js'), options: { name: 'World' } } } Useful this APIs: this.resourcePath, this.emitFile, this.addDependency, this.getOptions, this.callback, this.async, this.emitWarning, this.emitError, this.mode, this.sourceMap. Guidelines: keep loaders single-purpose, stateless, cacheable, and chainable. Return JavaScript (the last loader in the chain must output JS unless a type rule handles it). \---

heading: 32\. Interview Questions and Answers
text: 1. What is Webpack? A static module bundler that builds a dependency graph from entry points and emits optimized bundles. 2. Loader vs plugin? Loaders transform individual files (per-module, run in a chain). Plugins hook into the compiler/compilation lifecycle to perform broader tasks (bundle-wide optimization, asset generation, environment injection). 3. In what order do loaders run? Right to left / bottom to top (like function composition), with a pitching phase going left to right first. enforce: 'pre' and 'post' adjust ordering. 4. Difference between \[hash], \[chunkhash], \[contenthash]? hash is per build, chunkhash per chunk (including its dependent modules, even CSS), contenthash per file content. Use contenthash for long-term caching. 5. What is tree shaking and what's needed for it? Dead-export elimination. Requires static ESM, production mode (or usedExports + minifier), proper sideEffects flags, and not transpiling ESM to CJS. 6. How does code splitting work? Via multiple entries, dynamic import() creating async chunks, and SplitChunksPlugin extracting shared/vendor code. 7. Explain HMR. The dev server pushes updated modules over a WebSocket; the HMR runtime fetches the update manifest and chunk, replaces modules, and runs accept handlers, preserving app state. 8. What is the runtime/manifest chunk? Webpack's bootstrap code (module registry, chunk loading). Splitting it out keeps vendor and app hashes stable. 9. What are source maps and which devtool do you pick? Mappings from generated code to source. Dev: eval-cheap-module-source-map. Prod: source-map or hidden-source-map. 10. How do you speed up builds? Filesystem cache, narrow loader scope, swc/esbuild, thread-loader selectively, avoid expensive devtools, profile with --profile. 11. What is Module Federation? Runtime sharing of modules between independently built applications; powers micro-frontends with shared singleton dependencies. 12. What are externals? Dependencies excluded from the bundle and supplied by the environment (global, CDN, Node). 13. resolve.alias vs TypeScript paths? Aliases are a Webpack runtime concern; TS paths only affect type-checking. Keep them in sync. 14. How do you handle environment variables? --env for config logic; DefinePlugin/EnvironmentPlugin for app code; never embed secrets. 15. What changed in Webpack 5? Persistent caching, asset modules, Module Federation, better tree shaking, deterministic IDs, no automatic Node polyfills, output.clean, top-level await, and web worker support via new URL. 16. What is scope hoisting? ModuleConcatenationPlugin merges ESM modules into a single closure, reducing wrapper overhead and bundle size. 17. publicPath vs output.path? path is the output directory on disk; publicPath is the URL prefix used at runtime to fetch assets/chunks. 18. How do you debug "why is this module in my bundle?" webpack --stats-reasons, the bundle analyzer, or stats.json inspection. 19. How does Webpack resolve a bare import like import x from 'pkg'? Via enhanced-resolve: checks resolve.alias, searches resolve.modules, reads the package's exports (then mainFields), applies extensions. 20. Why might CSS appear out of order or duplicated? Import order across chunks plus MiniCssExtractPlugin; solve by consistent import order or ignoreOrder for CSS Modules where order doesn't matter. \---

heading: Yarn
text: A practical, in-depth reference for the Yarn package manager: what it is, how it works internally, how to use it day to day, how to run it in CI and monorepos, and how it stacks up against npm (with a short note on pnpm). Version note: Yarn's feature set differs significantly between Yarn Classic (1.x) and Yarn Berry (2.x, 3.x, 4.x). Commands and behaviors below are labeled where they differ. Always check the official docs for the release you're using, since details change between minor versions.

heading: 1. What Is Yarn?
text: Yarn is a package manager for JavaScript and TypeScript projects. It installs, updates, and removes dependencies declared in package.json, resolves the full dependency tree, records exact resolved versions in a lockfile, and runs project scripts. It is compatible with the npm registry (registry.npmjs.org), so every package published to npm is installable with Yarn. Core promises: Deterministic installs: the same lockfile yields the same dependency tree on every machine. Speed: parallel downloads, a global/offline cache, and (in modern Yarn) installs that skip creating node_modules entirely. Correctness: strict dependency resolution (especially with PnP) that prevents code from importing packages it never declared ("phantom dependencies"). First-class monorepo support through workspaces. ---

heading: 2. History and Versions
text: Era Name Version Status --- --- --- --- 2016 Yarn Classic 1.x (latest 1.22.x) Maintenance mode. Receives only critical fixes. 2020 Yarn Berry 2.x Rewrite in TypeScript; introduced PnP by default, plugins, constraints. 2021 Yarn Berry 3.x Performance and ergonomics improvements. 2023+ Yarn Berry 4.x Current line. Requires a modern Node.js (18+). Background: Yarn was created at Facebook (now Meta) with Google, Exponent, and Tilde to fix npm's problems at the time: non-deterministic installs, slow installs, and weak offline support. It pushed npm to adopt lockfiles (npm 5, 2017) and many other improvements. "Berry" is the codename for Yarn 2+. It is a ground-up rewrite, not a drop-in upgrade from 1.x. The yarn binary you invoke is a thin shim that loads the version pinned by the project. Classic and Berry have different configuration files (.yarnrc vs .yarnrc.yml), lockfile formats, and many command names/flags. Rule of thumb: for new projects choose Yarn 4 (Berry) or npm/pnpm. Avoid starting new projects on Yarn 1.x unless a constraint forces it. ---

heading: Recommended: Corepack
text: Corepack is a tool that manages package manager versions per project. It shipped with Node.js for many releases. Newer Node.js releases (starting with Node 25) no longer bundle it, so you may need to install it yourself. # Install Corepack if your Node.js doesn't bundle it npm install -g corepack # Enable shims for yarn/pnpm corepack enable # Pin Yarn for a project (writes the packageManager field in package.json) corepack use yarn@stable # or a specific version corepack use yarn@4.9.2 Pinning happens through the packageManager field: { "name": "my-app", "packageManager": "yarn@4.9.2" } Anyone running yarn in the project then automatically gets that exact version, with no global install and no version drift between developers and CI.

heading: Alternative: yarn set version
text: From within a project (with any Yarn available): yarn set version stable # latest Yarn Berry yarn set version 4.9.2 # specific version yarn set version classic # Yarn 1.x This downloads the release into .yarn/releases/ and records it as yarnPath in .yarnrc.yml. Commit that file so the whole team uses the same version.

heading: Other options
text: npm install -g yarn installs Yarn Classic 1.x (not Berry). Fine for bootstrapping; use yarn set version afterward. System packages (Homebrew, apt, Chocolatey) tend to provide Classic and lag behind.

heading: Verify
text: yarn --version ---

heading: 4. Core Concepts
text: package.json: declares the project, dependencies (dependencies, devDependencies, peerDependencies, optionalDependencies), and scripts. Lockfile (yarn.lock): records the exact resolved version, checksum, and dependency graph. Cache: compressed archives of every package version. In Berry it is a first-class, optionally committed artifact (.yarn/cache). Linker: the strategy for making installed packages available to Node.js (PnP, node_modules, or pnpm-style). Workspaces: multiple packages in one repository sharing one lockfile. Resolution vs. fetch vs. link: Yarn's install is three phases. Resolution computes the dependency graph and updates the lockfile; fetch downloads archives into the cache; link makes packages importable. Descriptors vs. locators: Berry terminology. A descriptor is a request (lodash@^4.17.0); a locator is a concrete resolution (lodash@npm:4.17.21). You'll see both in yarn.lock and error messages. ---

heading: 6. Install Strategies
text: Yarn's nodeLinker setting (in .yarnrc.yml) controls how installed packages are exposed to Node.js: nodeLinker What it does Pros Cons --- --- --- --- pnp (default in Berry) No node_modules. A .pnp.cjs map tells Node where each package lives (usually inside zip archives). Fastest installs, strict correctness, tiny disk footprint, enables zero-installs Tooling compatibility issues, needs editor SDKs, some packages need patches/unplugging node-modules Classic hoisted node_modules layout. Maximum compatibility with existing tools Slower, bigger, allows phantom dependencies pnpm node_modules with symlinks to a content-addressable store (like pnpm). Strict-ish, saves disk, high compatibility Less battle-tested than the other two within Yarn # .yarnrc.yml nodeLinker: node-modules Practical advice: many teams (especially with React Native, certain Jest/webpack plugin ecosystems, or legacy tooling) start with nodeLinker: node-modules for a smooth migration, then evaluate PnP later. ---

heading: How node_modules works (and why it's problematic)
text: Node resolves require('x') by walking up the directory tree looking for node_modules/x. This implies: Huge numbers of files and directories to write on every install. Hoisting makes undeclared packages accidentally importable (phantom dependencies), causing "works on my machine" bugs. Resolution is a filesystem search at runtime.

heading: How PnP works
text: At install time Yarn already knows the entire graph, so it generates a single file, .pnp.cjs, containing a static lookup table: "package A may require package B, located at path P." Node is patched at runtime (via --require .pnp.cjs, handled when you launch through yarn) so resolution uses the table. Benefits: Strictness: a package can only import what it declared. Undeclared imports fail loudly. Speed: installs write mostly just the lockfile, the cache, and .pnp.cjs. Startup resolution avoids filesystem walking. Smaller footprint: packages remain as zip files in the cache.

heading: Practical considerations
text: Run things through Yarn: yarn node script.js, yarn tsc, yarn jest. Running bare node won't know about PnP. Editor support: run yarn dlx @yarnpkg/sdks vscode (or yarn sdks) so TypeScript/ESLint/Prettier work in your editor. Packages that need real files: use yarn unplug or declare in package.json: { "dependenciesMeta": { "some-native-pkg": { "unplugged": true } } } Broken packages: fix missing dependency declarations via packageExtensions in .yarnrc.yml rather than forking: packageExtensions: "some-pkg@*": dependencies: missing-dep: "*" ESM and loaders: modern Yarn supports ESM under PnP via loader hooks; occasionally edge cases appear with experimental Node flags. Fallback mode: pnpMode: loose lets packages access hoisted undeclared dependencies as a migration crutch (not recommended long-term). ---

heading: 8. Zero-Installs and the Offline Cache
text: Yarn Berry stores every package as a compressed archive in the cache (.yarn/cache by default, configurable via cacheFolder; or a global cache when enableGlobalCache: true). Zero-installs means committing .yarn/cache and .pnp.cjs to version control. After git clone or git pull, the project runs without running yarn install. Pros Cons --- --- No install step in CI or after pulling branches Repository grows (often tens to hundreds of MB; use Git LFS cautiously) Fully offline, reproducible builds Noisy diffs when upgrading many packages Dependency changes are visible/reviewable in PRs Needs discipline: always commit cache changes together with the lockfile Not everyone should use zero-installs. A common middle path: don't commit the cache, but cache .yarn/cache (or the global cache) in CI between runs. Typical .gitignore for a Yarn 4 project that does not use zero-installs: .yarn/* !.yarn/patches !.yarn/plugins !.yarn/releases !.yarn/sdks !.yarn/versions .pnp.* For zero-installs, also keep .yarn/cache and .pnp. tracked (remove them from the ignore list). ---

heading: 9. The Lockfile
text: yarn.lock is committed to version control.

heading: Yarn 1 format (custom, indentation-based)
text: lodash@^4.17.21: version "4.17.21" resolved "https://registry.yarnpkg.com/lodash/-/lodash-4.17.21.tgz#..." integrity sha512-...

heading: Yarn Berry format (YAML)
text: __metadata: version: 8 cacheKey: 10c0 "lodash@npm:^4.17.21": version: 4.17.21 resolution: "lodash@npm:4.17.21" checksum: 10c0/... languageName: node linkType: hard Key points: Multiple ranges that resolve to the same version are merged into one entry. Berry records checksums of the archive (not just the registry's integrity hash), verified at install time. Berry includes workspace entries (languageName, linkType: soft for workspaces/links). Never hand-edit the lockfile except for resolving merge conflicts; after merging, run yarn install to normalize it. Yarn can resolve most lockfile merge conflicts itself in Berry. --immutable fails the install if the lockfile would change. Use it in CI. Lockfile formats are not interchangeable with package-lock.json. Yarn has no built-in command to convert from npm's lockfile, but running yarn install in a project that has only package-lock.json resolves fresh (and Berry can import some data from an existing package-lock.json or Classic yarn.lock). ---

heading: 10. Configuration (.yarnrc.yml)
text: Yarn Berry uses .yarnrc.yml (project-level, plus an optional user-level /.yarnrc.yml). Yarn 1 used .yarnrc and also read .npmrc. Yarn Berry does not read .npmrc for its own settings (it has its own npm settings). Example: # .yarnrc.yml yarnPath: .yarn/releases/yarn-4.9.2.cjs # set by `yarn set version` nodeLinker: node-modules # pnp | node-modules | pnpm enableGlobalCache: false # store cache in project vs ~/.yarn/berry/cache enableTelemetry: false enableImmutableInstalls: true # (also default true on CI environments) compressionLevel: mixed defaultSemverRangePrefix: "^" # "" for exact versions by default npmRegistryServer: "https://registry.npmjs.org" # Scoped / private registries npmScopes: mycompany: npmRegistryServer: "https://npm.pkg.github.com" npmAlwaysAuth: true npmAuthToken: "${GITHUB_TOKEN}" # use env vars, never commit secrets # Per-registry settings (e.g. proxies, Artifactory, Verdaccio) npmRegistries: "//registry.internal.example.com": npmAuthToken: "${INTERNAL_TOKEN}" npmAlwaysAuth: true # Safety enableScripts: true # set false to ignore lifecycle scripts for all deps enableStrictSsl: true # Fixes for misbehaving packages packageExtensions: "some-pkg@*": peerDependencies: react: "*" # Plugins plugins: - path: .yarn/plugins/@yarnpkg/plugin-workspace-tools.cjs Notes: Environment variables can be referenced as ${VAR}; use ${VAR:-default} for fallbacks. Any setting can also be provided as an environment variable YARN_ (e.g. YARN_NODE_LINKER=node-modules). yarn config prints/reads resolved values (yarn config get nodeLinker, yarn config -v for descriptions). Recent 4.x releases added supply-chain-oriented settings (for example, hardened mode and a minimum package age gate, npmMinimalAgeGate). Check yarn config -v or the docs for what your version supports. ---

heading: Protocols (Berry)
text: Protocol Example Meaning --- --- --- npm: "react": "npm:^18.2.0" / alias "my-lodash": "npm:lodash@^4" Registry package (default); can alias workspace: "@acme/ui": "workspace:^" Link to a workspace in this repo file: "lib": "file:../lib" Copy from a local path link: "lib": "link:../lib" Symlink local folder (its deps aren't resolved) portal: "lib": "portal:../lib" Symlink local folder and resolve its dependencies patch: "pkg": "patch:pkg@npm:1.0.0#./.yarn/patches/pkg.patch" Apply a patch to a dependency git: / github: "pkg": "github:user/repo#semver:^1.2.0" Git dependency exec: "gen": "exec:./gen.js" Generated at install time by a script

heading: workspace: ranges
text: workspace: always links to the local workspace. workspace:^ / workspace: get replaced with a real semver range (^1.2.3) at publish/pack time, so published packages are valid for consumers.

heading: Forcing versions: resolutions
text: { "resolutions": { "minimist": "^1.2.8", "**/lodash": "4.17.21", "foo/bar": "2.0.0" } } Use to patch vulnerable transitive dependencies. npm's analogue is overrides; pnpm uses pnpm.overrides. resolutions is supported in both Yarn Classic and Berry (syntax is slightly different).

heading: Patching dependencies
text: yarn patch lodash # prints a temp folder; edit files there yarn patch-commit -s /tmp/xyz # writes .yarn/patches/*.patch and updates resolutions This is built in, so patch-package isn't needed.

heading: Peer dependencies
text: Yarn Berry is strict: a package with unmet peer dependencies will warn, and under PnP an undeclared peer is genuinely unavailable. Use yarn explain peer-requirements to debug. ---

heading: 12. Workspaces and Monorepos
text: Declare workspaces in the root package.json: { "name": "monorepo", "private": true, "packageManager": "yarn@4.9.2", "workspaces": ["packages/*", "apps/*"] } Directory layout: monorepo/ ├── package.json ├── yarn.lock ├── .yarnrc.yml ├── apps/ │ └── web/package.json └── packages/ ├── ui/package.json └── utils/package.json All workspaces share a single lockfile and a deduplicated install.

heading: Referencing sibling packages
text: { "name": "@acme/web", "dependencies": { "@acme/ui": "workspace:^", "@acme/utils": "workspace:*" } }

heading: Common workspace commands (Berry)
text: yarn workspaces list --json # discover workspaces yarn workspace @acme/web add react # run a command in one workspace yarn workspace @acme/web run dev yarn workspaces foreach -A run build # all workspaces (-A, --all) yarn workspaces foreach -At run build # -t: topological (dependencies first) yarn workspaces foreach -Ap -j 4 run test # -p: parallel, -j: concurrency yarn workspaces foreach --since=origin/main run lint # only changed workspaces (+ deps/dependents with flags) yarn workspaces focus @acme/web # install only what @acme/web needs yarn workspaces focus --production # production deps only (e.g. in Docker) Related tools often paired with Yarn workspaces: Turborepo, Nx, Lerna (now maintained by Nrwl/Nx), and Changesets for versioning. Yarn alone gives you dependency management, running scripts across workspaces, and version bump workflows (yarn version), but not remote caching or sophisticated task pipelines.

heading: npm equivalents
text: npm supports workspaces (7+): npm install -w packages/ui, npm run build --workspaces, --workspace=..., --include-workspace-root. It lacks Yarn's foreach topological/parallel orchestration, focus, and constraints, so teams typically add Turborepo/Nx. ---

heading: 13. Scripts, Binaries, and Running Tools
text: { "scripts": { "build": "tsc -b", "test": "jest", "lint": "eslint .", "prepare": "husky", "postinstall": "node scripts/setup.js" } } yarn build and yarn run build are equivalent. Binaries from dependencies are available directly: yarn tsc, yarn eslint. Under PnP these resolve correctly because they run inside Yarn's environment. Lifecycle scripts: preinstall, install, postinstall (for dependencies, run at install time), and prepare/prepack/postpack (for the project itself). Berry runs dependency lifecycle scripts only for packages that need them and with enableScripts controlling the global switch. You can disable scripts for specific packages through dependenciesMeta: { "dependenciesMeta": { "esbuild": { "built": false } } } Pre/post hooks: In Berry, automatic pre/post scripts for user-defined scripts (e.g. prebuild) are not run (only the standard lifecycle ones); Yarn Classic and npm do run them. Call the steps explicitly instead. Argument passing: yarn build --watch forwards args to the script. Berry does not require -- separators. yarn dlx : downloads and runs a package in a temporary environment, like npx (does not touch the project's dependencies). Environment: Yarn exposes env vars such as npm_package_name, INIT_CWD, and PROJECT_CWD in scripts. Some legacy npm_package_ vars are only partially supported in Berry. Cross-platform shell: Berry ships a portable shell interpreter for scripts (supports &&, , pipes, env var assignment like FOO=bar cmd, globs) so scripts behave identically on Windows and Unix. Exotic bashisms may fail; call a real script file for complex logic. ---

heading: Plugins
text: Berry is built around plugins; many core features (e.g., workspace-tools, interactive-tools, typescript) are bundled or optional. yarn plugin list yarn plugin import https://example.com/my-plugin.js yarn plugin import typescript # official plugin: auto-adds @types/* yarn plugin remove @yarnpkg/plugin-typescript The TypeScript plugin automatically adds corresponding @types/ packages when you yarn add a package that lacks bundled types. Plugins live in .yarn/plugins/ and are referenced from .yarnrc.yml. Commit them.

heading: Constraints
text: Define repo-wide rules in yarn.config.cjs (JavaScript API) or constraints.pro (Prolog, legacy). Examples: "all workspaces must use the same React version," "every package must have a license field," "no workspace may depend on package X." // yarn.config.cjs /** @type {import('@yarnpkg/types').Yarn.Config} */ module.exports = { async constraints({ Yarn }) { for (const dep of Yarn.dependencies({ ident: "react" })) { dep.update("^18.3.1"); } }, }; Run yarn constraints to check and yarn constraints --fix to apply fixes. Neither npm nor pnpm provides an equivalent built-in system. ---

heading: Supply-chain practices
text: Lockfile + --immutable in CI to prevent unexpected version drift. Checksums: Berry verifies archive checksums on install (--check-cache re-verifies the cache against the registry). Lifecycle script control: set enableScripts: false globally and opt in for specific packages that truly need build steps, since install scripts are the most common supply-chain attack vector. (With scripts disabled, packages that require a build step, such as native addons, won't be compiled.) Auditing: yarn npm audit # Berry yarn npm audit --all --recursive # include all workspaces yarn npm audit --severity high yarn audit # Classic Provenance and trusted publishing: publishing with provenance/OIDC is mainly an npm registry feature; Yarn Berry supports provenance on yarn npm publish via --provenance in recent versions. Verify support for your version. Pin and review: consider defaultSemverRangePrefix: "" (exact versions) and use Renovate or Dependabot for controlled updates. Strictness helps: PnP and pnpm-style linkers block phantom dependency access, which reduces accidental reliance on transitive packages that could be swapped. Registry authentication: store tokens in environment variables or a user-level /.yarnrc.yml, never in committed files. Malicious/typosquatted packages: neither npm nor Yarn can fully prevent them. Review new dependencies, use scoped private registries, and consider package-age gates and allow-lists where supported. ---

heading: GitHub Actions (Yarn 4, no zero-installs)
text: name: CI on: [push, pull_request] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 cache: yarn # caches Yarn's cache folder - run: corepack enable # use the version from "packageManager" - run: yarn install --immutable - run: yarn build - run: yarn test Tips: Run corepack enable before setup-node's cache: yarn step in some setups, as the cache step calls yarn to locate the cache directory. If you see errors, reorder or enable Corepack first. --immutable is the default in CI environments (Berry detects CI). Be explicit anyway. Use --immutable-cache with zero-installs to ensure no cache changes are needed (yarn install --immutable --immutable-cache --check-cache). Cache .yarn/cache (or the global cache) keyed on yarn.lock. For monorepos use yarn workspaces focus and yarn workspaces foreach --since to avoid doing unnecessary work.

heading: Docker
text: FROM node:22-slim AS base WORKDIR /app RUN corepack enable # Install dependencies with good layer caching COPY package.json yarn.lock .yarnrc.yml ./ COPY .yarn ./.yarn RUN yarn install --immutable COPY . . RUN yarn build # Production image FROM node:22-slim WORKDIR /app RUN corepack enable COPY --from=base /app ./ # For monorepos: yarn workspaces focus --production @acme/api CMD ["yarn", "node", "dist/server.js"] Consider multi-stage builds, yarn workspaces focus --production, and keeping the Yarn release/cache in the build context only when needed. ---

heading: 17. Publishing Packages
text: yarn npm login yarn npm publish --access public yarn npm publish --tag next yarn pack # create a tarball locally to inspect it yarn npm whoami yarn npm tag add pkg@1.2.3 latest Notes: workspace: ranges are rewritten to concrete versions in the published tarball. Use publishConfig to alter main, types, exports, or registry for the published manifest (for example, to point main at dist/ while developing against src/). Versioning workflow: yarn version patch minor major for single packages. For monorepos, use yarn version check with the "deferred versioning" workflow (yarn version --deferred, yarn version apply --all), or Changesets. ---

heading: 18.2 Architecture Differences
text: npm builds a hoisted tree in node_modules (a "flattened" layout where shared deps are moved up as far as possible). It's simple and universal but allows undeclared imports and has dedupe edge cases. Yarn Classic uses the same hoisted layout but with a faster, more deterministic algorithm and an offline mirror feature. Yarn Berry models the install as resolution → fetch → link with swappable linkers. PnP removes node_modules entirely.

heading: 18.3 Determinism
text: Both npm (since v5) and Yarn use lockfiles. npm ci and yarn install --immutable are the "install exactly this" commands. Berry's lockfile includes archive checksums; npm's includes the registry's integrity hash. Both detect tampering of tarballs. Historically, lockfile drift between package manager versions caused spurious diffs; pinning the package manager (packageManager + Corepack) avoids this for both.

heading: 18.4 Performance
text: Real-world numbers depend on project, network, disk, and cache state. Directionally: Cold install, no cache: the three are in the same ballpark; Yarn Berry (PnP) and pnpm often edge out npm because they write far fewer files. Warm cache / CI with cache: Yarn Berry with PnP or zero-installs is typically fastest; npm has improved considerably. Disk usage: PnP stores zipped archives in one cache; hoisted node_modules duplicates package contents per project. pnpm also uses a global content-addressable store with hard links. Benchmark in your own repo before deciding; published benchmarks vary by methodology.

heading: 18.5 Developer Experience
text: Aspect npm Yarn (Berry) --- --- --- Setup friction None (bundled) Needs Corepack or version pin Error messages Improving Detailed, with explain tooling (yarn explain) Editor integration Works everywhere Requires SDK setup for PnP Documentation Large Comprehensive but version-split (Classic vs Berry docs) Interactive upgrade No built-in yarn upgrade-interactive Debugging deps npm ls, npm explain yarn why, yarn info, yarn explain

heading: 18.6 Compatibility Gotchas with Yarn Berry/PnP
text: Tools that read node_modules directly (some bundlers, native module loaders, Jest plugins, old Storybook/React Native tooling) may break. Use nodeLinker: node-modules or unplug. Packages with undeclared dependencies need packageExtensions. Node's own --require / loader behavior interacts with PnP; start scripts through yarn. Docker/serverless environments need .pnp.cjs and the cache present at runtime (or use node-modules linker for deploy artifacts). IDEs need yarn sdks.

heading: 18.7 Where npm Is Better
text: Zero setup, universally documented, default in CI templates. Reference implementation of registry features (provenance, trusted publishing, npm audit fix, npm pkg, npm query). Max compatibility with tools and tutorials. Simple projects don't benefit from Yarn's complexity.

heading: 18.8 Where Yarn Is Better
text: Monorepos (workspace tooling, foreach, focus, constraints, workspace: protocol). Strict dependency correctness (PnP). Offline/zero-install workflows and fast CI. Built-in patching, plugins, and portable scripts. Fine-grained configuration for registries and scopes. ---

heading: 19. Yarn vs npm vs pnpm (Quick View)
text: npm Yarn 4 pnpm --- --- --- --- Storage Per-project copies in node_modules Zip cache + PnP map (default) Global content-addressable store + symlinked node_modules Strictness Loose Strict (PnP) Strict (non-flat node_modules) Compatibility Highest Good (PnP caveats) Very high Monorepo features Basic Rich Rich (--filter, catalog:) Unique strengths Bundled, registry features PnP, zero-installs, constraints, plugins Disk efficiency, speed, strictness with fewer compat problems If you want Yarn's strictness without PnP's tooling friction, evaluate nodeLinker: pnpm or pnpm itself. ---

heading: 20.1 npm → Yarn 4
text: # 1. Pin Yarn corepack enable corepack use yarn@stable # or: yarn set version stable # 2. Choose a linker (safe start) echo "nodeLinker: node-modules" >> .yarnrc.yml # 3. Remove npm artifacts rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json # 4. Install and generate yarn.lock yarn install # 5. Update scripts/docs/CI: npm ci -> yarn install --immutable, npx -> yarn dlx, etc. Checklist: Replace .npmrc registry/auth settings with .yarnrc.yml equivalents (npmRegistryServer, npmScopes, npmAuthToken). Replace overrides with resolutions. Replace npm run a && npm run b in scripts with yarn a && yarn b (or keep npm run only if you truly want npm). Replace pre/post custom hook scripts with explicit calls. Update CI cache keys from package-lock.json to yarn.lock. Update .gitignore as in section 8. Run tests with nodeLinker: node-modules first, then try PnP.

heading: 20.2 Yarn Classic → Yarn Berry
text: yarn set version stable yarn install # upgrades the lockfile format Differences to handle: .yarnrc → .yarnrc.yml; .npmrc-based auth must be re-declared. yarn install --frozen-lockfile → yarn install --immutable. yarn upgrade → yarn up. yarn audit → yarn npm audit; yarn publish → yarn npm publish; yarn info → yarn npm info. yarn global is gone. yarn licenses, yarn outdated, yarn list: use plugins or alternatives (yarn info, yarn upgrade-interactive, third-party tools). resolutions syntax mostly carries over (use /pkg globs carefully). Start with nodeLinker: node-modules. The official migration guide recommends this as the incremental path.

heading: 20.3 Yarn → npm
text: rm -rf node_modules yarn.lock .yarn .pnp.* .yarnrc.yml # remove "packageManager": "yarn@..." from package.json (or set npm@...) npm install # generates package-lock.json Convert resolutions → overrides, workspace: ranges → plain version ranges or , and Yarn-only commands in scripts/CI. ---

heading: 21. Best Practices
text: Pin the package manager with the packageManager field and Corepack. Commit the lockfile, always. Never .gitignore it for applications. Use --immutable (Yarn) / npm ci in CI. Declare every dependency you import. Treat PnP strictness as a feature. Prefer nodeLinker: node-modules initially when migrating, then reassess PnP. Use yarn dedupe periodically (and in CI with --check) to reduce duplicate versions. Keep dependencies updated with Renovate/Dependabot or yarn upgrade-interactive. Use resolutions sparingly and document why each exists; remove when upstream fixes land. Restrict install scripts (enableScripts: false with explicit allowances) for security-conscious projects. Never commit auth tokens. Use env vars in .yarnrc.yml. Use workspace:^ for internal deps so published packages have correct ranges. Run tools via yarn (yarn node, yarn tsc) when using PnP. Use yarn workspaces focus in Docker/CI to limit install scope. Keep one package manager per repo. Add a guard (e.g., only-allow, or a CI check that rejects foreign lockfiles) to prevent mixed lockfiles. Document the workflow in your repo's README: install, test, and release commands. Decide on zero-installs deliberately, weighing repo size against install-free workflows. Review lockfile diffs in PRs; unexpected changes can indicate supply-chain issues. ---

heading: 22. Troubleshooting
text: Symptom Likely cause Fix --- --- --- Cannot find module 'x' under PnP Undeclared dependency or tool not run via Yarn Add the dependency, add packageExtensions, run via yarn, or use nodeLinker: node-modules The lockfile would have been modified by this install, which is explicitly forbidden --immutable and lockfile out of date Run yarn install locally and commit yarn.lock Usage Error: This project's package.json defines "packageManager": "yarn@x" ... but the current global is ... Corepack not enabled or a global Yarn conflicts Run corepack enable; remove/uninstall conflicting global Yarn Editor can't resolve imports / TS errors PnP SDK not configured yarn dlx @yarnpkg/sdks vscode, select workspace TypeScript version Native module fails (node-gyp, missing binary) Scripts disabled or package zipped under PnP Enable scripts for that package, yarn unplug pkg, or use nodeLinker: node-modules Peer dependency warnings flood output Packages with undeclared/mismatched peers yarn explain peer-requirements, add the peers, or use packageExtensions Different results on CI vs local Different Yarn/Node versions or stale cache Pin versions, clear cache (yarn cache clean), reinstall with --check-cache YN0028 / lockfile merge conflicts Git merge conflict in yarn.lock Resolve conflict markers if possible, then run yarn install; Berry can auto-resolve many conflicts Jest/webpack/Metro can't find modules Tool incompatible with PnP Use a PnP-aware plugin/config or switch linker to node-modules Slow installs Cold cache, network, antivirus scanning many files Use a CI cache, enableGlobalCache, PnP, or a private registry mirror Auth errors for private registry Config in .npmrc ignored by Berry Move to .yarnrc.yml (npmScopes / npmRegistries) yarn global not found Removed in Berry Use yarn dlx or project-local tools Useful diagnostics: yarn --version yarn config # effective configuration yarn why <pkg> # who depends on it yarn info <pkg> -R # dependency details yarn install --inline-builds # show build script output YARN_ENABLE_INLINE_BUILDS=1 yarn install ---

heading: 23. Decision Guide
text: Small app or library, want zero friction: npm. Monorepo with many packages and a need for strong tooling: Yarn 4 (or pnpm). Strict dependency hygiene, fast CI, offline builds: Yarn 4 with PnP. Need maximum tool compatibility but better efficiency than npm: pnpm, or Yarn 4 with nodeLinker: node-modules/pnpm. Existing Yarn 1 project: upgrade to Yarn 4 when you have time to test; there's no urgency if it works, but Classic is no longer evolving. React Native or other ecosystems with heavy native tooling: start with node-modules linker. You need npm provenance/trusted publishing flows: npm CLI for publishing is the safest path (you can still develop with Yarn). ---
